title: Amanda Owen - a shepherdess with nine children - is TV’s most unlikely superwoman
body:
Amanda Owen, otherwise known as the Yorkshire Shepherdess, is an unlikely television star. Her day job as the guardian of a thousand sheep and mother to nine – yes, nine – children doesn’t exactly scream glamour. Nevertheless, she’s the author of five bestselling books and formerly the face of the hit Channel 5 series Our Yorkshire Farm (watched by an average of three million people over five series). To the millions who adore her, she’s a superwoman.

Tonight, she returns to TV after two years – and it’s a bigger deal than it might seem. In 2022 she announced that she and her husband (and father of those nine children), Clive – who, until this point, had been her steadfast co-star – were separating. Rumours of Amanda having had an affair swirled, but the couple never gave them any attention. Instead, Clive has said that the reason for their split was “constant fighting” and the fact that he couldn’t be the confidante his wife needed at the time. Which is why it’s surprising that the pair have reunited – on screen, though not romantically – to front Our Farm Next Door: Amanda, Clive and Kids.

The new More4 series follows the former couple’s renovation of a huge but very derelict farmhouse for their children to live in when they grow up, a couple of fields over from their original homestead Ravenseat in Swaledale, Yorkshire. The programme itself is as you’d expect – like a drawn-out episode of Grand Designs (though the Owens have a much more traditional sense of style than the designers on Kevin McCloud’s series) with a bucolic edge. But it’s not really the house, as gorgeous as it’s going to be when it’s finished, that we’re interested in – it’s Amanda.

She embodies the “having it all” fantasy that countless women have dreamed of and yet will never feel like they could ever achieve. Never a part of the corporate rat race, and spending all her time out in the countryside instead of the city smog, Amanda has a life most of us could only dream of. Even a separation from her husband of 22 years (the pair are still legally married) isn’t enough to burst her bubble – aside from the odd snipe at one another here and there, they seem to work together just fine in the new series.

None of that pedestal raising is Amanda’s doing, though. On TV – as, I imagine, in real life – Amanda is brutally honest about the realities of living and working on a remote 2000-acre farm. Spoiler alert: it’s really difficult. Add in raising nine children and her media career and you’ve got one hell of a busy woman. Yet she takes it all in her stride – dodgy plumbing, poorly lambs, shouting children and being snowed in are just something to deal with, not have a meltdown over.

But vulnerability peeks through, too. In one 2021 episode of Our Yorkshire Farm, Amanda was visibly upset by the loss of one of the family’s Shetland ponies, Little Joe, who unexpectedly died of a heart attack. She’s gruff, but never heartless.

All this adds up to paint a very human portrait of a woman who has become an idol to her fans. But perhaps the strongest quality that attracts us to Amanda is that she is normal – a very rare quality in the entertainment industry. She makes no bones about how hard she has to work to keep the wheels turning and yet she still manages to make it look easy. In a world where the “having it all” fantasy feels more and more like a delusion, the Yorkshire shepherdess is one of the few people keeping the dream alive.

‘Our Farm Next Door: Amanda, Clive and Kids’ continues next Monday at 9pm on More4.
topics: Channel 5, Farming, More 4, TV Opinion

title: Why is it so rare to see two old gay Black men on TV?
body:
This adaptation of Bernadine Evaristo's novel is a wonderfully complex series, elevated by captivating performances from Lennie James and Sharon D Clarke

I remember reading Bernardine Evaristo’s electric novel Mr Loverman when it was released in 2013 and feeling the thrill of discovering a new perspective on the Windrush generation immigrant story.

It told the story of Barrington “Barry” Jedidiah Walker, a 74-year-old, Antiguan-born man living in Hackney, east London, working up the courage to finally leave his wife Carmel (Sharon D Clarke) of 50 years to be with the love of his life. The problem for Barry was that his other lover was a man.

In the BBC’s eight-part adaptation, Barry is played by Lennie James (The Walking Dead) as an eccentric, full of life in his dapper suits and delivering Shakespeare quotes with a knowing smirk.

Since Barry was a teenager in the 60s, he and his best friend Morris (Ariyon Bakare) have led a double life, keeping their love a secret. But just as Barry is about to finally break the news to Carmel (Sharon D Clarke) and their two children, Donna and Maxine, his wife learns that her father is on his deathbed in Antigua.

She leaves to be with him and Barry – having declined her plea to accompany her – is left to wrestle with the potential repercussions of coming out. How would his wife react? Would his daughters accept him? Would he be safe as an old, gay Black man out in the world?

Directed by Hong Khaou (Lilting), Mr Loverman captures a slice of British Caribbean family life in London with plenty of rum and goat curry, God and gossip – and misogyny and homophobia.

While the book was set in 2010, Khaou subtly brings it forward to the modern day via Deliveroo drivers, references to the gentrification of London and conversations about same-sex marriage and “gay rappers”.

The series starts slowly and only truly starts to find its footing three episodes in when Barry’s conflict starts to be explored: can he overcome the years of trauma that have made him understandably resistant to publicly identifying as a gay man? “I’m not a homosexual, I’m a Barrysexual”, he says half-jokingly, half-defiantly to Morris who is pushing him to come out.

In one of the most intense scenes, Barry is woken by his grandson having a party in his home with some friends who are playing drill music with homophobic lyrics.

Barry is irate and when one of the friends calls him a “cocksucker”, we see the burning rage explode in Barry after decades of feeling hated by society.

The drama is at its best when it dials in on the impact growing up in a hostile, bigoted world has had on Barry and Morris. Through flashbacks, we see the two men being caught together first in Antigua, and then later, by Morris’s wife who leaves him and takes his kids with her.

There is also a quietly devastating sequence in which Barry, walking through Hackney to meet Morris, passes a corner where years earlier he found a man killed who was “cheating on his wife with a batty man”.

He also goes by Abney Park, a known cruising area for men, where he was once brutally attacked. His life is full of painful reminders of how difficult and dangerous life was (and still is) for many Black gay men on the margins of society.

Mr Loverman is a wonderfully complex series that weaves together issues of marital breakdown, intergenerational conflict, infidelity, racism and sexuality. But while it is faithful to the original, it doesn’t quite capture its magic. It is dragged down by its reliance on voiceovers to convey the inner monologues of characters – they’re more distracting than insightful.

And while the script itself is serviceable, there is some clunky dialogue (like the awkward dinner date Donna goes on where the man says “marriage is hard” and she replies “marriage is a vehicle for female oppression”), and one scene between Barry and his grandson discussing a victim of knife crime that comes off as a bad public safety campaign.

Barry and Carmel’s daughters are also not fleshed out as much as they should be and so the series relies on the tired tropes of “life in order older sister” and “messy younger sister” to fill in the gaps.

What lifts show above lots of what’s on television right now are the utterly captivating central performances by James and Clark. James embodies all of Barry’s charisma and charm, alongside his damage and shame, while Clark conveys all of Carmel’s heartache, bitterness and sacrifice of staying with a man who she knows is a “cheat”.

The tension between the two is so thick that it’s easy to understand why Barry calls their home “the lion’s den”. The chemistry between James and Bakare is equally palpable; every stolen glance, smile and touch of hands convey the depth and tenderness of their relationship.

It is rare and powerful to see two elderly Black gay men on-screen in love – and having sex. Mr Loverman is part of a changing cultural tide that is bringing the stories and histories of Black British gay men to the mainstream (alongside podcasts like We Were Always Here and books like Revolutionary Acts). It should be celebrated that the BBC is bringing the lives of Black gay men out of the shadows.

‘Mr Loverman’ starts tonight at 9pm on BBC One. All episodes are streaming on BBC iPlayer
topics: BBC One, TV Reviews

title: Godfather fans will love Al Pacino's memoir
body:
The Oscar-winning actor's occasionally evasive memoir is one for avid film fans

A little over a decade ago, the Oscar-winning actor Al Pacino was living in Beverley Hills and discovered he was broke. “I had fifty million dollars and then I had nothing.” Pacino, who had grown up poor in the South Bronx, New York, and struggled to keep his finances in order his whole career, suddenly found he was paying for 16 cars even though he had just two, and 23 mobile phones he didn’t know about. “There’s almost nothing worse for a famous person – there’s being dead, and then there’s being broke.” It turned out he had a crooked accountant as well as a poor eye for figures, but what did Pacino do? He went back to work, of course.

As for why a superstar actor with a reputation for being intensely private might write a memoir, in the case of 84-year-old Al Pacino’s Sonny Boy, the answer could be for the money. Pacino is refreshingly honest about his attitude to the thing most stars are cagey about. Despite his difficult childhood – his Italian-American parents were teenagers when he was born, both died young, but not before his mum attempted suicide, and three of Pacino’s best childhood friends died of drug overdoses – he never set out to make money. “It was a language I didn’t speak.”

But coming from the background he did, Pacino was also a hard worker. In his youth he had been a bicycle messenger, a house-mover, a cinema usher. He was also wildly literary, despite leaving school early, becoming obsessed with Chekhov after seeing The Seagull on stage as a young adult. He took to carrying playwrights’ books around thereafter, and used to read obsessively in the library, where he went to stay warm before the fame and the money come along. Throughout the book he casually quotes Molière, Brecht, Shakespeare. He is a passionate scholar, minus the education.

Although the memoir is occasionally frustratingly evasive (he irritably shrugs off the Method acting he became known for; we might guess the bad-mannered Noughties superstar producer who remains nameless), it is good at giving us a sense of Pacino’s voice, flipflopping between the type of self-assuredness that lent itself to endlessly falling out with directors (“See a pattern here?” he notes wryly) – and at the same time struggling with attention.

Pacino was entirely unbothered by fame, loathed it even. As his star rose, he developed anxiety, panic attacks, and a drinking problem. He gained a reputation for being aloof after he failed to attend the Oscars following his first nomination for Best Supporting Actor in 1973 (for The Godfather), but the man that emerges from the pages is more painfully shy. “The world wouldn’t let me be shy,” he laments.

There are meaty anecdotes about stars – annoying Philip Roth, flat-sharing with Martin Sheen, watching Marlon Brando eating chicken cacciatore with his hands (“gobble gobble gobble”), getting together with Diane Keaton, inexplicably holding out his hand like a Roman emperor for Jackie O to kiss one night after performing Richard III. But there are also lengthy passages devoted to just how a film came about and how it was financed, or which particular aspect of it Pacino didn’t approve of. This is really a book for avid film fans, not so much for the general public.

The section likely to please all readers, though, is his trial by fire on The Godfather. Paramount didn’t want him for the part of college graduate turned gangster Michael Corleone, and he nearly lost it while filming. “By the end of the film I hoped that I would have created an enigma,” he says carefully about his now iconic performance, but he knew at the start it wasn’t quite cutting it.

Perhaps another motivation for the book was legacy. After a lifetime spent living stubbornly in the present, he is all reflection and nostalgia as the book comes to a close, particularly following a near-death experience with Covid when he briefly had no pulse. “I returned and I can tell you there’s nothing there. It’s over.”

Although the memoir ends with memories of family and friends, it’s clear it’s his films he wants most to be remembered by. This is a book less about a man than an actor through and through. As he writes here, he was asked in an interview once what he thought God would say at the pearly gates. Pacino replied: “I hope He says rehearsal starts tomorrow at 3pm.”

Published by Century on 15 October, £25
topics: Book Reviews, Books, Film

title: Ryan Murphy used to be a TV genius - now he's TV poison
body:
Nothing is certain in this world except death and taxes. And Ryan Murphy‘s endless parade of lacklustre TV shows.

This year alone, TV’s most prolific writer and producer has developed more TV series than most showrunners create in a lifetime. These include 9-1-1 (with the bee-nado), Grotesquerie (starring Taylor Swift’s footballer boyfriend Travis Kelce), AHS: Delicate (Kim Kardashian’s latest distraction), American Horror Stories (the spinoff no one watches), Feud: Capote vs. The Swans (Naomi Watts wishing she’d been cast in season 1), and American Sports Story: Aaron Hernandez (tough to watch in more ways than one).

Murphy was once a visionary writer and producer who shook up Hollywood with defiantly queer shows that pushed the boundaries of television. These days, the only thing Murphy’s pushing is people’s buttons.

Murphy’s latest, the controversial Monsters: The Lyle and Erik Menendez Story, has been a huge hit for Netflix: it racked up 19.5 million views in the first week alone, and is currently the most watched on the streamer worldwide. The true-crime series, based on the murder of Lyle and Erik’s parents, José and Kitty Menendez, baited viewers before it even started with a homoerotic poster that depicted the two leads shirtless and intimate – a Murphy staple – invoking an incestuous relationship (which the brothers have since vehemently denied).

Monsters – both this series and the first, Dahmer – consistently exploits queerness to generate headlines. In doing so, it detracts from the actual abuse the Menendez boys suffered at the hands of their parents, twisting the facts to conflate these horrors with sexual identity. As a loud voice in queer media, Murphy is the last person who we would expect to see feed into harmful myths that suggest homosexuality can be traced back to sexual abuse.

The Lyle and Erik Menendez Story has provoked outrage from critics and viewers alike, but also from the titular “Monsters” themselves, who have decried the show’s “dishonest portrayal” of their crime in a statement released by Erik from prison.

Twenty-four members of the Menendez extended family have since criticised the series, describing the second chapter of Netflix’s Monster anthology as a “a phobic, gross, anachronistic, serial episode nightmare that is not only riddled with mistruths and outright falsehoods, but ignores the most recent exculpatory revelations”.

Ryan’s response? “I’m used to being controversial,” he told People magazine. “It’s not new to me.”

The families of Jeffrey Dahmer’s victims were similarly dismayed by the first series of Monster, with one, Eric Perry, arguing that the show was effectively “retraumatising [the families] all over again”. Nevertheless, the series gained one billion views in just 60 days, making it the third most-watched Netflix series of all time. A second season was inevitable.

Controversy has long been Murphy’s bread and butter. His first show, a biting teen melodrama named Popular, wasn’t as, well, popular as it should have been, but it did pave the way for 2003’s Nip/Tuck, a campy yet horrific medical drama, which became a blueprint for Murphy’s signature depraved style. From a diarrhoea-filled hot tub to a self-performed mastectomy, this ridiculous (and ridiculously watchable) series about two morally bankrupt plastic surgeons became one of the definitive watercooler shows of the Noughties.

Then came the camp high-school musical melodrama Glee about a bunch of misfit teens competing for acceptance as the state’s premier choir. It became a global franchise that spawned live concert tours, a reality show spin-off, and turned its young stars – including Lea Michelle and Diana Agron – into household names overnight. The whole world was paying attention to Ryan Murphy.

Not content with just one global phenomenon, Murphy decided to create another, American Horror Story, which channelled the camp trash vibes of Nip/Tuck with a queer, grotesque spin on horror. The anthology franchise launched the careers of Sarah Paulson, Lily Rabe, and Adina Porter, and featured legendary turns from acting royalty including Angela Bassett, Kathy Bates, and of course, the one-and-only Jessica Lange. Lady Gaga’s acting career was launched in season five, Hotel.

The first four series – Murder House, Asylum, Coven and Freak Show – represented the very best of Murphy’s singular vision, bringing him more acclaim, Emmys, and cementing his status as a queer cultural icon. But even these seasons often ran out of steam halfway through.

If there’s one thing Murphy struggles with more than controversy, it’s pacing. His best ideas inevitably sour by the end. American Horror Story fans who are still watching, 13 years in, actively expect the story to dip midway as plot points are dropped or switched up with alarming regularity.

Throughout the 2010s, Murphy continued to churn out TV, winning Emmys for The Normal Heart, Feud: Bette and Joan and the first two seasons of American Crime Story, The People v. O. J. Simpson and The Assassination of Gianni Versace. And then there was Pose, a landmark show about New York’s trans ball culture which marked a turning point in the career of the man who apparently never sleeps.

Co-created by Steven Canals, Pose made history by hiring the highest number of transgender actors in one TV cast, leading to Michaela Jaé Rodriguez’s historic 2022 win at the Golden Globes. Pose also made history because it’s one of the very few Ryan Murphy productions that actually improved as time went on, becoming one of the most important and joyful queer shows ever created.

It was no surprise that in 2019, Netflix announced a $300m (£210m) partnership with Murphy. At the time, it was an exciting prospect for fans. Just imagine what his brilliantly sick, twisted mind could conjure up with the freedom (and cash) a huge streamer could provide.

Not a lot, it turned out. The Politician, an exhausting teen satire starring Ben Platt, was neither as smart nor as funny as it thought it was (Jessica Lange’s “butt-munch speech” aside) and Sarah Paulson’s Ratched – an unnecessary One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest prequel – wasn’t the surefire win it should have been either. Historical drama Hollywood turned out to be even more vapid than its namesake, and Halston, a series about the eponymous American fashion designer who diluted his own brand beyond repair, starring Ewan McGregor, was the most tedious of the lot.

Each show had the promise of Murphy’s winning formula still, where gore, decadence, and fabulous divas in fetching hats combine to maximise the story’s inherent camp appeal, but there was always something missing. Take 2022’s true crime thriller The Watcher, which played it safe and ended with a twist that made us regret watching it at all.

A new Ryan Murphy project used to be an event, something daring and provocative that was always worth watching. Now he’s lost the signature bite of his early shows, despite the freedom his success and Netflix’s deal provided. It’s lazy.

It’s a shame that it’s the problematic shows that gain the most attention. When he’s not causing controversy for the sake of a few million streams, Murphy has worked as a producer on a number of vital queer documentaries including Circus of Books, A Secret Love, and Pray Away as part of his deal with Netflix. These films are far more interesting than Monsters, yet I bet this is the first time you’re hearing of them. At a point in his career when the writing no longer resonates as much as it once did, this should be Murphy’s focus.

Instead, the endless deluge of typical Murphy fare continues, including (but not limited to) Doctor Odyssey (a cruise ship medical drama), All’s Fair (a divorce lawyer drama also starring Kim Kardashian), American Love Story (based on JFK’s short-lived marriage to Carolyn Jeanne Bessette-Kennedy), and The Beauty (set in a world where catching a STD can make you gorgeous. Yes. Really). And of course, the next chapter of Monster is on the way, starring Charlie Hunnam as serial killer Ed Gein, who used to fashion keepsakes from the bones and skin of his victims.

Will any of these shows actually be any good? That doesn’t really matter anymore. Because when the nuclear apocalypse finally hits, leaving nothing behind but Cher and cockroaches, there’ll still be Ryan Murphy, toiling away on yet another controversy-baiting show designed to snatch headlines and fulfil his endless Netflix contract. If that’s the case, at least I won’t be around to watch it.
topics: American Horror Story, Netflix, Ryan Murphy, True Crime, TV Features, TV Opinion

title: On TV tonight, a documentary revealing a year in the life of Gaza Strip residents
body:
Also, Lorena Bobbitt reflects on her crime in 'I Cut Off His Penis' and it's Caramel Week on 'Bake Off'

9pm, BBC Two

With the first anniversary of the 7 October massacre having recently passed, we’ve had a flurry of powerful documentaries about the atrocity and ensuing conflagration in the Middle East. BBC Two’s Surviving October 7th: We Will Dance Again, Channel 4’s State of Rage and ITV’s Israel and Gaza: Into The Abyss are now followed by a documentary in which cameras were handed to four residents of the Gaza Strip to film their experiences as they live through the ongoing conflict. Filmed over the course of a year, it follows Aya, Khalid, Adam and Aseel and their families as they endure bombing raids, evacuations, family separations, deaths and even a birth.

8pm, Channel 4

It’s Caramel Week in the tent, Paul Hollywood informing us that the sticky goo needs to be “a rich colour… almost the colour of my skin”. Is that a spin on the old saying that “if he was made of chocolate, he would eat himself”? But as the bakers attempt a caramel biscuit signature, a pear tarte tatin technical and mousse cake showstopper, the brickbats arrive faster than a deflating soufflé.

9pm, ITV1

An eye-catching – not to say eye-watering – title for a documentary investigating cases of so-called “penicide”, where a woman cuts off a man’s penis. Going beyond the often sensationalist headlines, we hear the personal testimony of both women and men who have witnessed and felt the impact of this act, including the surgeons who re-attached the penises, and ask why this very specific act of violence is committed.

9pm, Channel 5

The empathetic presenter begins a fresh run of his series by returning to the wilds of Queensland to visit Bette who, despite being in her eighties, continues to live alone in a run-down house. Two years later, Fogle is relieved she is still there, despite nearly losing everything in a flood.

9pm, Sky History

A two-part look at how the Channel Island of Alderney became a preoccupation of Nazi leader Adolf Hitler and, under German control, was transformed into one of the most heavily fortified places on Earth. Away from prying eyes, the Nazis also established the only concentration camp on British soil.

9.15pm, Channel 4

The fathers and sons spend their first night sleeping wild, putting up their hammocks before trying to sleep amid a cacophony of bugs, insects and howler monkeys, not to mention a visit from a passing snake. Between all the practicalities, Jethro realises just how good the outdoors has been for Dexter, who has been getting in trouble at his school.

10.40pm, BBC One

The latest double-bill of this terrific third series of the banking saga begins with a pivotal episode in which Robert (Harry Lawtey) finds himself facing a parliamentary select committee grilling over the Lumi bailout and discovers that he’s been set up as the Pierpoint fall guy (“He’s a young man… he’ll recover,” says Ken Leung’s Eric). Elsewhere, Yasmin (Marisa Abela) is in a confessional mood, and Harper (Myha’la) undertakes some industrial espionage in the ladies’ washroom.
topics: TV Guide

title: I ditched after school activities - kids should be at home, not building a CV
body:
My kids' faces lit up when I cancelled their ballet and football. Clubs are a middle-class arms race that parents should resist

There are so many things that you do as a parent only because you think you ought to. Crazy toddler birthday parties, the trampoline in the garden, the sleepovers, the endless after-school clubs. Other parents grumble about them, sure, but rather than being off-putting, it ends up seeming like such a rite of passage that, perversely, you feel like you’re missing out if you refuse to take part.

Peer pressure and the herd mind are such powerful things that even I, not very susceptible to them, found myself pushing my children to do after-school clubs when they were in primary school.

Surely we ought to be exhausted and over-scheduled like everyone else, racing hither and thither, bags of football kit and ballet kit and Suzuki maths kit and jujitsu kit dangling from our arms – isn’t that just what you were supposed to do?

Luckily, my children pushed back against this. No, after school they did not want to go to origami club or swimming club. They wanted to come home and eat biscuits in front of Charlie and Lola.

I quickly saw their point of view. My daughter did brief stints at ballet and brownies, and my son did an after-school football club. All of these were a pain in the neck: the taking there, the getting changed in damp, sweaty, smelly rooms, the hanging about, the wrestling into the car and then out of the car and then arriving home tired and jangly and then immediately having to start on dinner for ratty, hungry children.

My children were seven and nine when the pandemic arrived and we dropped our meagre after-school clubs, plus all playdates, birthday parties and sleepovers like hot bricks. And we never looked back.

“You mean,” said my children, “we didn’t have to do those things?”

“No,” I replied. “They are all optional.”

Their little faces lit up. They didn’t actually want to do the after-school things, or even the playdates or the birthday parties or the sleepovers. It turned out that these were all sources of stress in their lives. They confessed that what they really wanted was to come home, shut the door on the world and just be left in peace until such a sad time came as having to leave again.

This also gave me pause to see the extra-curricular club thing more clearly for what it was – a sort of mania, brought on by an amorphous fear many parents have that their child is somehow falling behind, that success in later life requires everyone to start filling up their CV aged six.

Or perhaps the ECC arms race is fuelled by working parents who don’t trust nannies or au pairs not to get children home and immediately stick them in front of the telly.

Or maybe all of the so-called enrichment is simply down to the fact that many parents have got the busy-is-good bug and measure their worth by how packed their schedules are. This has always struck me as a wrong-headed and strange way to go about life, which is hard enough as it is: to inflict this mindset on children is extra weird.

I also suspect many see it as a status thing: after-school clubs are expensive and often require help – either a hands-on dad or more likely not just a nanny but a nanny who can drive.

Whatever the reason behind it, I washed my hands of the whole business completely and have no regrets.

But now both my children are at secondary school and after-school clubs have roared back at us. This time some of them are not optional. My son is required to be at football and cricket club and has opted into Table Tennis Club and choir. My daughter is embarking on her Bronze Duke of Edinburgh Award, which requires activities on Monday, Tuesday, one Wednesday a fortnight, and Saturday. And we haven’t even started on the volunteering criteria yet.

And, oh my god, I’m very pleased that my weeks haven’t looked like this up until now. After-school time, which has for the past thirteen years been mostly for lazing about reading comics and drinking tea, is now a rigid timetable. Some evenings the entire family isn’t back until 8pm. Eight PM, London Time! That’s time for bed!

Not only that, life has become one endless fox, chicken, grain logic problem. My husband arrived in the kitchen yesterday and said, “If Sam starts winter cricket training on Mondays from 6pm, will you be back in time from dropping Kitty at Art to be home when he’s brought back by Henry’s dad?”

My day is now split into two separate days: my working day, from 9am to 3pm and then a brand-new day of manoeuvring four people around north London on trains, in cars and on buses, while somehow also making dinner and not forgetting to pick anyone up.

School has been back for just over a month and the situation is becoming intolerable. The worst thing is, my children are enjoying it! “I think I’ll do rock climbing for ever,” said Kitty the other day, as I gently slid off my chair and crumpled to a heap on the floor.

So my message to you, if you have small children, is this: put off after-school clubs for as long as possible. When the time comes, there will be no getting out of it and trust me, you’ll want to be as well-rested as possible.
topics: Features, Lifestyle, Parenting

title: 11 easy ways to be healthier in your 50s - from tai chi to squeezing a tennis ball
body:
We might be living longer than ever but are in worse health than previous generations. Here are ways to turn it around, starting today

We’re living longer, but are spending that extra time enduring more ill health than our predecessors, according to a large-scale study.

Researchers at the University of Oxford and University College London found that levels of serious illness, disability and chronic disease for people in their 50s, 60s and 70s have increased throughout the past century. Not only that, but health concerns such as heart disease, cancers and type 2 diabetes are affecting people at younger ages than before, despite advances in medicine and public health campaigns.

So, what can you do to turn your health around? Here, we look at the surprising science-backed advice that can help you live better after middle-age, with minimal effort…

People in Britain and Europe now in their 50s and above are 1.5 times more likely to suffer heart problems than previous generations. But drinking more ‘builder’s tea’ could help, says dietitian Carrie Ruxton.

New advice from The European Society of Cardiology recommends people with heart disease increase their flavonoid intake. “In the UK, tea is the largest dietary source of flavonoids – a powerful type of polyphenol, a plant bioactive,” says Dr Ruxton, who is also a member of the Tea Advisory Panel.

“Studies indicate that diets rich in flavonoids can reduce the risk of chronic conditions, like heart disease, by up to 19 per cent.” Black or green tea, brewed for at least one to two minutes, drunk four times a day “is the sweet spot”, says Dr Ruxton. Eighty-five per cent of us already drink two to three cups a day, so just one extra cuppa a day could reap benefits.

All adults over the age of 65 are offered the flu jab for free and, last winter, getting vaccinated cut the risk of this age group being hospitalised by as much as 30 per cent.

Considering the flu was associated with around 18,000 deaths over the past two winters, getting jabbed is worthwhile. But there is a way you can make your flu jab even more powerful: have the vaccine in the morning, says Russell Foster, professor of circadian neuroscience at the University of Oxford and author of Life Time: The New Science of the Body Clock.

“[In one study] elderly individuals were vaccinated against the N1H1 flu virus either in the morning – 9 to 11am – or in the afternoon – 3 to 5pm,” he says. “Those individuals who were vaccinated in the morning showed an antibody response three times higher than those vaccinated in the afternoon.”

Risks to brain health from dementia or stroke can severely impact quality of life as we age, but by boosting our neuroplasticity – the ability of the brain to reorganise and make new neural connections – we can protect against the symptoms or recover better from these injuries.

“The brain thrives when it’s challenged in unfamiliar ways and creates new neural connections – this is what neuroplasticity is,” explains Dr Faye Begeti, a neurology doctor and neuroscientist at Oxford University Hospitals. “You can boost neuroplasticity by learning a new skill unrelated to your everyday activities – such as playing a musical instrument, cooking a new cuisine or learning a language.

“When we reach midlife, we tend to stagnate and repeat tasks we’ve already mastered. It doesn’t matter how good you are at the new skill, it’s the challenge itself that leads to neuroplasticity. Bonus points for activities like dancing, Pilates, yoga or tai chi, which also improve coordination, essential for reducing the risk of falls.”

One in two British women aged over 50 are affected by osteoporosis, a loss of bone density that puts them at much greater risk of fracture should they fall.

To help combat this risk, “combine prebiotic foods with foods that are rich in plant sources of calcium,” says Dr Megan Rossi, a gut health scientist at King’s College London and founder of The Gut Health Doctor and The Gut Health Clinic.

“In your 50s and 60s, calcium becomes even more critical for maintaining and supporting bone health. Research shows that prebiotic foods – what feeds the good bacteria in your gut – help to increase calcium absorption in the gut, which, in turn, can help reduce the risk of conditions like osteoporosis (especially in menopausal women where oestrogen levels drop). Try pairing prebiotic-rich dates with calcium-rich almonds or prebiotic-packed artichokes with creamy cashew nut dressing.”

“A significant, yet often overlooked, danger is high blood pressure,” says Dr Faye Begeti. “Most people with high blood pressure are diagnosed in midlife. People can have high blood pressure without noticeable symptoms, making it easy to ignore. Over many years, high blood pressure can damage the blood vessels that supply the brain with oxygen and nutrients.

When a large vessel is damaged, it can lead to a stroke, but the accumulation of damage to many small vessels can result in both movement and memory issues in later life – these conditions are known as vascular parkinsonism and vascular dementia. Treating high blood pressure with tablets can reduce the risk of that damage occurring.”

A reading of less than 120 / 80 is considered normal; anything above is considered elevated and worth discussing with your GP.

Last year, the number of people living with type 2 diabetes in the UK exceeded 5 million for the first time – and that number again are suspected to be living with pre-diabetes. Rates shoot up from the age of 50 onwards, but your approach to what you eat can help control blood sugar and even, over the long term, reverse type 2.

One simple way to do this is by pairing high glycemic index (GI) foods, known to cause a pronounced blood sugar response, with fats and proteins, which research has shown can dampen that response. So put peanut butter on your toast instead of having it plain (or worse, with jam), and make your heart-healthy porridge oats even better with a dash of milk or cream and a sprinkle of nuts or seeds, says Dr Carrie Ruxton.

“For a long time, a curious link between social isolation and health has been noticed,” says immunologist Dr Jenna Macciochi in her book, Immunity: The Science of Staying Well. “A number of illnesses, from heart disease to cancer to some neurodegenerative disorders, have been linked to loneliness.”

This is thought to be because loneliness triggers inflammation throughout the body. Estimates put as many as 30 per cent of people in the UK as being chronically lonely, a statistic that rises with age. So “prioritise social engagement,” says Dr Faye Begeti.

Research shows that maintaining strong social connections can not only alleviate all manner of health risks, it can also help halt cognitive decline. “Engaging in meaningful conversations, joining group activities, and fostering long-term friendships keeps neural circuits active, reducing isolation and the accompanying risk of dementia.”

Grip strength, a lesser-known measure of healthy ageing, has also declined among the current generation of 50-plus-year-olds. A reliable predictor of overall strength, bone mineral density and mental function, its decline is associated with an increase in health issues, including arthritis, heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers.

So spend five minutes each day working on improving yours: you can buy a grip strength tool from Amazon for a couple of pounds or try “dead hanging” from a pull-up bar.

“Other easy exercises include stretching your wrists and hands by squeezing a tennis ball for 10 seconds, a desk press where you position your palms face up under a desk and push up, or working the small muscles in your hands simply by clenching your fists,” suggest trainers at Pilates studio Heartcore.

“While there isn’t a universal ‘brain health test’, one key area often neglected as we age is hearing checks,” advises Dr Faye Begeti.

“Untreated hearing loss is linked to a higher risk of cognitive decline and dementia because it can lead to social isolation and reduced brain stimulation. If you notice any issues with your hearing, please get it checked and, if needed, use hearing aids (don’t avoid or be embarrassed by them) to stay engaged with your environment and keep your brain active.”

“Muscle mass decreases by around three to eight per cent per decade after the age of 30, and the rate of decline only increases in your 60s and beyond,” says Dr Megan Rossi.

“Plus, as you age, your body becomes less efficient in building muscle and digesting protein (which supports muscle growth and maintenance). Given that eating a portion of protein has been shown to stimulate muscle growth, and having smaller portions helps support protein digestion in the gut, it becomes more important to spread your protein intake across several meals as we age – so have, for example, half a chicken breast at lunch and another half at dinner instead of one full breast at dinner.”

Rates of bowel cancer – the fourth most common cancer in the UK – rise from the age of 45. Screening is essential, but 30 per cent of people eligible for free screening in England neglect to take the test.

“In England, around nine in 10 people with bowel cancer survive their disease for five years or more, if it’s diagnosed at the earliest stage,” says Sophia Lowes, a health expert at Cancer Research UK. “However, this falls to around one in 10 when bowel cancer is diagnosed at the most advanced stage.

“We encourage people to take up the offer of bowel screening when they are invited. But it’s also important that any time you notice any changes that are not normal for you, don’t ignore it; talk to your doctor. In most cases, it won’t be cancer, but if it is, diagnosing it at an early stage can make a real difference.”
topics: Features, Health, Illness, Lifestyle, Wellness

title: Having triplets cost me £18k in the first year alone
body:
Megan Smyth is a single mother to three boys. She said the costs are huge and there should be more help for parents

When Megan Smyth fell pregnant four years ago, she knew that twins ran in her family – but never banked on the one in 200 million possibility that she would have identical triplets, conceived naturally.

Neither had she considered just how much it would cost to take care of three babies. Between car seats, cots, high chairs, a specialist triplet buggy, clothes, nappies, wipes, formula, bottles – plus a new car to fit the babies, as well as her six dogs – costs for the first year racked up to at least £18,000.

That’s not including the new house they needed to move to, as well.

“My mum and dad helped a lot, and my ex-partner’s mum and dad, because just having one child costs crazy money, let alone three,” says Megan, 35, from Derbyshire.

“It’s super expensive. I’ve been trying to decide whether it’s getting better or worse, because they eat more now that they’re three years old. They’ll probably have two sandwiches each for lunch, for example, and that’s times three. We go through two loaves of bread a week. Some weeks I’ve had to borrow money off my mum for a food shop. We scrape by.”

Taking care of a single baby can cost up to £7,200 in the first year, according to MoneyHelper, but parents of twins and triplets must budget for more as they can’t wait for hand-me downs, as in the case of conventional siblings.

Research from the Twins Trust found that having twins can cost parents up to £20,000 in the first year, and up to £30,000 for triplets, when taking into account not just basic babycare and life essentials, but also new cars and houses to accommodate the expanding family.

In Megan’s case, finances are particularly stretched. Since the triplets were 18 months old, she has been their sole provider after splitting from their father.

Receiving no financial support or child maintenance from her ex, Megan’s salary working four days a week as an NHS procurement assistant has to cover everything, from the mortgage to groceries, clothing, medical bills and activities.

She buys the boys’ – Rico, Colby and Odyn – clothes secondhand from Vinted, and in turn sells clothes they’ve outgrown. She shops savvily, buying the cheapest food products from Aldi, but her weekly bill still comes to £80.

Days and even meals out are rare, as the cost of everything is multiplied by three – not to mention birthdays and Christmas, which she needs to buy for throughout the year to make it manageable.

“Some things are getting easier as they get older. For example, they are toilet trained so I don’t need to buy nappies any more, and they will be in school soon, so I won’t have to pay nursery fees and I will be able to work full-time. But there are still other things that are becoming more expensive, for example, they’re clothes as they get bigger,” says Megan.

“Days out are not cheap at all when there’s three of them. I recently looked at taking them to a theme park and it was going to cost £25 each, so that’s £75 before I even get myself there, or pay for petrol and lunches.

“We’re going to the circus on the weekend, as they’re doing a deal where kids are free if you go at a certain time. Deals where kids eat free don’t usually work for us as it’s based on one paying adult getting a free meal, and there’s only one of me and three of them.”

Extra-curricular activities are just not affordable with three sets of fees to pay for, which can make Megan upset that the triplets miss out on opportunities simply because there are three of them.

“I looked into signing them up to football, but it would have been £90 without the kit. Going beyond the essentials becomes unachievable.

“I don’t want them missing out just because there are three of them. It feels like I’m penalised for having triplets, because it’s not like I chose it. I tried to have one baby and ended up with three,” says Megan.

“I try my hardest, but there are certain things I just physically can’t do without the money, and there’s nothing I can do about it. I can’t change it. I’m trying to look at other ways that I can earn money from home, because I can’t do anything that would require more childcare, just so they can have the extra bits that other kids would have.”

Megan has also at times felt isolated by the lack of support for triplet parents, especially single ones, apart from Twins Trust and a Facebook group for triplet parents she’s joined, through which she’s made friends.

“We’ve had no help with the fact we go through three times the amount of nappies, or three times the amount of food. After they were born, we didn’t receive any more midwife or health visitor appointments than anyone else, we were on our own. But after they were in the neonatal intensive care unit, I learnt how to get them into a feeding and sleeping routine, so that was really helpful,” says Megan.

Twins Trust is lobbying the government for more support for parents of multiples, from making maternity pay per baby rather than per pregnancy, increasing funded childcare hours, and providing additional mental health support – a luxury for Megan, whose only break is on a Friday night when her mum takes care of the triplets.

For now, she’s doing the best she can with what she has. “I used to do a lot of sport before the kids came along, but I don’t have any hobbies any more. It’s just one of those things. Money’s tight at the moment. I just remind myself, that it’s not for ever – it will get better at some point.”
topics: Bills, Children, Pregnancy

title: How can we limit the tax we pay when taking my partner's £700k pension?
body:
A reader wishes to know how they can reduce the tax they will need to pay on their pension

In this series, readers can email in with any question about their finances to be answered by our expert, Charlotte Ransom. Charlotte has 30 years of experience working in financial services and wealth planning, including 10 years as a partner at Goldman Sachs. She co-founded Netwealth, which specialises in low-cost investing and financial planning advice. If you have a question for her, email us at money@inews.co.uk.

Question: My 59-year-old spouse has a deferred pension worth £525,000 from their previous job, plus other pensions adding up to £700,000 in total. What strategies are available to limit the tax we pay when we start to draw down?

Answer: Throughout our working lives we can implement various strategies to be as tax-efficient as possible, and it’s the same in retirement. It’s a good move to evaluate your situation now, as it gives you plenty of time to adjust your approach if needs be. A timely assessment also puts you on the front foot if you need to make changes as a result of this month’s Budget.

A deferred pension, for the sake of other readers, is simply a pension you are entitled to draw from should you choose to, or you can instead leave it invested to continue to grow. You can access most personal or workplace pensions from age 55 but many people are still working at that age and prefer to leave their pensions to continue to accrue. On the other hand, the state pension age is now 66, rising to 67 in April 2028, so if you retire early you may need to access your personal pension to support your income needs.

You mention your spouse has £700,000 in total through separate pensions. As neither of you may be accessing these funds for potentially 10 years or so, it makes sense to consider the merits of consolidating these different pots into one place. There are many reasons for doing so, but let’s start with the most crucial: to ensure your money works as efficiently as it can to maximise your pension’s worth.

While we can’t control how investment markets perform or know how well they may do in future, we can reasonably assume a return of 5 per cent per annum over time. A recent FTSE 100 analysis showed it returned around 6.3 per cent a year annualised over the past 20 years, while the US S&P 500 index averages around 10 per cent a year over the long term. Assuming a 5 per cent return over the next 10 years, therefore, is not being overly ambitious. We should then assess an aspect of investing that we can control: what we pay in fees.

In 10 years, with your £700,000 pot growing by 5 per cent a year, and paying 1 per cent in total annual fees, it would reach just under £1.04m. However, if you pay all-in fees of 2 per cent a year (this is typical with a traditional wealth manager), your funds would grow by almost £100,000 less – reaching just over £940,000. Of course, any further regular pension contributions could also boost your pot meaningfully while you continue to take advantage of the tax breaks your spouse has benefited from up until now.

Making these efficiency changes is a key benefit of consolidating different pension pots. Don’t assume your smaller pots are not worth thinking about – the value of bringing them all together could be significant. You may also find it more convenient and easier to oversee a single pot. In addition, when you are evaluating your options you can ensure that your pension portfolio is appropriately diversified across a mix of global assets to help drive extra resilience and further growth opportunities.

Later, when you and your spouse are ready to start taking money from your pensions, this is where you need to be thoughtful. In retirement, we must generally pay tax on our income, just as we do throughout life. This is based on our total income, including the state pension, and we all have an allowance of £12,570 before we pay the basic tax rate of 20 per cent, with the higher rate of 40 per cent kicking in at £50,270.

A crucial exercise for you to do in advance is to estimate how much you think you might need to live on to enjoy a comfortable retirement – and then to structure your income so you don’t pay any more tax than you need to.

For example, your spouse’s potential pension pot of around £1m or so could generate a sum that drives them into the higher rate bracket, while you may decide an income of £40,000 to £50,000 is sufficient for your needs. You will also benefit from the first 25 per cent of the pension being tax-free – this is a considerable sum in itself and could be spread out over a number of years before you have to pay any tax at all.

Even in retirement, you and your spouse should also take advantage of the annual ISA allowance of £20,000 (£40,000 for a couple) – the funds you accrue in an ISA can then be taken as a tax-free income as and when needed. As you can see, there are a few permutations and you may find it is a complex task to juggle the options on your own. Clarity is key, and this might be easier to obtain with professional financial advice.

Taking advice now could help you to enhance the value of your assets in the years before you draw from your pension – and steer you away from costly mistakes. As well as your own state pension, you may have other savings or investments you would like to optimise. As a couple, you may also wish to minimise your exposure to capital gains tax (CGT) and potential inheritance tax (IHT) liabilities. These two areas in particular (along with potentially other aspects of pension rules) may need a closer assessment after Labour’s first Budget in 14 years on 30 October.

While we don’t know exactly what areas of the nation’s finances will be impacted, we expect that better-off individuals will bear more of the burden. It is therefore sensible to assess whether some scenarios could impact you and your spouse. How would you be affected if the CGT rate rises to 40 or 45 per cent? Could your calculations for a comfortable retirement be altered if the pension tax relief is lowered substantially? Would a stricter IHT regime affect your plans for gifting money to children?

Whatever the actual outcome of the Budget, we would urge caution in making overly quick decisions since there should be time to digest any changes that are introduced and consequent action. It is reassuring that you and your spouse have a decent nest egg to build on towards retirement – and you can ensure you maximise its potential in the years ahead by taking appropriate action now as well as taking the time to consider what your needs in retirement are likely to be and how that might affect your plans.
topics: Investing, Pensions, Retirement

title: More people are living to 100. Here's how much you need to save in your pension
body:
People are living longer but many people, including 54-year-old Audrey, don't want to because they fear their pension pots may run out

More people are living to 100 than ever before. While for many this will be good news, it does mean people need to have much larger pension pots to fund their longer lives.

Based on figures published earlier this year from the Office for National Statistics (ONS), the cohort of those aged 65 and above is expected to grow by just under 40 per cent between 2023 and 2050.

During the same period, this growth may increase to 90 per cent for those aged 80 and above, while the number of centenarians is expected to rise by 200 per cent.

A new report from Canada Life found that while 47 per cent of UK adults feel positive about the prospect of celebrating their centenary, 74 per cent agreed that, should they live to 100, they would worry about their quality of life – and whether they have enough money to fund their retirement.

So how much do you need to save for a long life and will we all have to work longer?

The Pensions and Lifetime Savings Association (PLSA) estimates that a single person would need £31,300 a year in retirement for a moderate income.

This includes around £55 a week for groceries, a three-year-old small car and a fortnight’s holiday each year in the Mediterranean.

If you get the full state pension of £11,502, which is currently set to the age of 66, then you’d need £19,798 from a private pension each year to make up the difference.

Experts at PensionBee looked at how much someone currently aged 25, 35 and 45 would need to put away each month to ensure their pot is big enough to give them a moderate standard of living in retirement.

Becky O’Connor, director of public affairs at PensionBee, told i: “Building a pension pot large enough to sustain a comfortable standard of living into your 100s is entirely achievable but, for most people, this goal requires a significant and sustained effort.”

The key, according to O’Connor, is to start saving as early as possible and to contribute as much as you can afford throughout your working life.

So, a 25-year-old with an existing pot of £10,000 would need to make contributions of £706 a month to generate a pot worth £511,582, which would give them £31,300 a year up until the age of 100.

A 35-year-old with an existing pot of £20,000 would need to contribute £1,050 a month – from 35 to 68 – to achieve an overall pot size of £511,582 to give them £31,300 a year up to the age of 100.

And a 45-year-old with an existing pot of £50,000 would need to contribute £1,410 a month to achieve the same pot size.

These assumptions assume investment growth at 5 per cent each year, and one annual management fee of 0.7 per cent taken from your pension each year.

For those who have smaller pots, or no pot at all, they would need to save even more each month to reach this for a moderate retirement.

Additionally, those who wished to have a more luxury retirement would need to save up even more money.

The high sums could prove difficult for people to put away consistently each month, which then leaves many working later than they initially expected.

One such person who is worried they will not have enough saved is 54-year-old Audrey.

She told i: “The chance to live to 100 is exciting as I’m lucky to be in good health and, as long as that continues, I will be around longer to watch and support my children and, maybe one day, grandchildren.

“However, I might not be able to support them financially as much as I’d like to. Equally, living to 100 is a scary thought. I’m aware of the financial cost of living that long, not only personally but also to public services.

“The additional cost of ageing to the NHS and the Government will be astronomical, so I expect that I’ll see higher taxes to subside this.”

Working longer certainly isn’t something Audrey, who lives just outside of Bath, wants. She said: “I plan to retire in the next two to three years, when I’m 56 or 57.”

Audrey is the director of a construction business and works 40 hours a week.

“I would love to spend some time travelling and perhaps spend time with future grandchildren. I don’t feel I am overworked yet, but I have been working since I was a teenager and am looking forward to relaxing in my retirement years and enjoying life while I am healthy enough – both physically and financially – to do so.”

She told i she had been in the working world since she was 16 and had always taken her pension contributions seriously.

“Collectively, my company and I add in 15 per cent to my pension pot – 10 per cent myself and 5 per cent my employer. I joined my first pension scheme when I was 18 years old as I knew even then how important it was to start building up a pension pot.

“The importance of savings came a little later on once I got married. Both my husband and I took saving very seriously while also ensuring we didn’t miss out on anything we needed.

“We both invested any bonuses we received, and this has since been used to clear our mortgage at the age of 42. We’ve since been able to save and invest all our savings.”

Despite being diligent with her finances, Audrey still does not feel confident she has enough to live a very long life.

“Looking back, I’m really pleased with how diligent we were with our savings, but I do not feel financially prepared to live to 100. When I started thinking about my future and retirement, I thought that if I lived to see 90, I’d be doing well.”

The state pension age is currently 66 years old for both men and women in the UK. It is scheduled to increase from 66 to 67 between 2026 and 2028, and then from 67 to 68 between 2044 and 2046.

There are concerns this could be pushed back even further in the coming years.

According to Canada Life’s report, 69 per cent believe retiring in their sixties will soon become a thing of the past, while 25 per cent disagree that living longer means we should work longer.

Lindsey Rix-Broom, CEO of Canada Life, said: “The prospect of a longer life should fill us with a sense of optimism. We can easily imagine people pursuing life with a sense of purpose, guiding younger generations and nurturing fulfilling relationships with loved ones.

“At the same time, we need to be realistic about how we approach improved longevity from both a financial and practical perspective, especially if it’s unexpected.

“The solution begins with a conversation involving us all – our customers and clients, financial professionals, the wider industry, and even policymakers at the highest levels of Government.”

Utilise tax relief

Pension savings benefit from tax relief, meaning money you save into a pension is free of income tax on the way in.

Pensions can be an especially tax-efficient way of saving for higher rate taxpayers. For example, if you earn £65,000 a year and put £10,000 into a pension through salary sacrifice, the whole £10,000 would go in as a contribution.

But if you wanted to save that £10,000 elsewhere or spend it, 40 per cent income tax and 2 per cent national insurance would be charged first, leaving you with a tax bill of £4,200 and only £5,800 to spend.

Max out employer contributions

If you are employed, your first step should be to check the pension benefits your employer offers. All employers must provide a workplace pension scheme and contribute a minimum of 3 per cent of your salary by law.

But some employers will be more generous than this. Some may pay in a percentage that is well into double figures, or will offer to “double match” your contributions up to a certain amount.

For example, they may pay in 16 per cent if you contribute 8 per cent.

Check national insurance contributions

To get the full state pension of £221.20 a week, you need at least 35 qualifying years of national insurance contributions. You will need at least 10 years of contributions to get any state pension.

Check your national insurance record through your personal tax account on the gov.uk website to see if you are on track.

You can top up gaps in your national insurance record for the previous six years. Some can buy back missing national insurance years dating from 2006. This may be worth doing to help you get the full state pension.

title: State pension set to increase higher than predicted at £473 from next April
body:
The Office for National Statistics has revised its wage growth figures up, increasing how much pensioners will receive under the triple lock

The state pension is set to be higher than expected for millions of pensioners as a result of revised earnings figures.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) today revealed that average wage growth in the three months to July is 4.1 per cent, up from its previous estimate of 4 per cent.

This is the crucial figure that is used in the state pension triple lock calculation and means pensioners are likely to see an even bigger boost to their pots in April next year.

Under the triple lock, the state pension increases every April by whatever is the highest – inflation, earnings growth or 2.5 per cent – and this year the earnings growth figure is expected to be the highest of the three.

Inflation figures will be released tomorrow, which, if higher would be used instead. However, it is expected to be below two per cent and so not used.

As a result of the revised wage figures, and provided they will be used to uprate the triple lock, it means those on the new state pension will get £473 more a year as of next April, compared to the previous estimate of £460 a year.

It means the weekly rate will increase from £221.20 to £230.30, a total increase from £11,502 to £11,975 a year.

For those on the basic state pension, the increase will be from £169.50 to £176.45 – £6.95 more a week and an extra £361 a year.

This will be an annual hike from £8,814 to £9,175.

Although good news for pensioners, it will cost the Government an estimated extra £100m.

Steve Webb, partner at LCP said: “A slightly higher rate of increase is welcome for pensioners, though will be an unwelcome £100m extra cost for the Chancellor as she prepares her Budget.

“The rate of the new state pension will now be close to £12,000 per year, very near to the £12,570 tax-free personal allowance. This is likely to put extra pressure on the Chancellor to take action on tax allowances in the coming years”.

Chancellor Rachel Reeves said yesterday that the state pension will rise by around £450 a year, adding she would announce the exact level of the state pension at the Budget on 30 October.

She insisted that the uplift would more than compensate for the loss of the winter fuel payment – worth up to £300 a year – suffered by most pensioners.

title: I moved to LA - and discovered what loneliness is
body:
When Lucy Pearson moved to the metropolis with a boyfriend, she was excited to immerse herself in its glamour. The reality was different

While Selling Sunset might be responsible for peddling an unrealistic image of Los Angeles in today’s Netflix era, I blame my own high hopes on growing up as an avid reader of the Sweet Valley High books. After devouring the series in its entirety, I soon after moved to the Saturday morning TV series, and so, spent a large part of my younger years fantasising about spending weekends in shopping malls, boys named Brad, and driving around California beaches in an open-top Jeep.

I’d always dreamed of moving to America, though I never knew under what circumstances it would happen. Yet, as the years passed by and my twenties were consumed by the hustle and bustle of London, I found myself living a very different reality. I fell in love with a boy I met on a boat in Sydney, and moved halfway around the world to be with him, and began to think that perhaps the American dream of my teenage years wasn’t meant to be after all.

But life has a funny way of unfolding. After eighteen months in Australia, a new opportunity arose: my boyfriend at the time, a driven and ambitious hip-hop dancer, landed a job at a dance studio in LA. Suddenly, the idea of living in America didn’t seem so far-fetched. He was seven years younger than me, and moving to LA had always been part of his long-term plan. It felt like opportunity and adventure were within reach, and we bit the bullet.

A few weeks later we moved to Hollywood. I was 31 at the time, my boyfriend was 25, and while he was eligible for a working visa, I went on a tourist one, which meant I didn’t have any working rights. We had saved enough ahead of moving there to ensure all our basics were covered, and my plan was to focus on my book blog – for which I’d won an award earlier that year.

It would be an understatement to say that my first day in LA didn’t go as planned. My boyfriend had flown out two days earlier to get things set up in the apartment we were subletting in North Hollywood. But as I went through passport control – a nerve-wracking experience at the best of times in America – I was directed to a side room. There, I sat watching as several people were arrested in front of me, while I waited my turn to be questioned. Despite having the correct visa, a return flight booked, and accommodation that we’d fully paid for, I had to endure a grilling on why we had chosen to move to LA. It was only after much pleading that I was allowed to pass through to arrivals.

One of the first mistakes we made was not listening to the people who insisted we needed a car. Like most people who’d lived in London for any stretch of time, my licence had been gathering dust for years, and I figured if I could survive in both London and Sydney without wheels, I’d be able to do the same in LA. And so, we didn’t bother getting a car, initially thinking we could survive on Uber rides and public transport. Big mistake. LA is sprawling in a way other cities aren’t, and it could take hours – due to the unreliability of public transport – to get from one neighbourhood to the next.

While my boyfriend threw himself into his new life at the dance studio, I found myself feeling more isolated than ever, struggling to navigate a city designed for drivers while I gave up leaving our neighbourhood unless we did so together. I was so frustrated at not being able to work that I ended up doing an unpaid internship at a travel website in Santa Monica in a bid to build my writing portfolio – but the commute was a four-hour round trip by public transport, so I only went in twice a week, making it hard to fashion any real friendships.

We had secured our apartment ahead of moving there, and paid way over the odds because we booked it through Airbnb. While our apartment was big, and we had access to a swimming pool, we were paying around £2,500 a month for a place that had very little within walking distance.

For the first time in my life, I tasted the true flavour of loneliness. While my boyfriend was busier than when we lived in Sydney, spending long days in the dance studio, I was more isolated than ever. I’d trained as a yoga teacher when I first moved to Sydney, and a happy by-product had been the tight-knit group of friends I’d made there.

Soon after landing, I signed up for further yoga teacher training at Wanderlust in West Hollywood – hoping it might give me the same social circle I’d found in Sydney. But most of the people I met through the studio lived on the other side of LA, meaning trying to forge any sort of friendship beyond a brief acquaintance was more effort than it was worth. According to Cat Moore, human connection specialist and director of belonging at the University of Southern California, I’m not alone. “There’s a revolving door feeling about lots of spaces in LA,” she says. “There’s a sense of scale that can become overwhelming, and people often come in and spin out.”

I spent a lot of my time in the Starbucks in Studio City, drinking syrupy iced coffees and watching the cloudless sky darken as the afternoon slipped into dusk. It was sitting at my favourite outside table that I would meet the only person whose face I remember for my time living in LA. His name was Sam, and he was a homeless man who always offered me half of the same sandwich he would buy every afternoon, despite my insistence I hated egg. I would buy him a coffee most days, and walk home to an empty apartment, and I’d often find myself wondering where he slept at night, if there was anything more I could do to help, or if he, too, felt the loneliness that seemed to permeate the city.

While LA is often portrayed as a glamorous metropolis such as in Selling Sunset, my experience was far more mundane. The city is undeniably beautiful in parts – endless blue skies, dramatic sunsets over the Pacific, and palm-lined streets – but it also has a grittier, more difficult side.

The vast distances, the endless traffic, and the glaring divide between the rich and poor were stark reminders that LA was not the dreamscape I had once imagined. Sure, there were beautiful houses and fancy cars, but there were also tents lining Venice Beach, and people like Sam, as well as Uber drivers who told me they were one minor car accident away from being unable to pay their rent. While in the UK we have the NHS, in the US, the lack of public healthcare means that one slip or fall could lead to complete financial ruin.

Autumn came. As the leaves began to fall, and the branches were bare against the sky, the vibrant energy of our early days in LA began to fade. Decaying pumpkins now sat in the stead of brightly lit jack-o-lanterns that had flickered an amber glow through our neighbourhood in the lead-up to Halloween. Our time in LA was coming to an end.

We had only ever planned on spending six months there; a trial run to see what the reality of living somewhere we’d both dreamed about was like. But while my boyfriend had thrived, I couldn’t wait to leave, and I went back to London for six weeks to spend time with my family, before returning to my boyfriend in Bondi. Six months later we broke up, and he moved back to LA.

And yet, for all its challenges, there is something undeniably captivating about LA. Despite the traffic, the expense, and the isolation, there’s no denying the creative energy that pulses through the city. I eventually came to appreciate the quiet beauty of LA – the sunsets over the Pacific, the diversity of its neighbourhoods, the endless inspiration of living in a city that is constantly reinventing itself. For all its flaws, LA does have a certain magic.

Still, when I look back at my time there, I can’t help but think about how different it was from the version of the city I had imagined. The LA I read about as a teenager was a carefully curated fantasy, a far cry from what life there was really like. I didn’t find what I’d hoped to when I first arrived, but I left with a deeper understanding of myself and the world around me.
