title: I'm a private school head - state schools need us
body:
Fee-paying schools share sports grounds, arts facilities and teachers with the state sector, says the warden of a £13,000-a-term secondary

Alastair Chirnside, warden of St Edward’s School in Oxford, is one of many private school headteachers to have choked on their cornflakes at Bridget Phillipson’s latest tweet. The Education Secretary, in defence of the Government’s proposed VAT levy on school fees, wrote: “Our state schools need teachers more than private schools need embossed stationary.”

I can confirm there isn’t so much as a branded pen on display in Chirnside’s study at St Edward’s when I interview him. There’s no budget for posh writing paper or pens, he insists when I suggest he’s hidden them; the school has more pressing initiatives to fund – such as the school’s teacher training programme for modern languages, maths and physics teachers, most of whom move straight into the state sector. And the art classes, sports coaching, free meals and facilities it provides to 35 local state primary and secondary school partners.

Sending up private schools as islands of privilege where money is frittered on marketing material, is not only spiteful and divisive but inaccurate, Chirnside explains, as the sector supports thousands of state school children every year. Staff from his secondary school, which has 800 pupils and costs from £13,395 per term, run large-scale sporting events for 2,000 local primary school children each year, while 3,500 local young people use the school’s arts centre. Each week, lower sixth formers are dispatched into the community for a 90-minutes service as part of Teddies Collaborates – they stack shelves in food banks, work in charity shops and provide learning support at primary schools, as well as assisting with social media management and events planning for local charities. “These aren’t superficial gestures – we’re working in partnership with local organisations, and children in both sectors are benefiting,” he says.

The question of how helpful partnerships between state and private schools really are remains a subject of some debate. Chirnside, who took over as warden of the school in 2021, believes they are worth more to the Government than VAT from parents who are already struggling to afford school fees.

A 2023 study by the Private Education Policy Forum, a think-tank that aims to reduce inequalities in education, suggested that most partnerships were superficial and offer little public benefit. Of 277 state schools that responded to the researchers’ Freedom of Information requests, only 3 per cent said they had benefitted from accessing or borrowing private school facilities.

Chirnside refutes this. He says his sixth-formers hold their community placements for eight months, enough time for a reception child to have gained more fluency in their reading, for example: “No school sets out to pay lip service; they work with state partners because they believe in doing so.”

Rather than punishing private school parents with VAT, he suggests the Government look to formalise partnerships between the two sectors. There could be a contractual requirement for private schools to share facilities such as theatres and pools with state schools, for example. “I think they’d be surprised to discover that in many cases they’re only formalising what is already in place,” he says.

He concedes there are challenges and barriers to partnerships; it’s no good a private school offering its pool to a state school, for example, if the school in question can’t provide transport or staff. Yet in most cases there will be a way around it, he says. “If neither time nor money can be found it doesn’t become a real thing, which is why schools must prepare and plan in advance to ensure what they’re offering the state sector is truly accessible.”

If Phillipson were part of our conversation today, I suspect she’d be rolling her eyes. Chirnside is Labour’s very definition of privilege: he went from the Dragon, one of the most prestigious prep schools in Britain, to Eton and on to Oxford, where he was awarded a half-blue for rowing. Yet his parents were both grammar school-educated and worked tirelessly to pay school fees; no different, he says, from many families in the private school system today. (One survey by Premium Credit suggests nearly half of parents with children at private schools today rely on family help to afford the fees.)

“There are some private school parents with significant wealth but not many; most are forgoing lots of things,” Chirnside says.

Parents are now facing an extra 20 per cent on the cost of their school fees, so I ask him if the school will be scaling back its partnership work. Not if we can help it, Chirnside says. Social responsibility is intrinsic to the school’s philosophy, he explains. “The most important public benefit from our school isn’t the teacher training we provide or the loan of our facilities but the nature of the people we send out into the world,” he explains.

Yet he admits his staff are working harder than ever to keep down the costs and ensure that any initiative they run is mutually beneficial to the community and pupils at St Edward’s. “Lavishing money on another school simply in the spirit of munificence would be impossible to justify,” he says. “When we donate money to local charities, it’s because our pupils have raised it.”

St Edward’s currently offers fee support to around 100 pupils. Unlike smaller private schools in less wealthy areas, which are having to cut bursarial assistance for new starters to help existing families afford the fees, the school plans to grow the bursary pot to help a further 60 pupils in the coming years. This is the equivalent of one in five pupils receiving financial assistance.

“We’re fully committed to breadth of access – in our view, a narrow, exclusive community is not the right place to grow up – and, thankfully, our parents are committed to supporting this,” Chirnside says. The school is lucky in that there are philanthropists among the parents and alumni who are keen to donate to the bursarial fund, he says. “I know this goes against the view that wealthy people are not on the side of society but the truth is we observe the opposite here.”

Increasingly, parents are questioning the point of it all – I know this because it’s all my fellow fee-paying friends talk about. We’re paying ever-increasing fees only for our children to be discriminated against by university admissions tutors when they leave.

Families have not left St Edward’s or asked for fee reductions due to the VAT levy, but Chirnside believes this is only because of its demographic and location; there are plenty of examples in other schools where pupils have been pulled out or haven’t taken up places in reception or year seven. Figures from the Independent Schools Council suggest there are 10,000 fewer children in private schools ahead of the VAT policy. “There is a lot of diversity within the sector; lots of specialist schools and smaller establishments in deprived areas – one of the many issues with the VAT policy is that it’s one size fits all,” Chirnside says. “There will be closures. It’s going to be a very difficult period of time.”

Private school parents will find themselves paying more for other aspects of their children’s lives, he says, from ballet and music lessons to health checks if they continue to do them at school. “Then there’s the fairness of those who choose to pay for a state boarding school being let off VAT and the question of what happens to those aged 16 to 18 in further education. Private tuition isn’t subject to VAT yet to me it seems very similar to paying for education. And what about not-for-profit schools like us – should the VAT outcome be the same?”

He fears the VAT levy will damage the private sector, a valuable export worth £16.5bn to Britain’s economy and associated with 328,000 jobs, while providing no real benefit to the state. He is also concerned by the rushed timing, with Labour insisting on imposing VAT on fees from January. “All schools – and parents – are working to budgets and financial plans which were set months ago, so the sudden imposition of VAT will be financially and administratively disruptive to a very great degree,” he says. “There still seems very little clarity on the detail and there are still very many important questions to be answered.”

title: The cheaper, quieter alternative to Cornwall for a UK holiday this autumn
body:
Northumberland received about a third as many visitors as the south-western favourite – but there's plenty on offer

As my children dig like puppies in the soft, biscuit-coloured sand of Alnmouth Beach, big grins stretching across their faces, I feel pretty smug. Holiday chat at the gates of our Home Counties school often references Dorset and the South West. But I rarely hear Northumberland mentioned.

It’s curious – this quietest of counties (England’s least densely populated, but one of its largest) is home to historically important and wildlife-rich islands, a National Landscape that’s ripe for adventure and more castles than any other English county.

While Cornwall welcomed more than four million holidaymakers in 2023, Northumberland, received 1.8m overnight guests, with more than 80 per cent of its visitors on day trips. And while London and the South West have long attracted the lion’s share of domestic holidaymakers in the UK, declining numbers in Cornwall are in contrast to a small increase in Northumberland.

Meanwhile, Visit Britain’s short-term rentals survey revealed that accommodation in Northumberland is, on average, £74 lower per day than that in the south-west.

I could instantly see the appeal of this glorious county – Alnmouth is one of several vast and largely empty beaches that make up the Northumberland Coast National Landscape, providing perfect bucket-and-spade days as well as plenty of space for out-of-season wildlife walks. You’ll never find yourself whingeing about crowds.

There’s also a ready supply of family-friendly days out. Yes, you might have to layer up and prepare for rain in autumn or winter, but the wild North Sea coastline is spectacular. A 38-mile section of the King Charles III England Coast Path – from Bamburgh to the Scottish Border – opened last summer, via Holy Island.

During our family trip, my six- and four-year-old were mesmerised by the Duchess of Northumberland’s fantastical Lilidorei play village and its “Lililympics” challenges and miniature houses inhabited by nine invisible clans. The eye-opening attraction – the subject of Channel 4 documentary, The Duchess and her Magical Kingdom last year – is the world’s largest play structure, with suspended cages, towering spires and vertiginous slides. It’s transforming into “Spookydorei” in time for Halloween and half term.

We crossed the wobbly bridges to the whimsical Treehouse Restaurant, then explored the gardens for their dancing fountains, bamboo labyrinth and many horticultural gems such as the fascinating Poison Garden, where toxic, intoxicating and narcotic plants are nurtured – a great October half-term option (adult admission is also two for the price of one this month).

At the castle, my mini witch and wizard joined a broomstick training session while girls dressed as Hermione posed for selfies against the castle’s famous backdrop.

Of Northumberland’s natural attractions, the Farne Islands – an important Grey Seal and seabird sanctuary – are a must-see. Inner Farne reopened this spring after a two-year bird flu closure, but summer is the best time to visit, when you’ll see puffins and migratory birds.

However, in winter, there’s still the chance to see seals and their pups on boat tours from Seahouses, a seaside town which, along with the dinky village of Craster, is renowned for its traditional smokehouses. We joined one of Billy Shiel’s Boat Trips and ticked off guillemots, kittiwakes and puffins from our checklist. While the affectionately nicknamed “Tommy Noddies” head to the open sea in autumn, the end of October is prime time for spotting some of the 3,000 fluffy grey seal pups which are born here each year.

The captain took us to the spot where local heroine Grace Darling helped rescue survivors of the 1838 SS Forfarshire shipwreck. Her life is honoured in the RNLI Grace Darling Museum, in Bamburgh, the location of one of the county’s spectacular castles, and where our children were fascinated by a Saxon combat lesson, as part of a pop-up living history weekend.

Between Seahouses and Alnwick are the sprawling ruins of Dunstanburgh Castle, on a remote headland buffeted by the North Sea. The huge, ruined castle was built in the early 14th century by Earl Thomas of Lancaster, possibly in a show of might against his adversary King Edward II.

We finished our trip at Barter Books, a curious second-hand bookshop housed in Alnwick’s former train station, whose sprawl of shelves is packed to the rafters with pre-loved tomes in every genre. There’s a quaint tearoom, a miniature train that chugs along the shelves and – if you visit in the colder months – a roaring fire.

By the time I was back at the school gates, the kids had seen stunning wildlife, enjoyed interactive history lessons, stepped into a storybook and had swathes of beach all to themselves – just some of the reasons Northumberland is back on our radar for half term.

How to get there Berwick upon Tweed is on the East Coast Mainline, served by LNER trains between London Kings Cross and Edinburgh. Trains to Morpeth are operated from London Kings Cross and Edinburgh by Lumo.

Where to stay Five nights at Farne View Cottage in Seahouses, for a family of four in the week of 25 October, start at £676 with sykescottages.co.uk

What to visitThose keen to embrace spooky season will find loads of events going on across October, with many being easy on the wallet, too. Look out for free Halloween activities at sites including Bamburgh Castle, 15 per cent off at English Heritage-owned Warkworth Castle (when you book online) and free Halloween activities at National Trust properties such as Wallington Hall.

More information visitnorthumberland.com
