title: How electric cars fuel human rights abuses
body:
Electric car makers risk supply chains which expose workers and local communities to exploitation, health risks and environmental harm as mines needed for the battery metals expand

Car manufacturers are continuing to fuel human rights abuses by failing to responsibly source the key minerals critically needed for electric vehicle batteries, a report suggests.

As global demand for battery minerals soars, carmakers needed to identify and mitigate human rights risks in their supply chains in countries where minerals are extracted such as the Democratic Republic of Congo and Philippines, according to a report by Amnesty International.

Electric vehicle (EV) batteries contain minerals and metals such as cobalt, copper, lithium and nickel – essential for energy technologies which require a battery storage unit.

The International Energy Agency says demand for these critical minerals will increase nine-fold between 2024 and 2050. To meet this demand an estimated 350 new mines will need to be opened.

Amnesty warned the rush to extract minerals for the energy transition has a “dark side” including forced evictions, threats to health from environmental pollution, dangerous working conditions and abuse of indigenous people’s rights.

Mining for the minerals used in electric vehicles can entail huge risks for people and the environment. Amnesty research has shown how industrial cobalt is linked to forced evictions in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Amnesty is calling on car companies to use their massive leverage as global minerals buyers to influence upstream mining companies and smelters to mitigate these human rights risks.

A study of 13 EV manufacturers found none of them demonstrated “they are yet conducting adequate human rights due diligence on their battery metal supply chains”.

“While some progress was made, across the board, the scores were a massive disappointment,” it said.

China’s BYD, one of the largest and fastest-growing electric vehicle companies, ranked bottom of Amnesty’s assessment, with the German manufacturer Mercedes-Benz rated top. Tesla was the second highest rated EV maker.

“BYD’s disclosures show a serious lack of transparency on human rights diligence in its battery supply chains,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty’s secretary general.

“Other low-scoring firms, such as Hyundai and Mitsubishi, lack the necessary depth and information about implementation across key human rights due diligence areas.

“The commitments these companies report on… provide little evidence of meaningful action, showing they have a long way to go to meet international standards.”

“The lack of transparency around supply chains demonstrated by these companies is a serious problem considering the likelihood that they may be sourcing batteries made with minerals such as cobalt or nickel mined in conditions that could harm people’s human rights,” said Ms Callamard.

“The huge rise in demand for the metals needed to make electric vehicle batteries is putting immense pressures on mining-affected communities,” she added.

“Those lagging behind need to work harder and faster to show that human rights is an issue they take seriously. It’s time to shift gears and ensure electric vehicles don’t leave behind a legacy of human rights abuses.

While some of the companies assessed have taken positive steps to acknowledge their human rights responsibilities and align corporate policies with international human rights standards, a lot more needs to be done Amnesty said.

Major EV manufacturers could do more to show they’re actually implementing their policies through addressing human rights risks and providing effective remedy to affected people.

Amnesty’s assessment was based on each car maker’s publicly available reports, policies and filings. Their report does not capture every action companies may undertake.

Amnesty called for governments to introduce and enforce mandatory human rights and environmental due diligence legislation covering companies’ global operations and supply chains; ensure access to effective remedies for human rights harms linked to the impacts of EV manufacturers’ global operations.

Companies should also be required to implement environmental safeguards and rehabilitation plans; ensure protections for workers’ rights; as well as acting to address gaps and failures identified in the report and publicly disclose measures taken to mitigate human rights risks in the battery mineral supply chain.
topics: Amnesty International, Driving, Electric Vehicles, Environment, Human Rights

title: How Gaza and a Raving Loony unseated Jon Ashworth in Leicester South
body:
Three months after the shock election night defeat of one of Labour's big beasts, Jon Ashworth, i visited Leicester South and found questions still being asked about the campaign that toppled him.

It may sound bizarre for accusations of electoral wrongdoing to be associated with a candidate for the Official Monster Raving Loony Party. But as i revealed, the claims and counter-claims swirling around the general election race in Leicester South are serious.

During the campaign, few in the Labour Party expected they would have any trouble in defending a majority of more than 22,000 in the constituency.

But there was a problem, and it was a big one for the incumbent – and shoo-in for a position in Sir Keir Starmer’s cabinet -Jonathan Ashworth.

The issue, as for some other Labour MPs, was that Ashworth had abstained in a Commons vote on a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas in November last year, weeks after the October 7 attack.

Roughly a quarter of Leicester’s 369,000 population is Muslim. When the general election was called, independent candidate Shockat Adam was able to turn the heat onto his Labour opponent.

Labour’s then shadow paymaster general has claimed in post-election interviews that it was the “most vitriolic campaign” he had ever experienced.

He alleged that he was subjected to abuse and harassment from Adam’s supporters. At one point he claims he was forced to seek refuge in a vicarage as opponents to his campaign used megaphones to ensure everyone in the area could hear the opposition they were directing at him.

For Adam, however, who called on some of his supporters to cease any harassment, it was a legitimate campaign with robust questioning as part of a fair debate.

At least two of the clashes between Ashworth and those campaigning against him were shared widely on social media. Adam reposted at least one of them on X, formerly known as Twitter.

“He was asked questions,” Adam says in an interview with i. “There was no abusive language. There was no physical confrontation. I’ve seen the videos.

“This was robust questioning. I wouldn’t stand for any form of aggressive behaviour.”

However, some members of Ashworth campaign team claim they continue to be abused, with at least one local Muslim businessman facing calls for a boycott of his company due to his support for Ashworth during the campaign.

Adam calls on those, whether his supporters or not, to cease such harassment.

But, it was not only Ashworth who claims he was subjected to abuse from Adam’s campaign team.

Usman Ghani Admani, a local human rights lawyer and cleric, told i he felt he was “shadowed” by Adam’s team throughout the election and regularly faced pressure to quit the race to allow Adam to unite the Muslim community vote.

Admani, who joined the race as an independent candidate following Rishi Sunak’s firing of the election starting gun on 22 May, says: “Right from the beginning I was pressured by supporters of Shockat not to stand. But I was standing on a platform for all of Leicester South, not just on Gaza.

“I wanted to help people with their day-to-day issues. I was not just about an issue voters here feel passionately about but the issues they face every day. Housing, the cost of living crisis, jobs, public services.

“I refused to stand down, so everywhere I campaigned Adam’s campaign team would show up and continue to pressure me.”

Admani speaks of once incident where his son placed some of his campaign leaflets on a table at a local community centre. He claims Adam’s supporters then abused his son, both physically and verbally. Once again, Adam denies these claims.

In another video, supporters of Adam can be heard using a megaphone to campaign loudly outside the front door of his home.

Another candidate in the race, who asked not to be named, also claims they were intimidated by Adam’s campaign team and even asked by Adam himself to exit the race so he could have a clearer run at Ashworth’s majority.

Adam strenuously denies these claims.

“These unfounded allegations are nothing more than a straightforward political attack, which should be ignored by the public and responsible sections of the media,” says the new MP.

“We fought an upbeat, community campaign focusing on the issues important to the residents of Leicester South – the cost of living crisis, cuts to the NHS, housing, the failure of traditional politicians to represent the communities they serve and the ongoing genocide in the Middle East.

“Our campaign captured the imagination of residents, with hundreds of activists getting involved to deliver this victory for the people of Leicester South.”

For some observers, Ashworth himself has to shoulder part of the blame. They point to his frequent appearances on the airwaves extolling Sir Keir Starmer’s programme for a future Labour government and suggest he may have taken his victory for granted. They also claim he underestimated the rising anger at the events in the Middle East and how he was viewed as a political lightning rod.

Whatever the truth, Adam pulled off a remarkable victory, turning Ashworth’s 22,675 majority into a 979 one of his own.

Adam’s was not the only shock victory for new MPs that stood with a pro-Gaza message to voters.

Labour has lost five seats with large Muslim populations – four to independents and one to the Conservatives.

In Leicester East, the Conservatives benefitted from independent candidates picking up several thousand votes, particularly the area’s former Labour MP Claudia Webbe.

In Birmingham Perry Barr, Labour’s Khalid Mahmood lost to independent Ayoub Khan by 507 votes.

Independent candidates who made the conflict in Gaza central to their campaign also won in Dewsbury and Batley, as well as Blackburn, which both previously had healthy Labour majorities.

There were also close calls for the new health secretary Wes Streeting in Ilford North, as well as for Jess Phillips in her Birmingham Yardley constituency.

Did Adam expect to win?

“That’s a really difficult question to answer,” he says. “In the sense that we worked really hard for about five months.

“My campaign was a very grassroots campaign, and I must have knocked on hundreds of doors. My campaigners must have knocked on 1000s of doors, and we were getting very positive responses, and there was a momentum building.

“But I knew the magnitude of the task. We had no history behind us. We had no backing behind us, no political support behind us.

“There was a hope that we were going to win, but the expectation was we were probably not going to make it.”

A number of sources involved in the campaign have claimed to i that Adam’s campaign co-ordinated with Amaar Suliman, the candidate for the Official Monster Raving Loony Party who stood under the name Ezechiel Adlore.

From the origins of campaign leaflets, to free food at events held for voters and Muslim community leaders, there is a long list of allegations that are all robustly denied by Adam and Suliman.

While Adam admits that Suliman had occasionally volunteered for his campaign before standing as a candidate in his own right, he denies assisting him on his campaign.

However, the Labour Party, which wrote to Leicestershire Police to call for an investigation, remains unconvinced by Adam’s campaign tactics.

A spokesman for Leicestershire Police said: “The force has received a number of reports concerning election material distributed in the run up to the General Election on 4 July.

“All matters within the election period are dealt with expeditiously by specialist officers. Further enquiries are continuing to identify whether a criminal offence has been committed.”

Responding to the questions over his relationship with Suliman, Adam says: “Neither myself or any member of my team suggested he stand – this is a ludicrous allegation.

“I have not donated to his campaign nor have my campaign staff. I have no knowledge of who else my donors may have donated to.”

Suliman, who joined the Monster Raving Loony Party last November because it was the “only party honest about the ridiculousness of politics”, adds: “With regards to the MP, I remember having heard a local was going to run independently about a month or two after my campaign began and heard him speak .

“By ‘work’ he may be referring to me voluntarily helping collect the feedback cards they asked the audience to write on a couple of times, which I ended up summarising it to him.

“We spoke about the running of elections as I had already studied up on the commission and councils’ guidance.”

According to Suliman’s electoral expenses, which have been obtained by i, he was charged £1,825 for the flyers targeting Ashworth.

Suliman’s expenses also show that he donated £1,903.35 to his own campaign “to meet election costs”.

The connection between Adam and Suliman including their preference to both use 1 Key Solution for printed material are the concerns at the centre of Labour’s call on Leicestershire Police to investigate a possible breach of electoral law. Candidates have a legal requirement to accurately detail the expenses they spend during their campaign and providing false information can lead to the winning candidate being removed and a new election called

Answering the question on the extent of his relationship with Suliman, Adam denies any involvement in his campaign.

“Not at all,” he says. “That’s something you will have to take up with him. I can appreciate where you’re coming from, but there’s nothing there.

“Your implication that he was some sort of proxy for my campaign is both bizarre and false. It’s also a little insulting to Mr Suliman.”

Nick Delves, the treasurer of the Monster Raving Loony Party, told i that its candidates are not encouraged to engage in negative campaigning. He said he and the party’s leader, Howling Laud Hope, had suspicions about Mr Suliman motives for standing as one of their candidates.

“We don’t have a lot of vetting going on, and we tend to take what we can,” he says.

Delves added they would be reviewing Suliman’s campaign literature and if he asked to stand again for the party, he would probably be turned down.

Away from the allegations over Adam’s campaign, Shockat Adam is a precise and fastidious man.

Indeed, even wiping rain drops from reading glasses with a fleece sets him off. The MP, who owns a chain of opticians, twitches and leaps to his bag to find a cloth to ensure my lenses are not scratched.

This precise trait is demonstrated throughout the conversation.

Asked his personal view on a number of ethical and contentious issues – from gay and trans rights to whether or not Hamas and Hezbollah are terrorist organisations – Adam rarely provides a much insight into his thinking. He answers by referring to the consensus view in Parliament and throughout the country to seemingly justify avoiding a direct answer to direct questions.

But, while Adam was considered a single-issue candidate in his fierce rivalry with Ashworth, he does concede that MPs should answer questions on a wide range of issues that affect not just the Muslim community in his constituency, but all of the 71,000 that live there.

At least, on one moral and ethical issue he is forthright. On abortion, Adam is not alone among MPs in believing in the right to life of the unborn child.

“There are situations where an abortion may be the only solution,” he says. “If I was on the spectrum, I am more pro-life and I would respect that view more, but I am not binary from that question.”

He adds that in circumstances of a women becoming pregnant after being raped or if a mother’s life is at risk, then an abortion should be an option.

While he is candid on this moral question, he is not so open on the issue of gay and transgender rights.

Asked how he would vote on same sex marriage in the unlikely event that it ever came up before Parliament in the future, he says he would vote “with my constituents” because he believe in “consultative democracy”.

As a former local chairman of the Muslim Engagement and Development (MEND) organisation, he presided over a group that offered advice to parents seeking to prevent their children being taught about transgender issues in school.

“This is a topic that I will hold my hands up high, and say I need to inform myself a little bit more,” he says. “I think we have to have a conversation between the parents and the schools.

“Sex education has to be taught at an adequate age at schools. As long as there’s constant communication with parents and families, and there is respect between the two, I generally find there’s not an issue.”

As we sit together, Israel was preparing for its “limited” invasion across its northern border into Lebanon after two weeks of targeted hits on Hezbollah leaders and “military targets”.

During the latest escalation in the Middle East Lebanese authorities claim there have been more than 2,000 deaths with more than 9,000 injured in Israeli strikes. A further million people are said to have been displaced during the bombardment.

As a single-issue candidate who stood on a pledge to campaign for an immediate ceasefire at Israel’s southern border with Gaza, Adam does have a solution, possibly not as radical as some may have expected.

Despite sharing a stage at recent rallies with speakers who have called Israel a terror state and called for its destruction, Adam claims he does not condone such ambitions but says Israel “has committed acts of terror on the people of Palestine”.

He goes on to say that he believes in a two-state solution that returned to the pre-1967 war borders between Israeli and Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank.

“I would like to see a two-state solution, people living in peace side by side,” he says.

On this point he may well disagree with his brother, Ismail Patel, who before the October 7th attacks said he “saluted” Hamas for resisting Israel.

Does he side with the UK’s definition of Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen as terrorist organisations?

On this point he refuses to offer his personal view, saying these groups are “proscribed terrorists organisations as we speak”.

Pushed several more times, he adds: “You know, people will always stand up as resistance fighters and, in other people’s eyes, they’ll be terrorists. That’s always going to be the case.

“It has been since the world started and it’s all semantics. We want no more killings in those areas, for their safety, for their benefit, for the world’s safety.”

While Adam clearly identified Leicester South’s Muslim vote as his key to victory, there are two synagogues in his constituency. Now an MP, he says will represent all communities on his patch.

At the time of the interview the anniversary of 7 October atrocities by Hamas was a week away, and he says he is meeting with the community a year on from when 1,200 Israeli’s lost their lives in the attack.

“I am going to speak to the Rabbi and have a meeting with them at one of their events”, he says. “I see absolutely no association with my Jewish community or the Jewish faith with the actions of the Israeli army.

“I think we must stop conflating those two and weaponising these terminologies because it serves nobody.”

I asked Adam if he had met with Jewish community leaders around the anniversary of Hamas attacks but did not receive a response.

He then says that in the year since 7 October, the Israeli Defence Force has, according the Hamas-run authorities, killed around 40,000 Palestinians, including around 16,000 children.

Just a mile or so from Adam’s current office is Evington Road, an area where many in Leicester’s Muslim community choose to live.

Here Adam may have garnered significant support during the campaign, but the residents are not yet ready to pronounce on whether he is a good MP.

Rather than focusing on the war in the Middle East, Mohammed Islam, 54, wants Adam to fix things closer to home.

He says: “They are spending lots of money on the city centre, but for seven or eight years they’ve done nothing about the potholes around here,” he says, echoing a problem faced by all communities across the country.

“I’m glad Shockat got it, but let’s wait and see if he’s going to be good for the community. It’s good he will get Gaza up the agenda, but he needs to act closer to home too.”

Tarek Aziz is another Evington Road local, and he’s not ready to praise the new MP he voted for just yet.

“He is committed to us as we are minority, as the Muslim community, in England and we need somebody who can raise our voice,” says the 28-year-old.

“He’s doing that. He’s doing well, and I will keep supporting him but it has just been three months. There’s still a long way to go.”

Not everyone who lives in this area is a fan of Adam. Janice Tardy, 72, lives “just down the road” and is concerned what Adam will do for the non-Muslim community.

She also suggested Ashworth was seen by some as having taken the constituency for granted.

“I felt cheated by Labour,” she says. “I voted Labour all my life, but Ashworth didn’t show his face here.

“We didn’t see them campaign here and that’s why I think he lost. I feel like my vote was stolen. I’m not sure Labour will get my vote again.”

Asked if she was happy with her new MP, she adds: “He’s not going to support the interests of white people in this neighbourhood. End of story.”

Like any constituency, Leicester South is not just about one group or community. It is too simple to suggest Adam beat Ashworth because of the Muslim community turned out for him.

As Leicestershire Police considers Labour’s demand for an investigation into the Leicester South election campaign, Adam is confident there is nothing to find. Ashworth and Labour, on the other hand, are hoping if proof of an offence is found then it will allow them a second chance to win the seat.
topics: Gaza, Gaza–Israel conflict, General Election 2024, Israel, Israel-Hamas war, Jonathan Ashworth, Leicester

title: The first time Russians captured her, she wrote this. The second time, she died
body:
Journalists around the world have been paying tribute to Viktoria Roshchyna, a Ukrainian reporter who has died aged 27 while in Russian custody.

Roshchyna disappeared in Russian-occupied Ukraine in August 2023. Vladimir Putin’s forces only confirmed nine months later that they had detained her, without explaining why. Last week, her father was informed by letter from Moscow’s defence ministry that she had died, without being offered any explanation.

This was not Roshchyna’s first experience of being held captive by the Russian forces – which makes her determination to continue reporting seem even braver.

She had previously been captured in March 2022 while trying to reach the besieged city of Mariupol. In the article i is republishing below – originally written for the Ukrainian news outlet Hromadske, and translated into English for the group Index on Censorship which campaigns for media freedom around the world – Roshchyna described that traumatic ordeal.

By Viktoria Roshchyna, 5 April 2022

I was in Zaporizhzhia on the morning of 12 March. I wanted to get to Mariupol to write an article; I thought that I had to tell the truth from the blocked city. It was my initiative.

I found out that a humanitarian convoy was going to Mariupol. I went to the assembly point but the convoy had already left. I contacted the authorities and asked them if I could catch it up. They replied that I could try. I did not find a personal driver, so I left with another convoy heading to Polohy. We caught up the Mariupol convoy near Vasylivka, and I continued with them.

I came across the occupiers’ first checkpoint in Vasylivka. Russian soldiers thoroughly checked me. They made me unzip my coat and show the contents of my bag. They found a camera and asked if I was a journalist. I confirmed this. They told me that I had no business in Mariupol and that I should return to Zaporizhzhia. They inspected my phone and camera and found nothing. I asked permission to continue with the column. The occupiers did not mind. We stopped overnight in Berdyansk.

We continued our way in the morning but we were stopped near the city limits and we were told to wait for permission. We were waiting for two or three hours by a crossroads where the roads to Mangush, Energodar and Vasylivka go. Rumours started to spread that we wouldn’t be allowed to move.

Cars passed by and a woman from the convoy told us that she had found some local guys who were willing to drive us to Mariupol. When we arrived at the agreed place, the car was no longer there. The Russian military told us to wait and started talking with us.

I stepped aside. I was thinking of returning to the convoy but a Russian soldier approached me and asked me to show him my phone. He told me that he had instructions from above to check me.

He asked if I was a journalist. I did not lie as it could make things even worse. He asked to show him my WhatsApp account and he saw the contact of the security services of Zaporizhzhia. There was a message with a request to publish a video of a Russian soldier who had swapped sides to join Ukraine.

Some other soldiers began to interrogate me. Then they spoke with Metropolitan Luka [a priest of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church]. Luka and other clerics were leading the convoy. When they returned, they said I had to go with them. I was put into a prison van accompanied by four Chechen paramilitaries who took me to the Berdyansk district administration office.

“I had to tell the truth from the blocked city”

I was met by people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas. They seemed to be very young, less than 30 years old. They started to interrogate me, searching me and inspecting my phone and documents. They told me that I was not a journalist but a spy and a propagandist which I denied. It lasted for an hour. Then, one of them said: “Everything is clear with you”. I realised later they were from the Russian security services, the FSB.

One of the men in balaclavas brought in his commander. When I asked him who he was, he replied: “I am the man. You have two options: you either go to a jail for women or to a Dagestani military base.” I asked them what that meant. They did not explain. Then two men grabbed me, put a blindfold over my eyes and took me out of the room. I was crying, explaining that I was a journalist, that people would be looking for me, and that they would not get away with it. They took me to the local office of the SBU, the Ukrainian Security Service.

I was met by Chechens and Dagestanis who put me in a tiny room with a chair, a table and a window which they closed and told me not to approach it. They brought a blanket on which I slept on the floor. It was light and warm there. I was taken out only to the bathroom. Almost all my stuff was taken. When I asked when they would let me go, they answered, “When Kyiv is taken”. They added: “Luka is in charge of the convoy and he refused to take you”.

From time to time, I was interrogated by Russian occupiers.

“We have no conscience. The law does not exist for us,” the FSB guys said. “Ukraine does not exist anymore.”

They repeated this every day.

“If we bury you somewhere here, no one will ever find out. You will be lost forever,” they said.

“I was crying, explaining that I was a journalist, that people would be looking for me, and that they would not get away with it”

I had no fear. I knew they were trying to break me. But I felt desperate because I knew nothing about the outside world, and I was not able to do my job.

“We do not fucking care that you are a woman and a journalist,” they shouted.

But I knew the fact that I was a journalist restrained them.

At some point Chechens joined in with the daily moral pressure of the FSB guys. They guarded me and tried to convince me to cooperate.

“They are serious. They won’t let you go for nothing. You’d better to cooperate with them because you are so young. Otherwise, you will stay here forever,” they said.

They added: “We are the power. They are the brains.”

They brought me some food, but I refused. The first days I ate my remaining supplies from Zaporizhzhia. When it was finished, I took nothing but sweet tea. I felt my energy leave me. It was difficult just to get on my feet. During the last visit of the FSB men, I was not able to stand. But I continued to demand my release. When I cried too loud, one of the Chechens hit me and told me that I wasn’t at home, and I should watch my tone.

“When I cried too loud, one of the Chechens hit me”

There were a few empathetic men among them, nevertheless. They came to ask if I was OK, asked me to eat something and begged me not to kill myself.

I asked to be allowed to make a call. They refused. Afterwards, the FSB told me that there would be a neutral interview and then I would be released. I insisted that I wouldn’t lie. They agreed. They brought a camera after a while. They had a prepared text with them, and they demanded I read it. I did not agree with the wording “high probability of having saved her life”. Eventually I agreed to shoot the video and they dropped the previous demands regarding full support of Russian actions and accusations against Ukraine.

Once the video was completed, they took me to another place. It was the local jail in Berdyansk. They refused to return my phone and camera as they considered them “propaganda tools”.

I spent the night in a room with a Russian soldier, who was supposed to guard me. The electricity and heating were cut off during the night. It was very cold. With my flashlight I counted the hours until morning. The soldier told me that the people who had interrogated me were from FSB. He was afraid that I would kill him during the night. He asked me whether I considered them as occupiers. Then he put the Ukrainian flag and the national emblem near me and said: “This is to calm you down. You see, we did not destroy them.”

In the morning, they blindfolded me again. Then they took me out of the jail and showed me the direction to go. I reached the closest bus station and went to the location of an evacuation convoy. I left with them the next day to territory controlled by Ukraine.

I am sincerely grateful to everyone who put in their efforts to find me and release me.

© Hromadske

“I insisted that I wouldn’t lie”

When Viktoria Roshchyna was released, the incident did not scare her away from reporting on what was happening in her homeland and to her people. Instead, she continued reporting with tenacity, working for Ukrainska Pravda and other respected publications.

She was awarded the Courage in Journalism prize by the International Women’s Media Foundation in 2022.

Following the news of her death, her former colleagues at Hromadske shared some of her best work in an online tribute.

They said: “She was one of those journalists who do not wait for an editorial assignment. As soon as something was happening, Viktoria was already there. At rallies, skirmishes, sites of murders. She took on the most difficult challenges, loved law enforcement topics, attended high-profile and important court sessions.”

Index on Censorship and allied organisations said: “We welcome the opening of an investigation by Ukrainian authorities on grounds of ‘war crime combined with premeditated murder’ and demand that Russian authorities do the same to elucidate the circumstances of Roshchyna’s death and bring to justice all those who could be responsible.”

Jeanne Cavelier of the group Reporters Without Borders: added: “The Russian authorities have never provided any information about her detention, despite repeated requests from her family, the Ukrainian authorities, and RSF. They must shed light on all the circumstances surrounding her detention and death.”

Explanatory text by Rob Hastings
topics: Big Reads, Journalism, Media, Russia-Ukraine war, Ukraine

title: Number of senior university staff earning £100k doubles in four years
body:
The research comes after an i investigation found that university bosses claimed at least £1m in expenses in the past two years

Universities’ refusal to hand over details of their vice chancellors’ expenses has been described as “unacceptable” and prompted calls for limits on spending.

An i investigation found that bosses at leading UK universities claimed at least £1m in expenses in the past two years.

But the true figure is likely to be much higher as several institutions refused to provide their full expenses data.

John O’Connell, chief executive of the TaxPayers’ Alliance (TPA) campaign group, called for universities to place “much stricter limits on expense accounts” and to ensure “they’re fully open to reasonable requests for information.”

Higher-education bosses have warned of a looming cash crisis in the sector, with an estimated 40 per cent of universities expected to be in deficit this year.

But TPA research, shared exclusively with i, reveals that the number of university staff receiving more than £100,000 in total annual pay has more than doubled since 2020.

The TPA, which campaigns for lower taxes, found that across 99 universities across the UK, there were almost 10,000 members of staff receiving over £100,000 in total remuneration.

This compares to 4,112 members of high-earning staff identified in 2020.

Like i, the TPA faced a lack of transparency from a large number of universities: 52 universities out of 164 refused to respond to its Freedom of Information (FoI) requests. A further 13 provided unusable data.

i requested and successfully obtained copes of expenses receipts from a number of institutions. They revealed that university bosses, who earn more than £300,000 a year on average, had claimed for five-star hotel rooms, meals at trendy London restaurants, taxi fares of more than £200 and even luxury cookware – including a £39 herb chopper.

However, the request was blocked by other universities who argued it would be a breach of General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) rules to provide copies of these documents.

In response to i’s investigation’s findings, Mr O’Connell of the TPA said: “Taxpayers will be shocked by the free-spending attitudes of university vice-chancellors, but almost as shocking is the unacceptable approach that many are taking by refusing to release the receipts.

“At the same time as higher education institutions are going cap in hand to the government demanding an injection of taxpayer cash, their leaders are using the company credit card with reckless abandon. Just as egregiously, many are using every trick in the book to avoid the transparency that taxpayers expect.

“Universities should be placing much stricter limits on expense accounts, while also ensuring that they’re fully open to reasonable requests for information.”

The TPA’s University Rich List report is due to be published in the coming weeks and examines staff salaries, benefits and expenses across all universities in the UK. It uses publicly available data and FoIs.

Many academic staff are facing redundancy or have lost their jobs in recent years as institutions seek to cut costs. Students could also be hit with higher tuition fees, with ministers reportedly considering plans to raise the upper limit from £9,250 to £10,500 per year.

A spokesperson for Universities UK said: “There are over 240,000 academic staff working in UK universities and far more once non-academic professional staff are taken into account.

“Deciding on pay at this level of seniority is complex and includes clinical academic staff wages set by the Department of Health and Social Care, while senior staff members like VCs have their wages set by remuneration committees.

“Staff operating at this level are experts, working at a senior level within vast institutions that deliver billions of pounds worth of benefits to students and local communities. Their pay reflects the responsibility of these roles.”
topics: Expenses, News, Universities

title: Why Covid waves are still happening throughout the year
body:
With the UK on its fourth wave of the year - with a strong possibility of another one before the end of the year - i asked the experts why Covid keeps coming back

Nearly five years after Covid-19 reached the UK, the virus is in its fourth wave of 2024, with hospitalisations surging by more than 20 per cent in a week.

Hospital admissions are much lower now than they were earlier in the pandemic while an infection is generally far less serious. But new waves of the virus keep coming back and the results can still be severe, posing the risk of serious illness, death and long Covid, especially among the clinically vulnerable.

By contrast, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – a key cause of the common cold – and flu are seasonal viruses, meaning you can relax in the spring and summer and start worrying about them in the autumn.

Covid, meanwhile, is year-round, with the UK suffering two waves this summer alone, in June and July.

The conveyor belt of waves is driven by a constant stream of new variants and sub variants – working in conjunction with waning immunity against the virus – and the fact that Covid is intrinsically about three times more contagious than flu and RSV.

So a new variant comes along that is able to evade existing immunity built up from previous infections and vaccines better than are existing variants, which pushes up cases and can fuel a new wave.

In the following weeks and months, the wave of infections pushes up the nation’s immunity against the new variant and cases subside.

But that immunity starts to decline quite quickly and, because Covid is fundamentally much more contagious than flu and RSV, it doesn’t take much to start up a new wave.

“The problem with Covid is that it evolves so quickly. Its evolutionary rate is something like three or four times faster than that of the fastest seasonal flu,” professor Steve Griffin, of Leeds University, told i.

“So you’ve got this constant change in the virus, which accelerates the number of susceptible people. It’s creating its own new pool of susceptibles every time it changes to something that’s ‘immune evasive’.

“Every one of these subvariants is distinct enough that a whole swathe of people are no longer immune to it and it can infect them. That’s why you see this constant undulatory pattern which doesn’t look seasonal at all,” he says.

Adding in seasonal factors, such as cooler weather forcing people indoors and children returning to school, and the conditions are frequently conducive to a new wave.

These factors, along with the new variant XEC, have fuelled the current wave in the UK.

XEC is spreading so fast it is thought to be close to being dominant in the UK, if it isn’t already.

By contrast, because flu and RSV are fundamentally much less contagious – and produce far fewer new variants that can evade immunity – they need more extreme conditions to cause a wave.

There is also much more built-up immunity against these viruses, which have been round far longer than Covid.

As such, those viruses only really get going in November, peaking around Christmas and falling off sharply in January.

“We can either increase our immunity by making better vaccines or increasing our vaccine coverage or we can slow the virus down with interventions, such as improving indoor air quality. But we’re not doing either of those things,” said Professor Griffin.

As a result, there is no sign of Covid becoming seasonal, he said, adding he would be “pleasantly surprised” if that happened this decade.

“People often talk about viruses running out of evolutionary space, so it can’t keep changing. But the trouble with this one is that it doesn’t seem to have reached anything near that limit and it seems to have this huge capacity to change and keep changing.Like different branches of a very large tree,” he said.

“If it does become seasonal, it will take a long time based on the current rates. Whether it’s a disease of consequence as much in several years’ time – it hopefully won’t be.”

Professor Christina Pagel, of University College London, said: “Many people assumed it would become seasonal eventually, but the timescale for that could be years or decades.

“Covid is still intrinsically infectious enough and mutating fast enough and our immunity to infection wanes fast enough, that it can sustain waves throughout the year.

“I have no idea how long that will continue. Better vaccines, such as the new nasal ones being developed, might well help but who knows when they will become readily available?” said professor Pagel.

Professor Sheena Cruickshank, of Manchester University, said: “I would really like to see investment in vaccine technologies that may give more durable protection and that were offered more widely.

“Ideally we would be looking to develop or acquire more durable vaccines that confer longer-lasting immunity – such as nasal vaccines or multivariant universal vaccines that may be more resilient against the ever-evolving virus.”

title: Unemployed could be given weight loss jabs to get back to work, Streeting says
body:
Health Secretary reveals plans to trial latest generation of drugs like Mounjaro on worklessness and productivity

Unemployed people could be given weight loss jabs to help them get back to work, Wes Streeting has suggested.

In an opinion piece for the Telegraph, the Health Secretary said “widening waistbands” were placing a burden on the NHS by costing it £11bn a year.

“Illness caused by obesity causes people to take an extra four sick days a year on average, while many others are forced out of work altogether,” he wrote.

The latest generation of weight loss medicine, like Ozempic or Mounjaro, could be administered to people in order to get them back into employment, and to ease costs to the health service, he added.

He continued: “For years, governments have ducked the serious, long-term policy decisions required to tackle its debilitating effects. Fears of being labelled ‘nanny state’ have meant nothing has been done.”

His suggestion comes as the Government announced a £279m investment from Lilly – the world’s largest pharmaceutical company – on the day the Prime Minister hosted an international investment summit.

The plans announced at the summit will include real-world trials of weight loss jabs’ impact on worklessness, productivity and reliance on the NHS, according to the Telegraph.

A study by Health Innovation Manchester and Lilly, will examine whether being put on the drugs will reduce worklessness and the impact on NHS service use, and will take place in Greater Manchester.

The Health Secretary continued: “The reforms this Government will put in place will open the NHS up to work much more closely with life sciences, to develop new, more effective treatments, and put NHS patients at the front of the queue.”

In separate comments to Sky News, Streeting said he believed some of the weight loss “can be game changing in terms of tackling obesity,” but warned they should not be misused.

“Where I think we’ve just got to be careful, though, is that we don’t see these drugs as an excuse not to do the right thing in terms of our diet, nutrition, exercise or to use them as cosmetic drugs for the Instagram perfect body,” he said.

“It’s great the NHS is there for us and it’s free at the point of use… but that doesn’t mean that you should use it and abuse it.”
topics: Obesity, Unemployment, Wes Streeting

title: What UN peacekeepers do and their complicated role in Hezbollah strongholds
body:
The UN Interim Force in Lebanon (Unifil) has faced unprecedented attacks by the Israeli military, but has refused a demand to leave the border region

The UN Interim Force in Lebanon (Unifil) has frequently found itself in difficult situations, including threats and attacks from both sides of the conflict between Israel and Hezbollah.

Unifil faced unprecedented attacks last week that intensified over the weekend, resulting in five peacekeepers getting injured in a series of Israeli strikes.

On Sunday, Unifil said two Israeli tanks destroyed the main gate at a peacekeepers’ facility overnight before troops “forcibly entered the position” in Ramiya in southern Lebanon. It came a day after Unifil said its headquarters in the border town of Naqoura was struck by explosions.

The Israeli military is demanding that the peacekeepers leave the area, but Israel has faced international condemnation for repeatedly firing on them since the start of its ground operation in Lebanon two weeks ago.

Israel’s hostility towards Unifil is not new, as it has long viewed these forces as being under Hezbollah’s control, accusing them of failing to prevent Hezbollah from stockpiling weapons south of the Litani River, in violation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701, which was drawn up following a month-long war between Israel and Hezbollah in 2006.

Unifil consists of about 10,000 peacekeepers from 50 countries, who have been patrolling the border area between Lebanon and Israel for nearly 50 years. They are tasked with reducing tensions along the “blue line” dividing Lebanon from Israel and the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights.

The mission’s Spanish commander, Major General Aroldo Lázaro Sáenz, has repeatedly emphasised that Unifil has no mandate to use force, and, as such, its main task is to produce regular reports that are discussed every four months by the UN Security Council. So far, none of these reports have resulted in binding action.

Unifil’s relationship with Hezbollah is marked by caution, as the local population in southern Lebanon is predominantly loyal to Hezbollah. Unifil refers to this population as the “local community”.

The residents of southern villages and towns, who have benefited from Unifil’s services and training programmes for farmers and women since 1978, monitor the daily patrols with suspicion.

Some patrols have led to violent attacks, the most recent of which occurred in the southern Lebanese town of Al-Aqabiya in 2022, when residents killed an Irish soldier and destroyed a Unifil vehicle after it entered a side road, reinforcing suspicions that the mission was spying on them.

Allegations of espionage have always lingered among Hezbollah’s popular base, particularly since some patrols, especially the French and Spanish, have repeatedly attempted to enter private property to take photographs, only to be driven off with stones.

But Unifil has largely maintained peace in the border region for 18 years. That changed, however, on 8 October 2023, when Hezbollah decided to open a front against Israel in what it called the “support war for Gaza”, which over the past year has evolved into a full-scale conflict in Lebanon’s south, eastern Bekaa Valley, and southern Beirut suburbs, with parts of central Beirut also being bombed by Israel.

As a result, UN peacekeepers are under increasing danger and are being targeted by Israel, which believes Hezbollah has long enjoyed near-complete freedom of movement in areas under Unifil’s mandate, with support from Iran.

Over the years, Hezbollah has built an arsenal of weapons, launched rockets towards Israel and dug offensive tunnels under the Lebanese-Israeli border, among other activities.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has called on UN Secretary-General António Guterres to immediately withdraw UN peacekeeping forces from southern Lebanon.

“It is time for you to remove Unifil from Hezbollah strongholds and combat zones,” he said on Sunday.

Mr Netanyahu added that the Israeli army had repeatedly requested the withdrawal of Unifil forces, but their request was denied in order to “provide a human shield” to protect Hezbollah fighters.

This has made the situation for these forces very complex.

Andrea Tenenti, spokesperson for Unifil, said the peacekeeping mission was “committed to staying”.

He told i: “It is crucial for peacekeepers to remain in southern Lebanon. We are present here at the behest of the Security Council.

“Moreover, it is vital for the UN flag to fly in this region – not only to monitor the current, challenging situation but also to report back to the Security Council and to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid to the population in the south.”

He added that thousands of people remained trapped in villages, lacking access to basic necessities. “Thus, we will continue our presence.

“The situation is indeed challenging and concerning, yet peacekeepers will maintain their positions. Any decision regarding changes in the situation will rest with the Security Council, not with the peacekeepers on the ground.”

A senior international force official, speaking anonymously, said Mr Netanyahu “has no right” to request UN peacekeepers withdraw from their positions.

“The host government – in the case of Unifil, that is Lebanon – typically requests the Security Council to extend the mandate or deploy a peacekeeping force. This process is ongoing,” the official explained.

“However, that does not mean that the Security Council cannot make its own decision regarding Unifil. The Security Council always retains the authority to make decisions.

“If, for example, it determines that the situation has become too dangerous for peacekeepers, it may decide to relocate them or adjust their deployment. This is always within the Security Council’s purview, and we cannot question that.

“However, typically, the decision is made between the host government and the Security Council, not Israel, as it is not the host government.”

Lebanon’s ministry of foreign affairs issued a statement condemning the “systematic and deliberate targeting” carried out by the Israeli army against Unifil, saying the attacks on its headquarters in Naqoura “is an act that is condemned and illegal, violating the mandate defined by the UN Security Council”.

The ministry urged the UN Security Council, the international community and the countries contributing to Unifil’s mission to call for an investigation into the matter and to take a firm stand against the attacks.
topics: Hezbollah, Israel, Lebanon, United Nations

title: Election rule changes to Georgia vote count are a 'recipe for a coup'
body:
Poll workers fear the new hand-counting rule will bring unnecessary chaos in the swing state

IN GWINNETT COUNTY – It may be Zach Manifold’s job to get his staff to hand count ballots during this year’s US presidential election, but that doesn’t mean he agrees with it.

“It doesn’t make any sense to me,” says Mr Manifold, the election supervisor for Gwinnett County in Georgia, while speaking at his office in the suburbs of Atlanta.

The rule was approved in August, three months before the election, by three Republicans on a state board who were personally praised by Donald Trump as his “pit bulls”.

It is Mr Manifold’s job to implement the changes, which he will, even if he doesn’t see the point.

“At the end of the night, the number that’s on the ballot scanner is by far the most reliable number you’re going to get,” he says. “As opposed to three people, after a 16-hour day, sitting down to count sheets of paper.

‘”I will trust that scanner all day long over people who are tired and exhausted.”

That’s as close as Mr Manifold gets to frustration during an interview with i from election headquarters some three weeks before the vote.

His cool head will be an asset on 5 November given what’s been happening with elections in Georgia.

The swing state could decide the election and, in 2020, it was the focal point of Donald Trump’s efforts to overturn the result, which he lost by 11,780 votes.

Polls show that this year, across the state’s 159 counties and more than seven million voters, Trump has a one-point lead over Democrat Kamala Harris, the Vice President.

That is well within the margin of error, meaning any advantage could make all the difference.

In Georgia, critics say that includes Republicans making major changes to the state’s rules with just a few months to go until the election.

The state election board ignored the advice of its own legal counsel and Georgia’s top prosecutor to require hand-counting of the ballots and allow vaguely-worded investigations into the results, among other changes.

The result has been described as a “recipe for a coup”, which is no small thing in Gwinnett County, the second-most populous county in Georgia, which has dramatically swung in favour of the Democrats in the past decade.

Sylvia Albert, director of voting and elections at Common Cause, a non-profit that promotes voter access, claims that the election board’s goal was to “create confusion and distrust in the system”.

In effect, the board was “trying to make their own law and they can’t do that”, she said. “That’s a clear strategy and we need to call it out so voters know it’s happening.”

In Gwinnett County, concerns over the vote have centred on David Hancock, who was appointed to the county election board in May last year.

In March, he refused to certify the results of Georgia’s presidential primary but was overruled by the two Democrats and independent members of the five-strong panel.

According to reports in Rolling Stone, Mr Hancock’s Facebook posts include one from 2020 about 2,000 Mules, the documentary by right-wing activist Dinesh D’Souza, which contains discredited claims about the election that year.

Next to it, Mr Hancock allegedly wrote “those of us looking to expose what happened in the Nov. election are not going to stop on January 20th”, the publication reported.

Other posts reportedly include one in which Mr Hancock said that most people who attended the rally in Washington on 6 January 2021 that led to the storming of the US Capitol were “patriots who have done no wrong”.

Which brings us back to Mr Manifold.

The 43-year-old married father of two, who coaches little league baseball games in what little spare time he has, seems as far removed from a bureaucrat looking to steal the election from Trump as you can get.

Mr Manifold has been working in elections for 20 years and is so enthusiastic about his job he keeps an antique manual voting machine from the 1970s in his office.

He was optimistic about election night and said he was “pretty positive” the results would be accurate and timely.

His main concern was that there would not be another staff exodus, which is what happened after the 2020 election when about a quarter of his 40 employees left due to the “trauma” of the contested vote.

Now the office is back to 48 full-time employees and will hire another 125 temporary staff for the election, as well as 2,000 poll workers.

A tour of the election headquarters, a reassuringly drab municipal building on a strip mall next to a charity shop, rapidly becomes a ghost hunt for previous election conspiracies.

Outside, Mr Manifold points to the building next door. In 2020, it became the centre of wild speculation when a government worker who happened to be tasked with removing 300 old employee phones was followed home by people who thought he was removing election machines.

“He had to call the police,” Mr Manifold says.

Another conspiracy centred around a video posted online that some claimed showed a worker for Dominion Voting Systems, the company which makes and runs voting machines, was stealing voter data from the tabulation room.

In fact, he was transferring a data report from one computer to another in the tabulation room, where the computers are not even connected to the internet.

According to Mr Manifold, about 25 per cent of his job is now spent debunking misinformation, and it has brought him an odd celebrity status in Gwinnett County, even if it means he ends up talking about work when on a rare evening out.

“I miss the times when nobody wanted to know what I did,” he says.

In the past few weeks, Mr Manifold has been spending hours with his lawyers to try to interpret the vague wording of the election board’s rules.

As best as Mr Manifold understands it, the hand-counting rule requires that, at the end of election day, three poll workers will have to separate ballots into stacks of 50 and count them by hand to make sure they are accurate.

Previously, one election worker counted and checked their total against what the voting machines said.

Mr Manifold said the rule was unnecessary because his staff would be constantly checking those numbers as the day goes on.

In addition, there is a mandatory process where eight to 10 per cent of the ballots are randomly audited once the election is completed.

Mr Manifold says: “When we do the audit, every time that count is off I’ve never seen the machine off.

“It’s always been the people sitting at that table. It is. We do it in batches of 10 in the audit.

“The rule says batches of 50 for the election. There’s absolutely no way in a stack of 50 you’re going to get an accurate count.”

Efforts to change the electoral process date back to the chaotic weeks after the 2020 election when the Trump campaign filed dozens of lawsuits challenging the results.

Mr Trump made his now-infamous phone call to Georgia’s secretary of state Brad Raffensperger, who was in charge of the election process, telling him to “find me 11,780 votes”.

When those efforts failed, Mr Trump’s acolytes began planning how they would ensure he won next time by installing loyalists on county election boards.

Such boards are normally dull, bureaucratic affairs but the former president’s admirers saw them as an opportunity to, as critics claim, swing the election in his favour.

The changes began in earnest in 2021 when the state legislature, backed by a Republican majority, voted to remove Mr Raffensperger as chair of the election board.

In his place, the Republican party of Georgia installed three loyalists who now have the majority on the five-strong panel.

They were: Janelle King, a conservative podcaster with no experience running elections; Janice Johnston, a retired obstetrician-gynecologist, and Rick Jeffares, a former state senator.

In August this year, the board approved a rule that allows county election boards to conduct a “reasonable inquiry” into any irregularities before certifying the results, but the rule did not define what that could be.

Then came the hand counting rule followed by another that required county officials to meet by 3pm on the Friday after an election to review precinct returns. But that would be before the 5pm deadline for overseas and military ballots to come in.

That change deeply concerned Travis Doss, head of elections in Georgia’s Richmond County, and the president of the Georgia Association of Voter Registration and Election Officials.

Previously, his staff would wait until all the ballots were in before doing what the board now wanted to do themselves.

Mr Doss said his “biggest concern” was that one candidate might appear as though they were in the lead at 3pm on Friday, only for another candidate to be the eventual winner the following week.

He says: “Now this is where the speculation is going to come in; where did those votes come in, so and so was losing etc.

“It just brings in so much controversy that’s unnecessary… If that happens, it would be chaotic. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle once it’s out, and once it’s out there perception becomes reality. No amount of explanation can change that.”

Most of the new rules are being challenged in court by Democrats and voting rights groups but, as things stand, election officials have to continue as if they will be in effect.

They appear to have come from a near-complete breakdown in trust towards election officials that has, in part, been sown by Trump.

Like Mr Manifold, Mr Doss is diplomatic and is trying to see the best in the reasoning behind it.

“I want to believe that the people who are reintroducing the rules feel what they think needs to be done to make the election secure,” he says.

“I want to believe everybody is doing this in good faith and they’re doing it properly.

“The issue we have is that many of the concerns from the public can be mitigated if people understood the process.

“These rules are being introduced by citizens who don’t understand the process. They don’t understand the checks and balances we already have in place to make sure the elections are secure, fair and accurate.”

When asked if any “dead people” voted in the three countywide elections that have already taken place in 2024, a common refrain among election conspiracy theorists, Mr Manifold is emphatic. No dead people. No illegal immigrants. No fraud, as conspiracy theorists have claimed.

Mr Manifold was “feeling pretty good” about voting because of three uneventful elections in 2024 – then the election board began making changes.

“I bet I could count the complaints I’ve had about the elections this year on one hand,” he says.

“I’ve already had three elections; I don’t understand why they need to change anything.”
topics: Donald Trump, Georgia election investigation, Kamala Harris, US Election

title: Wild boar cull by archers sparks outrage in Spain's Costa del Sol
body:
The beasts are invading tourists areas, rooting through bins, damaging golf courses and causing car accidents

Protesters have objected to plans to use archers to kill wild boar that are invading tourist resorts on Spain’s Costa del Sol.

The porcine threat is troubling residents and tourists alike in Malaga, Marbella, Mijas and parts of Almeria.

Searching for food and water, the boars root through bins mostly at night, damaging golf courses and causing car accidents.

The marauding hogs are increasingly putting city dwellers at risk across Spain.

Shakira became another victim when she said she had her handbag stolen by two boars while out with one of her children in Barcelona in 2021.

There are believed to be about one million wild boars in Spain, according to the Hunting Resources Research Institute, which said this number could double by 2025 because of the soaring growth of this species.

To stop the invasion, Malaga council has paid archers £11,355 to bring them under control.

However, Ecologists in Action, an environmental group, veterinarians and an animal rights group have condemned this method of controlling the animals.

Librada Moreno, of Ecologists in Action in Malaga, said that employing archers to shoot boars in the 21st century was “barbaric”.

“If they are shot with arrows, these animals might just be injured and not die. It would be much better to use other methods like capturing them or introducing a sterilisation process,” she told i.

“Another thing which would help is if people do not put out food or water near where they live. These boars do not live in the mountains. They live in the outskirts of towns. They are a bother for people.”

Juan Antonio de Luque, president of the College of Veterinarians of Malaga, also opposed using archers.

“We are against hunting boars with archers. There is more chance that they will be injured and will die in agony,” he told i.

Mijas, a town which is popular with British tourists, employed archers to shoot wild boars and the method is used in other parts of the Costa del Sol.

PACMA, the animal rights party, has written to Francisco de la Torre Prados, the mayor of Malaga, asking that archers are not used to control wild boars.

In a statement, Malaga council told i that is had adopted “control measures to stop damage from wild boars and feral pigs. A temporary hunting emergency has been declared due to damage and health risks caused by these animals which…constitute a real risk to the ecosystem, livestock, agriculture and the population.”

Daniel González, who set up a private archery company to hunt the boars, told i they observe the animals and advise authorities to make sure food sources are removed.

“We will only sacrifice the wild boars when we need to. Not many die,” he said.
topics: Animal Rights, Animals, Hunting, Spain, Wildlife

title: The worst job in the world and why no one should ever take it
body:
Which job, with a reported salary of around £100,000 a week, which gives you first-class travel to all corners of the globe, and which offers you the opportunity to work with some of the world’s most talented performers in their field, would you think twice before accepting?

Well, if you are Lee Carsley, the interim manager of the England men’s football team, the answer would appear to be: permanent manager of the England men’s football team.

Following Gareth Southgate’s decision to leave the job after just short of eight years – 102 games, 61 victories, no major trophies, one West End play – the Football Association put Carsley, a journeyman professional player but a successful and respected manager of England’s under-21 team, in charge of the senior squad for six games. This was widely regarded as an audition for the job on a long-term basis.

We are four games into that run, and the evidence is not exactly conclusive – three wins against lesser opposition, but a humbling defeat at home to Greece. More significant, however, is the sense that Carsley is weighing up whether the job is right for him, rather than the FA deciding if he is right for the job. I know that, in the modern world, the balance of power between employer and employee has shifted, but this is something else.

“This job deserves a world-class coach who’s won trophies and been there and done it,” said Carsley after England’s victory in Finland on Sunday. “I’m still on the path to doing that,” he added, ostensibly exuding modesty and self-knowledge.

This seemed to underline his statement following the loss to Greece that he would “hopefully be going back to the under-21s” after his spell as interim manager concluded in November.

Carsley said that he was “definitely not” counting himself out. But unsurprisingly, the FA is now understood to have cooled on the idea of appointing him.

The bigger question for the FA, however, is less about Carsley’s apparent reluctance and more about understanding why this might be so. This is not about one man’s diffidence, but the more practical challenges involved in what, in the decades since England’s men last won a major trophy, the 1966 World Cup – has become something of an impossible job, defined by structural impediments, unrealistic expectations and unbearable scrutiny.

The Premier League, with its untold billions and unrelenting media focus, is, for many football fans, the only game in town: they abhor breaks in the season for international matches and resent club players coming back injured. For this reason, managers will withdraw players at the merest sign of a sniffle or a twinge.

While this gives the clear impression that the national team’s fortunes are of secondary importance to the domestic game, it’s not how we are led to think by much of the media and the game’s administrators.

We invented the game, the argument goes – a claim that’s not entirely true, by the way – and we have an inalienable right to be the best in the world. Our record since 1966 would tend to disprove this theory, but it doesn’t stop unreconstructed patriots believing it.

Finally – and Carsley had a small taste of this after the Greece debacle – the way in which the fans and the media turn against an unsuccessful England manager would be a cautionary tale for anyone thinking of taking the job.

Just remember how Steve McClaren – “The Wally with the Brolly”, as described by the Daily Mail – or Graham Taylor, characterised as a turnip in The Sun, were treated at the end of their reigns. Even the sainted Bobby Robson, in the wake of a draw with Saudi Arabia in 1988, was greeted with a headline that read: “In the name of Allah, go.”

Are all the riches in Christendom worth the private torment and public scorn of a challenge that so many, eminently more qualified, have tried and ultimately failed?

What’s more, the FA’s idea that a post which Carsley is reluctant to take might appeal to Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola is an example of the fantastical thinking and unrealistic ambition that has got us where we are today. Who can blame Lee Carsley for thinking twice?
topics: England Football, Gareth Southgate, Lee Carsley

title: England are ignoring the Yorkshire Rodri reinventing his game at Bournemouth
body:
Bournemouth midfielder Lewis Cook talks to i about adapting to play in a new, more deep-lying midfield position under Andoni Iraola

Doing the 92 is Daniel Storey’s odyssey to every English football league club in a single season. The best way to follow his journey is by subscribing here

Lewis Cook couldn’t stop crying – a feeling he says he had never experienced before. The Yorkshire-born midfielder was lying on the touchline of a Championship stadium and everything he wanted had fallen apart.

What was worse: he knew exactly what had happened and what it meant for the next year of his life. The crack, the tingle, the numbness, the medics; it made sense in the worst way.

Let’s wind back. Cook had always been tipped for elite-level football. He is one of a select band of English players who have featured for their country at every level from Under-16s up to the seniors. He joined Leeds United at eight years old after being scouted in his local Tadcaster, breaking into the first team when still a kid.

Then-Leeds manager Neil Redfearn recalls watching Cook in those early days, grabbing senior professionals and making them close down.

The team were losing 4-1 against Ipswich and Cook was leading the team at 17.

“I could see Cooky captaining England one day,” Redfearn said.

Then, nothing seemed likely to stop him. Cook joined Premier League side Bournemouth in 2016, got his first call-up for the England senior squad in 2017, made his senior debut in March 2018 against Italy and was on the five-man standby list for the World Cup in Russia that summer.

When Jermain Defoe arrived at Bournemouth and trained with Cook, then aged 21, he compared him to Luka Modric for his ball retention and protection. Let’s call it high praise indeed, albeit Cook laughs and says: “I think he probably must have only seen a glimpse, and only once.”

When Cook wore the armband for England’s Under-20s in 2017, he became the first England player since Bobby Moore to lift a World Cup trophy. It’s fair to say that the Football Association liked him. He has not played for England since. Plenty else has happened.

In December 2018, during a home Premier League win over Huddersfield Town, Cook made an innocuous challenge and ruptured his right anterior cruciate ligament. He was 21. During his rehabilitation, Cook visited four different countries for specialist advice and managed to get back fit in nine months, a remarkable effort given the severity of the damage. His professional world began to rebuild.

And then it happened again, two and a half years later: same innocuous challenge on him, same knee, same injury, only this time double the emotional heft. And so we arrive back at the tears. Shortly before turning 25, Cook had started 81 league games in five seasons at Bournemouth.

“The second one was tough, because I knew what the road ahead looked like from the start,” he says.

“I know how hard it is for players to come back from serious injuries. It’s a tough place to move away from. But once the crying and emotions were done, at least I knew what I had to do.”

In 2022, Bournemouth released a documentary about Cook’s recovery. Towards the start of the documentary, Cook looks into the camera: “I am Lewis Cook and I am relentless.” That is what jumped out most to Bournemouth’s medical staff and the coaches, this burning desire to get fit, stay fit, be the best.

“The main reason for me making it was that I knew what was coming this time,” he says. “It was for other people, really. By creating a documentary, it might help one or two others to come through similar experiences.

“It was invasive, but it wasn’t every second of every day. Hopefully it gave some insight and support into the mental, emotional and physical side of recovery.”

Now 27, Cook’s career has clearly been revitalised by him staying fit – 2023-24 was the first of his career with more than 30 league starts – but also by the arrival of Andoni Iraola to Bournemouth. Under Gary O’Neil, Cook was left on the bench 15 times in 2022-23 as O’Neil often rotated between Joe Rothwell and Philip Billing in central midfield.

Under Iraola, whose first-choice pairing is Cook and Ryan Christie, Cook has flourished. Last season in the Premier League, Rodri was the only regular outfield starter to recover the ball more often and Cook made more interceptions than any other Premier League midfielder. In raw numbers of ball recoveries, everyone else in the top 10 are regular internationals.

At the end of last season, with squad places for the European Championship being rumoured and with Jordan Henderson’s place seemingly up for grabs, Bournemouth expected Football Association representation at the Vitality Stadium that never came.

Instead, England went for youth in Kobbie Mainoo and Adam Wharton; Angel Gomes has since been drafted in. There are plenty at Bournemouth who feel that Cook’s consistency has been overlooked.

“I look back on the age group teams with a huge amount of happiness,” he says.

“I made friends with some excellent teammates and was mentored by some fine coaches. It was a great time. It also showed me that there was a pathway right through to the top and that I was capable of moving through it.

“It’s an amazing achievement to play for your country even once – I was so delighted to be around it, for my family as much as me. If you’re starting regularly in the Premier League as an English player, you should always be working to get into the senior squad, because if you’re playing every week then you can’t be too far away from it. And you never know. I’ll never stop trying to get there.”

The answer, obvious and simple, is to keep doing what you’re doing. Cook is in the top five for tackles and interceptions in the Premier League this season. Iraola loves his work rate and loves the distance he covers. In Christie and Cook, he has two selfless central midfielders. This is a player who Eddie Howe once said ran more than he had ever seen in a player before.

“It’s a requirement in the Premier League now,” Cook says about fitness levels that have repeatedly impressed Bournemouth’s coaches.

“We get our statistical data for every game, and lots get said online, but every player has to be at a point where they are physically elite. If you aren’t, you get run over and outmuscled. It’s an incredibly intense league and everybody I come against is a physical beast.”

But what’s most interesting is how Cook is being developed by Iraola. He has taken on a role as progressive passer in Bournemouth’s midfield alongside the physical work. He has never assisted more than three goals in a league season but managed two against Southampton when I was in attendance a fortnight ago.

The number of shots per game have almost doubled from last season to this. He’s almost matched his total touches in the opposition penalty area from last season in seven matches.

“When I came through I was a centrally defensive midfielder, but at Leeds I’d play some games as a No 6, then I’d be a No 10, sometimes on the wing. At Bournemouth, apart from in the Championship, I’ve never really played deeper like I am now.

“I’ve always thought that I could chip in with goals and assists, but previously I perhaps didn’t understand that I had the licence to go and make a difference in the opposition penalty area when playing deep. With Ryan [Christie] often coming deeper now too, I can do that. Obviously whenever I score, the next few games I’ll be shooting more! But if there’s a new way that I can make a difference, I have to do that.”

Perhaps England will come knocking again, perhaps they won’t. Perhaps he suffers a little for playing at Bournemouth, a club for whom he was the first England international in their history. Perhaps he is now in an age bracket, at 27, where the thoughts of coaches turn to those five years younger.

All of that seems a little harsh, if true. Cook was touted for stardom. The journey became longer and harder because of injuries that have threatened the elite careers of others, and yet here he is playing the best football of his life.

But Cook is sanguine enough to avoid any bitterness. The only answer, his mantra on repeat, is to work harder and longer to become stronger. When you have been through the tears and fears of 2018 and 2021, you learn to appreciate football in the present rather than focus too much on what might be. The best thing to do is play and play and play.

“The only target I have is to rack up as many matches as I can,” he says.

“I’m a hugely competitive person. When I do something I want to be the best at it.

“When you finish football you have to know that you did everything you could. That’s the only way you can live without regrets. When I come to look back on this career, that number will be what I look back on: how many appearances did I have? Goals and assists are nice, and of course you want to win games and stay in the Premier League. But it’s about playing as many games as I can.”

Daniel Storey has set himself the goal of visiting all 92 grounds across the Premier League and EFL this season. You can follow his progress via our interactive map and find every article (so far) here
