title: FA Cup draw in full as Wrexham, Birmingham and more discover first-round ties
body:
Everything you need to know about the FA Cup first round including a meeting between rivals MK Dons and AFC Wimbledon

The FA Cup first round proper draw has thrown up a derby clash between AFC Wimbledon and MK Dons as all 48 League One and League Two sides discovered their opponents.

Wimbledon won the most recent clash between the two sides 3-0, but a place in the second round will add extra needle to an already-tense tie.

Teams earn £45,000 for winning first-round matches, while losers still bag £15,000, which can be hugely impactful money for non-league sides.

Birmingham, the highest-ranked club currently in the competition at the top of League One, visit Sutton United – the Blues spent more on transfers this summer than Sutton have in their history.

Meanwhile Wrexham, who sit two points behind the leaders in second, are faced with a visit to League Two outfit Harrogate Town.

All games will take place between Friday 1 and Monday 4 November and Premier League and Championship teams don’t enter the competition until the third round.

Northern Premier League West side Hednesford Town are the lowest-ranked team left in the draw, but they will have to beat Gateshead in a replay if they are to make the first round proper.

They have been drawn against either Northern Premier League Premier Division side Gainsborough Trinity or National League Boston United, meaning this will become one of three all non-league clashes.

One of Tonbridge Angels of the National League South facing Southern League Premier Division Central side Harborough Town are also guaranteed a spot in the second round.

The same goes for Altrincham or Solihull Moors, who will face last year’s giant killers Maidstone.
topics: FA Cup, Sports News

title: Ineos cancel Sir Alex Ferguson's multi-million pound Man Utd ambassador contract
body:
United's most successful manager becomes latest victim of swingeing job cuts with global club ambassador role set to end after a decade

Sir Alex Ferguson is the latest victim of Ineos’ cost-cutting drive at Manchester United, with the legendary manager informed his multi-million pound club ambassador contract has been cut.

Sir Jim Ratcliffe‘s Ineos, who have taken control of football operations after buying a 27.7 per cent stake in United last February, have been making widespread cuts to reduce costs at Old Trafford, including 250 jobs.

Ferguson was in charge of United from 1986 to 2013 and had been kept on as a global club ambassador and director since stepping down from the managerial hotseat.

While he will remain a non-executive director at the club for the foreseeable future, he will no longer be paid beyond the end of this season, according to The Athletic.

In the only official description of Ferguson’s ambassadorial role, in the club’s 2014 accounts, it was outlined that he received £2.16m for his services annually.

Ferguson will continue on the club’s football board, a predominantly ceremonial body, but not on the official board – the football board also featured Sir Bobby Charlton before his death last year.

The Scot’s departure is reportedly amicable and the decision was wholly taken by Ineos, with the Glazers happy to continue paying Ferguson for his lasting impact on the club and its wider finances.

By Sam Cunningham, chief football correspondent

Sir Alex Ferguson joins the long list of Manchester United employees deemed surplus to requirements since co-owners Ineos took control of football operations.

The swingeing job cuts have led to morale sinking and insiders fearing things will get worse before they get better.

Here’s what we know about the cull:

Read the full story of Ineos’ first 10 months at Manchester United here

Ferguson was reportedly informed of the decision by Ratcliffe face-to-face and he is expected to continue attending both home and away matches when he can.

This is one of many cuts made by the new regime in charge of the football side, with senior executives losing access to club credit cards, the tradition free travel to the FA Cup final being ended and the staff Christmas party cancelled.

title: Jonas Eidevall resigns as Arsenal Women head coach
body:
Eidevall leaves under increasing pressure after three years in the role

Jonas Eidevall has resigned as Arsenal Women’s head coach after three years at the club.

The Swede won two League Cups and reached the semi-finals of the Champions League during his tenure, but a poor start to the season leaves Arsenal sixth in the WSL with one win from four games.

His assistant Renee Slagers will replace him on an interim basis.

After Arsenal’s 2-1 defeat to Chelsea on Saturday following a disappointing week which included a 5-2 hammering by Bayern Munich and a 0-0 draw with Everton, Eidevall said: “I gave absolutely everything today in preparation for this game.

“You can see the players gave absolutely everything on the pitch.

“That’s the part you can control as a coach. It’s just focusing on the next match and I just need to focus on the things I can control.”

But it was not enough, with the 41-year-old jumping before he was pushed after increasing pressure on his position.

Graffiti appeared on Hornsey Road by the Emirates after the Chelsea defeat reading “Jonas Out”, a clear sign that Arsenal’s massive and engaged fanbase had begun to turn against the coach.

Sporting director Edu Gaspar said: “We thank Jonas for his commitment to the club and achievements here since joining us in 2021.

“We have great respect for the dedication and commitment he showed to our women’s first team and recognise the role he has played in the growth and development of Arsenal Women. We all wish him the very best for the future.

“Our focus will now turn to the process of appointing a new Head Coach, and in the meantime, supporting Renee, as she takes interim charge of the team starting with two important fixtures this week.”

And director of women’s football Clare Wheatley said: “We’d like to say a huge thank you to Jonas for his hard work and dedication to Arsenal Football Club over the past three years.

“Jonas has brought us back-to-back trophies in the last two seasons, together with many memorable moments on the pitch.

“We wish Jonas and his family the best of health, happiness and success for the future.

“We have full confidence in Renée to take responsibility for the team in the interim period.”
topics: Arsenal FC, Sports News, Women's Super League

title: Inside Newcastle's transfer revolution 'worth millions if you get it right'
body:
Other clubs may lead the way in the Premier League arms race, but thanks to AI the Magpies are starting to close the gap on their rivals

Ted Knutson was involved when Newcastle United pressed the button on the first stage of their data revolution.

Knutson is one of the founders and the former CEO of Statsbomb, the football analytics firm used by some of the game’s biggest clubs. The cutting edge company deals in the sort of big data that helps clubs win games and buy smart but enthusiasm for buying in their service felt somewhat lukewarm in the parsimonious Mike Ashley era.

Then came the 2021 takeover and a chance to “flip” Newcastle.

“It had actually been simmering away in the background for a while,” he tells i.

“Newcastle’s recruitment group had been really, really interested in moving in a different direction even before the takeover went through but we didn’t know if the club as a whole were going to flip.”

Knutson took a personal role in talks, working alongside the sales team to get it done. Suddenly, post-takeover, they found themselves pushing at an open door at St James’ Park with the message coming back that Newcastle under new ownership wanted their “best in class” policy to extend to data provision.

Internally there was talk of building a “world-class” data operation to match the Premier League’s best. Plans to beef up the data team – which were followed through with a hiring spree – meant a “multi-year” partnership with Statsbomb was swiftly given the green light.

“We knew they were really, really interested when the [takeover] went through so it was great to make it happen. It’s one of the ones we were really excited about because we always felt Statsbomb can make a big difference and Newcastle is a great club.”

Knutson takes i on a quick look around Statsbomb’s IQ platform, which Newcastle have had access to for the last three years. The high-tech software is a treasure trove of insights, eight years and thousands of hours of programming in the making.

Data parsed from 120 competitions played across the four corners of the globe are at your fingertips. Every game has as many as 3,400 match events but thanks to artificial intelligence and some very clever programmers, here it is presented in a way that almost anyone could understand it easily.

Want to find a player who could do the same things as Bruno Guimaraes to replace him if he ever gets sold? Within a few clicks, you can do just that – and then dig deeper into his performance data.

On the platform it’s also possible to build a “Newcastle algorithm” which identifies players by position from every corner of the globe who would suit their style of play, technical requirements and experience level. That sits in the background, continually updating and acting as the starting point for deciding which players Newcastle’s scouts should take a closer look at.

It sounds simple but the complex job is identifying the right data to match up with the characteristics your head coach wants.

When Knutson worked in a previous role at Brentford they had a simple way of starting the ball rolling. They asked their head coach to forget about budgets and identify the five players in world football who would fit their way of playing the best. From that game of fantasy football, they could then start to build a picture of the sort profile the manager wanted.

Statsbomb and other tools like it have become hugely important. Right down to Conference South clubs are using it – the cheapest package comes in at £5,000 per year – and owners have confided to Knutson the transfer market “basically runs on our product”.

“You need to have so much information about players now, you can’t do it with just your scouts anymore, it’s impossible,” Knutson explains.

For Newcastle the impact became obvious when they signed Guimaraes.

“The first player that was signed off the back of that deal – and they’d been wanting to do something like this for quite a while but they were sort of stuck under the former ownership – was Bruno [Guimaraes],” Knutson explains.

“I used to work at Brentford and we arranged managers and clubs into different categories about where they would tend to go recruit-wise. Eddie Howe had a reputation as a manager with a preference for working with players with Premier League experience and the signings in that first January after the Statsbomb deal followed that trend but then Bruno came in and he was a great signing: a dynamic, electric signing at a really decent price.

“That was really the switch because if you look at who was signed before that it was Chris Wood, Kieran Trippier, Dan Burn, Matt Targett. These are all English players or players with a long history at English clubs. But then you start to see them shopping a little further afield.

“They have the confidence from that point to be able to go out and say ‘OK we understand what these players look like locally, we understand what their performance profiles look like afar, now the gap is how will they perform over here?’

“I think Statsbomb allowed them to be more comfortable with international signings and also probably pushed them to be that way. They think ‘We’re paying for this thing, our scouts are not scouting this thing, let’s see if we can get the best of it’ because that’s what the ownership also suggested they wanted when we signed the deal.”

Knutson is no longer at Statsbomb, having overseen the sale of the firm to Hudl this summer.

It has been a while since he spoke to anyone at Newcastle too but one of his new ventures, a free transfer analysis newsletter called Transfer Flow, has got him back into the front line of analysing clubs’ recruitment policies by using cutting edge data.

The tagline of the project is “We tell you when your director of football should be fired” so it’s safe to say they’re not afraid of offering an opinion or two. So what of Newcastle’s last few transfer windows?

“I think the club are using data somewhat but some of these buys, it feels like they don’t quite make sense,” he says.

“For the prices paid there were many other players you could have got for that price and done better off.”

Given the changes at St James’ Park in the summer, perhaps some of those in high places at Newcastle felt similar.

When Paul Mitchell was handed carte blanche by the club’s owners in the close season to overhaul Newcastle’s recruitment structures and system, it certainly felt significant.

Mitchell has since claimed that the first few months in his new role were spent working to someone else’s blueprint, operating off lists and within structures constructed before he arrived. Those comments proved controversial – causing tension with Howe to briefly bubble over after the transfer window closed – but actually got to the nub of what he was brought in to do.

Mitchell talked about many things in his September interview but what fell under the radar a little bit was his revealing admission that the club’s scouting needed to be more “data-aligned”. That was, insiders say, an important point.

Did it indicate Newcastle are to embark on stage two of their data revolution?

“It’s clear things are going to change under Mitchell,” one industry insider familiar with Newcastle’s work predicted.

“Newcastle are not novices at data by any stretch of the imagination. They do some excellent work but – probably because others were first to it – they’re not right at the leading edge of some of this stuff at the moment.”

It is generally accepted that Brighton, Brentford and Liverpool lead the way in the Premier League’s data arms race. The Reds have spent millions bringing in data scientists to build models which give them an edge on recruitment.

One example provided to i is that they have built a system that allows them to analyse relative strength of different European leagues so they can assess more accurately than most whether a player starring in the Eredivisie, for example, will be able to successfully perform at the same level in the Premier League.

“That is worth millions and millions if you get it right,” a source told i.

Brentford and Brighton, meanwhile, benefit from having owners whose core businesses are about sports gambling so they collect their own data that is different from their rivals.

Brentford are “fully aligned” on data from recruitment to coaching and match analysis. It helps them notice things others aren’t: those quick, goalscoring starts that everyone has marvelled at this season are partly formulated around performance data gleaned from Premier League games.

Newcastle? The feeling is they’ve come a long way but are “probably somewhere in mid-table at the moment”. Data is part of the recruitment process but is it a big part of the club’s talent identification right now?

Industry sources speak highly of head of data and insights Michael Emmerson, formerly of Chelsea and promoted to the role in the summer of 2023, as someone who has significantly improved Newcastle’s offer.

Other sharp minds work at the club and one insider says data is “absolutely” presented as part of the recruitment process and “definitely part of the club’s due diligence” on signings. Visualisations – the data wheels you often see highlighting player weaknesses and strengths – are looked at and “people are being listened to” at Little Benton. They compared that to Manchester United where “there is a big team of really good people but no-one ever seems to take much notice of them”.

For Mitchell, making changes before January feels crucial after he criticised aspects of what the model looked like before. Based on his past roles he is likely to make data a more important part of talent ID at the start of the process rather than as a so-called “sense check” at the end of it. Given his intention to bring in younger players from “untapped markets” such as France’s Ligue 2 at better prices, that feels like something of a non-negotiable.

To back all this up i understands Newcastle are looking to make at least one significant recruitment hire shortly but a huge influx of staff is not expected. Instead tweaking the outlook or work flows of some of those already in the building to match with Mitchell’s plan may be the way forward. The view of scouts on the ground, it’s emphasised, will still be hugely valued and important.

Looking at it from the outside, Knutson interprets Mitchell’s appointment as a clear signal that the ownership wanted structural change at St James’ Park.

He has been impressed by Mitchell’s CV – “He’s a good talker, he built a good team in a complicated situation at Monaco” – but feels it “may take him some time to solidify everything he wants to do”. The internal politics at Newcastle worry him but he says the club’s direction of travel feels clear.

“Even if they were not discussing things openly, the fact that they chose to bring in Paul Mitchell after Dan Ashworth suggests the ownership really want this model,” Knutson says.

“And so even if they’re not openly saying it, it’s clear that they don’t think the manager or head coach should have all the power and they need someone who does things longer term. Maybe they want that to be Eddie but they clearly don’t think that’s the case otherwise they wouldn’t have brought in Paul Mitchell, they’d have solidified Howe’s position.

“If Mitchell isn’t the guy, they’ve already made the choice that someone is the guy and this is the structure they want to do. Some of that is inherent reading into the actions of the owners, even if they’re not saying it.”

Is it a slap down for Eddie Howe? Knutson doesn’t necessarily see it that way, arguing a manager with “full power” at a club is becoming vanishingly rare.

Perhaps, he says, Newcastle’s summer decisions were about reversing that drift with Howe.

“Look, the head coach is a person whose job is inherently short-term,” he says.

“They’re judged every single week on results so their interests are in many ways significantly divorced from the owners, who are likely to want to limit losses.

“There are a bunch of misaligned incentives in football that Newcastle – and a lot of other clubs in the Premier League – are dealing with.

“There’s maybe five teams that have it figured out while the rest are scrambling to minimise the amount of money they are losing all the time or to try and get the on-pitch product really good but are dealing with massive amounts of waste like Chelsea are.”

On Saturday Newcastle will get a jarring reminder of the difficulties of getting the recruitment policy right when Yankuba Minteh, sold in the summer to solve a Profitability and Sustainability Rules (PSR) problem, lines up for Brighton.

Knutson is in disbelief that the club let him go.

“If they’re looking for a right winger they had the right person! They literally had him,” he says.

“It’s the biggest fumble they could make. It literally might have been better to be docked points than lose him.

“They flipped their money and got a 4x profit on it which is really good in most circumstances but Minteh’s profile is one that looks like he might be a top 10 right winger in the world in the next three years. Brighton clearly think that because they have him in the first XI.

“I was shocked by how much I love this kid because of his control inside of the box. You were watching [Jamal] Musiala at the Euros at the time who had that element of being impossible to touch in the box because you don’t know which way he will go, he can finish quite well and the fact he is left footed makes him super valuable by himself.

“Now what I expected Newcastle to do was keep him and as long as Eddie didn’t ship him out – which would have been a mistake, but we’ve seen that before with Saliba at Arsenal who was out on loan too long – I expected him to come in the last 25 minutes and really change the game, especially against the tougher teams you could stretch them.”

Given Newcastle’s PSR problems, they didn’t feel there was anywhere else to turn during their frantic June scramble to raise funds. And that’s part of the problem with recruitment – even when you lean into the data, emotion and optics can be just as important to Premier League clubs.

“If you had to make a choice I think selling [Anthony] Gordon was probably the right one. But it’s hard, it’s extremely difficult to pilot all this stuff and find the right path,” Knutson admits.

“The fact [Michael] Edwards and his team at Liverpool were able to do it for so long was laudable. Some groups do it once and then can’t repeat it.

“If you can repeat it, that’s when you know you’ve got a good recruitment group.”

His advice to Newcastle? Whoever is identifying overseas talent needs to be listened to.

“Their international signings seem sharp,” he says.

“The two names rumoured in the summer for centre-back from overseas – Malick Thiaw [AC Milan] and Antonio Silva [Benfica] – seemed really good.

“Thiaw is raw but physically suited to the Premier League. He needs to read the game a bit better but the kid from Portugal they had on their shortlist: that dude looked like one of the best centre backs in the world.

“Benfica sell really high but they’ve kept him. Now you get to look at him a little bit longer but he looks like one of the best cultured centre backs around, and a threat at set pieces too.

“You have to give credit to the recruitment team, the names they are rumoured to be linked with are really good.”

title: Ailish Tynan is a tour de force in ENO's The Turn of the Screw
body:
The cast in Benjamin Britten’s chilling opera The Turn of the Screw is brilliant - and director Jessica Bywater adds a layer of ambiguity to the story

Benjamin Britten’s The Turn of the Screw, based on Henry James’s ghost story, is – usually – a taut, tense and terrifying opera, concentrated into just seven singers and an orchestra of 13.

ENO’s new production, directed and designed by Isabella Bywater, is blessed with a splendid cast and a raft of mostly strong ideas as the Governess tries to save her two young pupils, Miles and Flora, from the vengeful spirits of their deceased abusers, the servant Peter Quint and the former governess Miss Jessel.

Bywater solves some problems but creates others in having the Governess experience the drama as a series of flashbacks from her bed in a psychiatric hospital. Projected images unfurl over her, moving through a grand country house and its grounds as rapidly as dreams.

One stroke of inspiration is the sheer ordinariness of the ghostly villains. Rather than pantomime ghouls, here Miss Jessel, magnificently sung by Eleanor Dennis, seems straight out of a Virginia Woolf novel, while Quint, the icily clear Robert Murray, is a caretaker plodding about in a brown coat, revealing his true self only when assaulting Miss Jessel on her desk.

As the Governess, soprano Ailish Tynan carries the show in a real tour de force. Her flashbacks depict her as mumsy and slightly out-to-lunch, her present as ploddingly institutionalised; throughout, her performance is generous, detailed and sung with ideal sympathy and warmth.

The child soloists singing Miles and Flora have their work cut out in the cavernous Coliseum, but Jerry Louth and Victoria Nekhaenko rise to the challenge splendidly, energetic and strong-toned (they alternate across the run with Nicolai Flutter and Holly Hylton). Gweneth Ann Rand is a dignified Mrs Grose and the tenor Alan Oke has a brief star turn in the Prologue.

The conductor Duncan Ward, making his ENO debut, leads a musical interpretation that, perhaps surprisingly, milks the piece for its most beautiful aspects: the 13 players from ENO’s mutilated orchestra (earlier this year made redundant and rehired for seven months of the year) offer rhapsodically phrased solos that contrast intriguingly with the social strictures evoked on stage, almost as if the score becomes the story’s subtext.

Speaking of subtexts, though, the staging seems to imply – with succinct details such as Quint mopping the hospital floor – that the Governess has imagined everything.

It would be a much more frightening story if she had not. Underneath, this is a tale about not just a paedophile, but the ghost of a paedophile, surely the worst supernatural bogey in British culture. Seventy years after the opera’s premiere, perhaps it is time to stop being coy about that.

To 31 October (eno.org)
topics: Arts Reviews, Classical Music, Opera, Reviews

title: Mr Loverman cast: Who stars in the BBC show and what is it about?
body:
Mr Loverman is a story of love, secrets and lies told through the life of Caribbean family man and Hackney resident Barry Walker

A groundbreaking story of love, secrets and lies comes to the BBC this week in the dapper form of Mr Loverman.

Barrington Jedidiah Walker (Lennie James), known to his friends as Barry, is a 74-year-old family man from Antigua, renowned for his fondness for retro suits and larger-than-life personality in his Hackney neighbourhood.

But Barry has a secret.

He has been in a long-term relationship with his best friend and soulmate Morris (Ariyon Bakare) for 60 years.

Based on the the novel of the same name by Booker Prize winner Bernardine Evaristo, the eight-part show chronicles Barry’s life as he faces difficult choices about how to live his final chapters.

Evaristo has described it as “a multi-layered exploration of sexuality and forbidden and hidden love and desire; the pressures of familial duty, sacrifice dynamics and secrets; conformity versus owning your individuality, and Caribbean masculinity and homophobia”.

Adapted for television by the man behind The Outlaws and Noughts+Crosses, Nathaniel Price and directed Hong Khaou, it stars Line of Duty actor Lennie James and three time Olivier Award-winning actress Sharon D Clarke.

Mr Loverman draws on a cast of well-known faces to British television audiences.

James leads the cast as Barrington Jedidiah Walker (Barry), a married family man leading a double life.

The British actor, who was born in Nottingham to parents from Trinidad, said he had been waiting for this part to come up since the book was first published in 2013.

“Any actor who saw and read Barry would like to play him as a character”, he said, “He’s everything that would excite an actor – complicated, funny, a good dresser and harsh.

“He’s also a contradiction – loyal but disloyal, a good and bad husband, a good and bad father, a good and bad man.

“He loves and hates in equal measure.”

The 59-year-old actor rose to fame playing Morgan Jones in the television drama series The Walking Dead and starred as DCI Tony Gates in BBC series Line of Duty. He also appeared in medical drama Critical and played Nelson Rowe in the drama Save Me.

Bakare plays Morris De la Roux, the best friend and long-term lover of Barry.

Discussing taking on the role, he said: “When I got the part of Morris, I went back to read the book again and I was just so touched by their relationship.

“You can understand this journey of these two men who are from Antigua, a country where it’s illegal to be gay, homosexuality is illegal – it has only just become legal over the past few years.

“So you understand why they hide their love for so long and how far they’ve gone to do that – marrying other people and having kids.”

Londoner Bakare, 53, played Dr Ben Kwarme in the long-running BBC series Doctors and has also appeared in Good Omens and Carnival Row.

He played Lord Boreal in the BBC adaptation of Philip Pullman’s trilogy His Dark Materials.

Sharon D Clarke plays Carmel Walker, the long-suffering wife of Barry and mother to Donna and Maxine. She is convinced her husband has been cheating on her with other women.

Three-time Olivier Award-winning actress Clarke played Lola Griffin in medical drama Holby City.

The 58-year-old, who was born in north London, has also appeared in Doctor Who and Showtrial.

She won the Oliviers for her stage roles in plays The Amen Corner, Caroline, or Change and Death of a Salesman. She was appointed an MBE for her services to dramas in 2017. The remaining cast includes:

Author Evaristo summed up Mr Loverman as “a novel about the consequences of not being true to yourself”.

She added: “More specifically, it’s about a 74-year-old gay Londoner, originally from Antigua, who is a married father and grandfather, who has hid his sexuality his whole life.”

Barry Walker has been married to Carmel for 50 years, they have two daughters Maxine and Donna and a grandson Daniel. Carmel has suspected for a long time her husband’s heart belongs elsewhere.

But she doesn’t know Barry has been in a secret, passionate affair with his best friend and soulmate Morris since they were teenagers in the Caribbean.

Now in his twilight years, Barry wants to spend his remaining days with true love. However, such a decision as ramifications for everyone in his family, not just Carmel.

Mr Loverman premieres on BBC One at 9pm on Monday 14 October, with the second of episode of the eight-part series following at 9.30pm. The remaining six episodes will be shown weekly on successive Mondays.

For those who can’t wait, all episodes of the show will be available on BBC iPlayer from 6am on 14 October.

title: Who was voted off of Strictly Come Dancing last night?
body:
Week 4 in the Strictly ballroom and the first 10s of the series made an appearance - but it was also time to hang up their dancing shoes for one celebrity

Strictly Come Dancing is now in full swing as week four brought with it all the high and lows of the dancefloor viewers have come to expect.

Model Tasha Ghouri and her professional partner Aljaž Škorjanec were riding high at the top of the leaderboard with a clutch of 10s, the first of the series, for their Charleston.

But for the only other couple performing a Charleston at the weekend, presenter Nick Knowles and his dance partner, Luba Mushtuk, it was a very different story.

We take a look at who nimbly side-stepped the dance-off this week and who waltzed straight in.

It was not Nick Knowles’ night on the dancefloor on Sunday.

The presenter of shows such as DIY SOS and Real Rescues found himself in the dance-off after missing last week’s show due to a knee injury.

The 62-year-old has been plagued by bad luck during his time on Strictly, having also sustained a shoulder injury before the second show.

On Sunday night, he faced Shayne Ward in the dance-off.

He performed his Charleston to “Rain On The Roof” from the Paddington 2 soundtrack with his dance partner Luba Mushtuk for a second time.

But it failed to impress the judges and he became the third celebrity to leave the show.

Speaking afterwards, he said: “I’ve really, really been surprised by how much I’ve loved doing it and by two things that happen.

“One is how much you care each week and the other is how much you don’t want to let down your partner.”

He praised his professional dance partner Luba and his fellow competitors, adding: “There are some amazing dancers up there, and I will love watching the rest of the series.”

Joining Knowles in the dance-off at the weekend was former The X Factor winner and actor Shayne Ward.

He scored 30 for his cha cha to “Ain’t No Love (Ain’t No Use)” by Sub Sub feat. Melanie Williams but nonetheless found himself in the bottom two following the public vote.

After both couples had danced again, judges Craig Revel Horwood, Motsi Mabuse and Anton Du Beke all chose to save Shayne and Nancy, with head judge Shirley Ballas agreeing with their decision.

After the departure of Nick Knowles at the weekend and singer Toyah Willcox and Olympic swimmer Tom Dean in previous weeks, there are now 12 couples left in the competition.

They are:

Week 4 in the Strictly ballroom saw the first 10s of the season make an appearance.

Model Tasha Ghouri and her professional partner Aljaž Škorjanec scored a near perfect 39, with 10s from Motsi, Anton and head judge Shirley, for their Coachella festival-inspired Charleston to “Unhealthy” by Anne-Marie, Shania Twain.

It was a good night, too, for opera singer Wynne Evans and dance partner Katya Jones, who came second on the leaderboard with 34 points for their tango to “Money, Money, Money” by ABBA.

EastEnders star Jamie Borthwick and his professional partner Michelle Tsiakkas wowed the judges with their salsa to “Danza Kuduro” by Don Omar ft. Lucenzo, also scoring 34 points.

And Gladiator and former Olympian Montell Douglas received 33 points with dance professional Johannes Radebe for their Viennese waltz to “Nobody Gets Me” by SZA.

Sitting mid-table were Shayne Ward and Nancy Xu, JB Gill and Amy Dowden and Chris McCausland and Dianne Buswell with 30 points and Pete Wicks and Jowita Przystal with 29 points, Sam Quek MBE and Nikita Kuzmin with 28 points, and Sarah Hadland and Vito Coppola with 27 points.

But languishing near the bottom of the leaderboard were former footballer Paul Merson and Karen Hauer with 23 points after their quickstep to “I Won’t Dance” by Fred Astaire and GP and i columnist Dr Punam Krishan and Gorka Márquez with their jive to “2 Be Loved (Am I Ready)” by Lizzo, scoring just 20 points.

title: We just don't trust Strictly anymore
body:
As someone who relies on Strictly during the winter months the way others might rely on a 10,000 lux SAD lamp, I had optimistically hoped that once Dave Arch and his orchestra had tuned up and southern Hertfordshire’s spray tanners had been conscripted and Claudia Winkleman had peeked wryly and reassuringly through her fringe, we would be able to start afresh and enjoy it with impunity.

I have maintained, throughout its grim summer of scandal, throughout the allegations and the investigations, and despite dark clouds over the future of this series, that come autumn we would once again be transported to somewhere happy and special and safe while the contestants gurned through their Charlestons or blithely Quickstepped to “Puttin’ On the Ritz”.

The BBC would clean up its act – it has to, this is Strictly – get some chaperones in, introduce some new professionals, stop the rot, and we would allow ourselves to be cocooned until Christmas in this joyful, playful little world where I, at least, belong. Many claimed it was doomed, that the magic was lost for ever. That is a future inconceivable to me.

Obviously, I was naïve. Because our fixation with Strictly – which has for many years been hysterical and totally disproportionate for a celebrity dance competition – has reached the point where it is no longer merely backstage rumours that threaten to derail the show but now every episode is dissected for evidence of the production’s institutionalised toxicity. Everything that is not slick, planned or perfect is proof of unsavoury behaviour, of souring relationships, of another brewing scandal it cannot afford.

I’m referring this time to opera singer and presenter Wynne Evans and his professional dance partner Katya Jones, who have reassured the public that they were joking around when, on Saturday night’s show, cameras captured first her moving his hand from her waist, across which it appeared to be creeping, and then later her snubbing his high-five and scowling at him.

Watch the videos for yourself – everyone else is. In fact I can currently see in the corner of my eye the clips being replayed on ITV News, a sign that, when it comes to Strictly, the kind of thing that might once have made a tabloid gossip item is now elevated to an incident of national importance.

The BBC says its welfare team has investigated the apparent tension between them and will not be proceeding further. Jones said in an Instagram post that “even the idea that it made me feel uncomfortable or offended me in any way is complete nonsense”.

And Evans said on his Monday morning Radio Wales show that he was heartbroken. “Katya and I are really, really close; we’re really good friends and, on Saturday night, we made a stupid joke. It was a stupid joke that went wrong. We thought it was funny. It wasn’t funny. It has been totally misinterpreted.”

Tricky one. Either you believe them, move on and everyone keeps dancing – because after all, these couples literally have to touch each other all the time and develop intense relationships quickly and there may well have been nothing out of the ordinary in either party’s demeanour.

Or, like those in the more vocal corners of social media, you believe that these denials are the result of some hasty diktat from a panicking production executive on high trying to avoid another PR disaster concerning men’s treatment of women on this programme; that we’ve heard of “rifts” between couples before that, too often, have indeed ended up being signs of something more sinister; or at the very least that Jones is the victim of a handsy bloke who is rightly being called out on the greatest and most public stage possible, the BBC’s flagship family show.

The brief footage is uneasy, and certainly awkward. And though I do think that as an engine of popular entertainment and with incredible influence, scrutiny of Strictly is well-justified, the only conclusion us spectators can draw from all this has nothing to do with the relationship between Wynne and Jones but about ourselves: we just don’t trust Strictly anymore.

No matter how well-oiled the machine or how sparkly the dancefloor or how reliably crap are Tess’s jumpsuits, the famous “magic” of this show relies, in the end, solely upon its audience’s belief in it as a place of secure, escapist delight.

This year, we watch in the knowledge of how much of that escapism and delight has been under false pretences. And that is something that will take a lot more than a few weeks of jolly group numbers to forget.
topics: Strictly Come Dancing, Subscribers

title: Lennie James: 'Did I enjoy the Walking Dead fame? No'
body:
Acting can, and invariably does, make unreasonable demands upon those who do it for a living. They might, for example, be required to bulk up, slim down, work with animals, or grow an unfetching moustache. Increasingly, they might have to perform in front of a green screen, surrounded by strategically placed tennis balls. All of it constitutes hard work, which is why they get the big bucks. But for Lennie James in his new BBC drama Mr Loverman, the craft demanded something that made him confront a fully existential discomfort: ageing up. James is 58; the character he plays on screen is in his mid-seventies. Rarely has James felt closer to the grave.

“It was weird, definitely,” he says, “but they did make me into a much better-looking older man than I will probably end up being, so I didn’t mind too much.” He smiles. “I was talking to an old friend of mine from drama school recently, and he reminded me that when we were doing A Winter’s Tale back when we were 21, we were playing men at 60 who had to age into their mid-eighties. It took a lot of effort back then. It took a lot less effort now.”

Mr Loverman is an adaptation of the 2013 novel by Bernardine Evaristo, about Barrington Jedediah Walker, a man who has been nursing a secret for much of his life. For 50 years, he has been married to Carmel, and is the father of two grown-up daughters.

If his wife has been deeply unhappy with him for a long time now, then it is with good reason. She believes him to be a carousing drunk and serial philanderer – which, granted, he is.

But what she doesn’t realise is that his philandering takes place with men rather than women, and with one man in particular: his lifelong friend Morris, with whom he has been in love since both were teenagers in Antigua.

Amongst this older generation, homosexual proclivity is the love that dare not speak its name. And so Barrington has long been required to hide in plain sight, causing not just great pain to him and to Morris – who wants nothing more than to set up home with Barrington, and, in these otherwise enlightened times, to marry him – but to his wife and children.

James does a terrific job of making the complicated, infuriating but fundamentally humane Barrington live, breathe, ache and yearn. Over eight episodes, we see him both as a carefree young man, and as a confused and tormented elderly one, for ever forced to keep the defining part of himself hidden away.

“The important thing for me was not to play his age but to play the person,” James says. “There needed to be a sense of consistency throughout. So we see him in his thirties, and his forties, but he was the same man then as he is now, in his seventies.”

Briefly, James pauses to frown. He raises his glasses to pinch at the bridge of his nose, and says: “I’m not hugely good at speaking about my technique, but when you act old age, it’s not just about the body – the knees, the back, the neck – it’s, it’s more general…”

In other words, the 74-year-old Barrington we see on screen, as performed by a man two decades his junior who has been rendered elegantly grey and skeletally stooped, brings a fully lived life to bear on the physical exterior?

“Exactly! I wanted to make him truthful, inside and out. Barrington may be keeping a secret, but he is someone who never wanted to be ignored in life. He is always putting on a show.”

Lennie James has been one of the UK’s best character actors for several decades now. Born in Nottingham in 1964, he was placed in care at the age of 10 after his mother died, and was later raised in south London. He often says that he was initially drawn to drama school because he liked a girl already in attendance there, but he took to it in a way that only cliché can best sum up: like a duck to water.

“It was never something I could even dream about doing, acting – not coming from my background,” he says, “but I loved it. I always loved it.”

He has been working consistently since the early 90s, his most prominent role coming in 2012 when he played a fatally bent cop in the first series of Line of Duty. In America, he became above-the-line famous after spending 10 years on the show The Walking Dead, which, he earnestly points out, “was the biggest television show in the world”. It precipitated a move from London to Los Angeles with his wife and three daughters, and he now divides his time between the two. When I ask whether he enjoyed the fame the zombie show brought, he shakes his head. “No. It was an experience, certainly, but all that has never been my aim.”

This is perhaps because James has always been someone who has taken his position, and the opportunities that have arisen from it, seriously. If he was going to remain an actor, he was going to do it well, and properly.

“I had some good advice when I was young that careers are built as much on what you say no to as what you say yes to,” he relays. “When I first started, I was aware of how quickly Black actors could be stereotyped, and so a lot of my effort in navigating things that came my way meant first considering what my family would think if they saw me do it.

“There was also this strong feeling within my community about what I, and other Black actors, were doing was representing them, and was saying something about our people, our culture and race. I was always very mindful about that.”

He has certainly navigated his path successfully, and with substance. James’ very presence has a tendency to elevate anything he is in, and if his roles tend to gravitate towards a certain sober seriousness, then he can also lift the mood simply with a beaming smile, which cracks his face open to reveal light and warmth.

In Mr Loverman, he gets to show both sides. He also shows a lot of flesh, for this is a drama that doesn’t just talk about forbidden love but spies on it, too. There are several sex scenes between Barrington and Morris.

“We had an intimacy coach, and that made a huge difference,” he says. “It’s hard to stay in character when you’re doing a sex scene, simply because you yourself feel so awkward about it.

“Back in the day, you’d just be given a shot of brandy or whiskey to help you get through it. But the intimacy coach introduced the degree of consent, and a degree of conversation. It helped.

“Playing Barrington,” he adds, “was challenging for many reasons, but I think he has been, for me, one of the most rewarding fellas whose shoes I’ve been lucky enough to put on.”

‘Mr Loverman’ starts tonight on BBC One at 9pm

title: A blood test told me I have high cortisol- is this the secret to curing my anxiety?
body:
Cortisol is the body's main stress hormone. Could reducing its production make us less anxious and tired? Eleanor Peake finds out

Stressed, burned out, anxious, gaining weight, sleeping badly. If social media is to be believed, these common problems can be blamed on one thing: cortisol – the body’s “stress hormone”.

Type the hormone into Instagram and all sorts of hacks appear, from cortisol-reducing workouts to cortisol-reducing recipes. Then there’s “cortisol face”. Apparently puffy cheeks are no longer a skincare issue but a direct result of too much of the stress hormone pumping through our blood.

Like most women, I sometimes have a puffy face. I am often tired and anxious. More than might be considered normal? It’s hard to say. Perhaps I am suffering from the dreaded high cortisol? It is a tempting thought. It would be nice to have something on which to blame all my woes.

According to a 2023 survey, 73 per cent of the UK population felt anxious in the previous two weeks, with 20 per cent feeling anxious most or all of the time. Are we all suffering from a chronically high cortisol crisis? Or are we all desperately looking for something simple to blame our stress on?

Cortisol is the body’s main stress hormone, produced by the adrenal glands. It has an important role in controlling metabolism and blood pressure, but chronically high levels are bad for your health – having been associated with weight gain and memory problems in research.

Naturally, with all the hype around cortisol, it’s never been easier to get your levels tested. So, I visited the London Regenerative Institute, an exclusive, private clinic by the Thames, to check mine out, via a blood test that costs £104.

Like testosterone, cortisol is a natural hormone in the body, with a natural cycle. Throughout the day it rises and falls. In the early hours of the morning, at around 3am, it begins to spike naturally, reaching its peak level half an hour after we wake up – giving us energy to get up and go.

From mid-morning, it slowly starts to decline in preparation for a good night’s sleep. But there are lots of things that can spike it throughout the day: a hangover, coffee, sugar or a stressful morning.

On my way to the appointment, I could sense that my stress levels were higher than usual. Perhaps unsurprising: I was downing an americano while fighting my way through a busy Tube station.

The previous night, I’d had a few glasses of white wine with friends, and so my sleep had not been at its best. I also hate blood tests. As I sat down in the luxurious doctor’s chair, my heart raced. Seconds later, the nurse extracted my sample.

The next day my results were in. I did indeed have a high amount of cortisol in my blood: 845 nmol/L. The average for that time in the morning is between 133 nmol/L and 537 nmol/L according to the clinic. Şebnem Ünlüişler, the London Regenerative Institute’s genetic engineer, tells me that this could be due to a lack of sleep, high anxiety, or possibly an infection in the body that I might not be aware of. To get a better picture, I would need to be tested again next week to see if this is a chronic issue.

But Dr Rachel Sumner, a senior research fellow and psychobiologist at Cardiff Met University, believes cortisol tests can be misleading. “That level of cortisol, without any other biological or behavioural context, is difficult to assess as ‘high’ or ‘low,” she says.

“It could depend on the last time you had some coffee or tea before the measure was taken, how much sleep you had the night before, and the last time you ate. It could also be affected by really specific things from that day, like whether you’re afraid of needles.” Other factors also include the amount of exercise I might have had that day, and whether I have a hormonal syndrome such as Polycystic Ovary Syndrome ( I do.)

This makes me feel better. “High levels of cortisol are often triggered by stress, but stress causes all sorts of different hormones and neurotransmitters to be released into the brain and body. Cortisol is just one of the hormones that is released,” Sumner explains. “It doesn’t necessarily cause the feelings that we associate with stress, such as a racing heart or sweaty palms. They’re more caused by adrenaline and noradrenaline.”

Wellness influencers often link high cortisol with feeling anxious, but that is rarely the case. “The types of processes that cortisol is involved in tend to take longer to go through the body. The signs tend to be a lot more subtle than the really big notifications that we get when we feel stressed,” says Sumner. She doubts whether cortisol would even cause a puffy face. “It’s very unlikely that the hormone would create changes that you would be able to visibly see.”

Cortisol face, then, is likely a myth – this symptom is seen in certain rare medical conditions such as the hormonal disorder Cushing’s syndrome, but not in healthy people who are a little stressed. But that’s not to say high cortisol can never be damaging.

“If we’re chronically stressed – and by chronic stress, we mean those types of stresses which don’t have an end, and which tend to cause pressure in a lot of different areas of our life over a really long period – [it] can damage cortisol regulation,” says Sumner. “Signs of this would be the onset of atherosclerosis, and abdominal fat [where the rest of the body is slim]. But they take a really long time.”

Reassuringly, it is rare to have a chronic cortisol condition. “If, for example, you happen to have really, really, high level of cortisol, a one-off test would be able to diagnose that. But to be honest, most people would know. You would be experiencing many other physiological and psychological symptoms,” says Sumner.

And high cortisol isn’t always a bad thing. “Most of the things that cortisol does is help provide energy to your brain itself. Cortisol instigates the release of fats and sugars into the bloodstream to allow that energy for us to fight or run away,” she says. Sometimes high cortisol can actually be an indicator of good physiological function. “When people are chronically stressed, we often observe a ‘blunting effect’ in cortisol levels,” she explains.

If we experience prolonged stress, in times of sudden danger, the cortisol produced by the body is actually lower than it should be, because the body is already in a prolonged state of stress. Spiking cortisol is a sign that the body is responding to stress in a healthy way.

To get a clearer idea about whether my high cortisol reading means I am under chronic stress, I would have to have my levels regularly tested. Ünlüişler advises that in the meantime, I take ashwagandha supplements, a herbal plant medicine, to reduce any possible anxiety in my body. Sumner supports this.

“Ashwagandha does show promise in regulating a variety of hormonal functions and has been used for thousands of years in Ayurvedic medicine for a variety of purposes,” she says. However, there is currently a lack of sufficient data from robust clinical trials to be able to tell how much impact it may have.

For those worried about their cortisol, Sumer advises frequent exercise and spending time in nature. “One of the other best ways that we can help regulate our physiological stress response is by exercise. Our fight or flight is geared towards it. Evolution created us to mobilise at a moment’s notice. Exercises that involve cardiovascular activity, or muscle yielding are really helpful in regulating bodily functions. Not just cortisol, but loads of other hormones too.”

Before my test, I was concerned that I might be suffering from constantly high cortisol. My puffy cheeks, I believed, were all the proof I needed. But it seems I have been taken in by my Instagram algorithm. Like much of our biology, cortisol is a complex and sensitive hormone that the body needs to function healthily.

And my high blood test result doesn’t mean I am chronically stressed. Neither can you diagnose dangerously high cortisol with just a puffy face and a bad night’s sleep. Ironically, our quest to reduce stress might just be increasing it.
topics: Anxiety, Features, Health, Stress, Wellbeing, Wellness

title: I'm 55, my kids have flown the nest, my wife is busy working, and I feel lost
body:
As i's Agony Uncle, Kenny Mammarella-D’Cruz - who has spent three decades listening to men talk about their feelings - gives his advice to a man struggling with his empty home

I have spent my whole life nurturing others, including my mother, aunt, eldest sister, wife and daughters. I’m 55, my youngest daughter has just left for university and I’m feeling a bit lost. I miss the house being noisy with their friends around and feel like the best days of my life are over.

My wife is career-driven and works longer hours than me; I only really work to earn money to enjoy life with the kids, though my colleagues are nice enough.

My wife and I lead quite independent lives and she doesn’t seem phased by this new stage, though she does seem busier than usual. We usually spend time together as a family or with friends, rather than the two of us together, so we haven’t really connected since dropping my youngest daughter off.

I’m happy and relieved the kids both sound like they’re having a great time – and I am thankful for social media and how easy it is to stay in touch – I just feel a bit like I’ve lost the most important role of my life.

Am I alone in feeling this way?

**

I’m not surprised you’re feeling lost: your role as primary caregiver is one of infinite value. It has defined your life over the past 18 years and you have filled your home with love. So no, you’re certainly not alone in feeling like this.

Rather than losing the most important role in your life, I’d celebrate a wonderful phase passing and look forward to the next phase of sharing your lives with your children through their stories and your own. Much as it may hurt, this is the time – as your letter suggests you recognise – to support them from afar as they enjoy newfound freedom and give yourself space to find what might bring you alive in your own life.

You have the time to take stock of your life. You sound like a man with a lot of love to give; now your children have gone, where’s it going to go? I’d recommend that the first, important thing for you to learn – perhaps for the first time in your life – is to share that love with yourself. To recognise, acknowledge and meet your own needs. To follow your curiosity and do things because you’re interested in them.

I’d take this opportunity to ask yourself about the shape of your life to come so you can shape it deliberately. Do you want to continue working? Would you consider starting a business? How would you like to express your creative energy? Where might you develop your skills?

Would you like to develop casual friendships with your colleagues? Do you have old friends you’d like to reconnect with? Do you have forgotten hobbies you’d like to re-explore? Sometimes one partner will feel the loss of children from the family home more starkly than the other: I wonder whether this is happening in your relationship?

It sounds like your wife is quite happy with the progress in your children’s lives, as they have a great time in university – and she’s busy getting on with her career. She may be grateful for the space to concentrate more on her work and the things she likes to do, but you won’t know this unless you ask her.

What’s interesting to me is that you seem to have spent your whole life nurturing women and I’ll bet you’ve got incredible empathy. I wonder what your relationship to men is and whether you have male friends, or prefer the company of women? I ask this because it feels as if there’s a hole in your need for connection.

I wonder whether at some level you’d like your wife to fill this hole. I’d caution that while this is an opportunity for you to reset your relationship, it is not a time to put all your social and emotional needs on her, rather than taking responsibility for them yourself. The newfound independence of children leaving would be somewhat stifled by a newly dependent partner.

Having said that, I hear what you say about spending time together only with other couples or for family occasions. Maybe your wife’s waiting for you to invite her to connect in whatever way you feel drawn to. It might be a good idea for you to have some nights out where you chat together and explore the next phase in your lives and in your relationship.

If you’re missing the noise of full home, do you want to start being more sociable and having friends around more regularly? Or perhaps get a dog both for companionship and the community among owners? Did you used to travel or play sports together before having children? Do you have common interests you could discover, or rediscover, together?

Have you asked your wife why she’s so busy at the moment? I’d recommend asking her straight if she wants to spend more time with you or if she still wants to develop her career? At least then you know the lay of the land, rather than hoping she might want one thing or avoiding asking directly. If your wife’s happy with her career focus, then carve out a space as a couple that includes both your needs for connection and space for you both to grow.

If you sense she is reluctant to spend time with you then I would recommend asking whether this is about her career, and whether she feels she needs to meet a milestone before she’s ready to change gear, or whether the issue is aspects of your relationship? If it is the latter, I would recommend that you seek good relationship counselling and take the time to explore your needs and unpick any unfulfilling habits or misunderstandings that might have built up over the past two decades.

But whatever the dynamic within your relationship, this is also a time to focus on yourself. While many parents neglect themselves to a certain extent, I wonder whether you’ve ever recognised your own needs when you’ve played the role of supporter, looking out for others. It might take practice to recognise what you’d like to do.

Now is a time when you can also flip this. As a parent-of-adults, ask yourself: “Who do I no longer need to be?” As you let go of those aspects of your life, new opportunities will surely show up for you to explore. As you’ve raised your children and tended to their needs, now you can inspire your children and share your life with them as they share their new lives with you.
topics: Features, Marriage, Parenting

title: Inflation expected to fall back below Bank of England's 2% target
body:
Experts think inflation will fall in figures released this week before rising later in 2024

Inflation is expected to have fallen back below the Bank of England’s 2 per cent target when figures covering the year to September are revealed on Wednesday.

Last month, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) unveiled that the consumer prices index (CPI) measure of inflation had held steady at 2.2 per cent in August, but economists now predict that September’s number will be lower.

Pantheon Macroeconomics has forecast that September’s CPI figure will be 1.9 per cent, while Deutsche Bank Research suggests it will likely by 1.8 per cent. Oxford Economics is forecasting 1.7 per cent.

The Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has previously said it expects a slightly higher figure of 2.1 per cent, but that forecast was made in summer.

In a note about its forecast, Pantheon Macroeconomics said: “All of the undershoot relative to the MPC’s call is accounted for by falling motor fuel prices.

“We expect the drop in motor fuel prices, following oil price falls through the summer, to cut 0.22 percentage points from headline CPI inflation in September compared to August.”

It is forecasting core inflation – which excludes volatile products like food and energy, to fall from 3.6 per cent to 3.5 per cent, and services inflation to fall from 5.6 per cent to 5.4 per cent.

Economists expect inflation to tick upwards later in the year.

Sanjay Raja of Deutsche Bank Research said: “Upward momentum will likely gather pace. The recent run of energy deflation will likely come to an end shortly. Indeed, pump prices are likely to reverse course in October, while dual fuel bills will see a hefty 10 per cent rise.

“The upcoming Autumn Budget also raises risks to short-term inflation, with alcohol and tobacco duty increases potentially in the offing.”

Pantheon Macroeconomics suggests CPI will reach 2.8 per cent by November, and could get to 3 per cent in 2025.

The Bank of England aims for inflation be around 2 per cent, and signs that inflation is falling can raise the prospect of it dropping interest rates – which are raised to counter high price rises.

Interest rates fell in August from their 16-year high of 5.25 per cent to 5 per cent, and economists think further falls are still to come.

Most economists think there will be at least one further fall this year, with another a possibility.

“We continue to expect the Bank of England to cut interest rates slowly in the coming months, from 5 per cent to 4.75 per cent in November, and thereafter perhaps by 0.25 percentage points at every other meeting,” said Ashley Webb of Capital Economics.
topics: Inflation

title: What you need to know before opening an account with Revolut
body:
Revolut is not yet a bank in the UK - here's the details on whether your money is protected

Revolut has come under fire after a BBC Panorama investigation told the story of a man who had £165,000 taken from his business account with the firm, and is yet to be refunded.

The e-money company said it cannot comment on the case as it is being looked at by the Financial Ombudsman Service.

In July, Revolut was granted a banking licence after a three-year wait for approval, though as of yet, its conversion is not yet complete.

If you are a customer, or are looking to become one, here is what you need to know about opening an account with them.

Revolut is a digital-only financial institution that doesn’t have a physical branch. It is also not yet a bank which means some rules apply differently to it.

The UK has a financial protection scheme called the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS). This entitles customers compensation of up to £85,000 if a financial services firm fails.

FSCS protection means customers get back their money – whether or not the bank actually has that cash itself to return to customers, as the funds come from the FSCS itself.

Currently, because Revolut is not yet a bank, deposits are not protected by the FSCS. They are instead protected by something called “safeguarding”.

With e-money institutions, funds instead are kept in a safeguarding account, meaning the provider – in this case Revolut – cannot lend it out to others and you should get your money back in case of a collapse. However, MoneySavingExpert.com has warned that this “could be minus some admin fees”.

The exception to this is Revolut customers who had money put in a Revolut Savings Vault – that money is deposited with a third-party bank, which held it on a saver’s behalf and was FSCS protected.

The situation is likely to change in the future, though Revolut needs to exit its mobilisation period first. Once this happens, funds will be protected by the FSCS.

There are other firms operating in the UK as e-money institutions rather than banks, with Wise being a prominent example.

Yes. New rules on fraud reimbursement from the Payment Systems Regulator came into play last week, and these still apply to Revolut, even though it is not yet a bank.

This is because the rules are also applied to payment firms – anyone using a system known as faster payments or Clearing House Automated Payment System (CHAPS) is covered.

Introduced last week, they cover something known as authorised push payment (APP) fraud, whereby someone is tricked into sending money to a fraudster.

Under the rules, payments that fall under an APP scam category are considered for reimbursement, providing certain tests are met.

These tests are designed to ensure that payees have not been negligent, for example, by ensuring they conducted basic checks before making payments.

Companies must ensure fraud victims are compensated up to £85,000 within five days under the new rules, and these rules apply to Revolut as well as banks.

As soon as you realise you have fallen victim to a scam, the Payment Systems Regulator says you should immediately contact your account provider to report it.

They will take all the relevant information from you and will “consider your case for reimbursement,” according to the PSR.

Your bank will investigate the issue and get back to you to let you know the decision they have made, but if you are still unhappy with their response, you can take the matter further by referring it to the Financial Ombudsman Service (FOS).

You can do this by using the FOS website.

A Revolut spokesperson said: “We are sorry to hear of any instance where our customers have been targeted by ruthless and sophisticated criminals. Revolut takes fraud and the industry-wide risk of customers being coerced by organised criminals, incredibly seriously.

“As a UK Payment Service Provider, Revolut abides by the same regulatory standards as any ‘high street bank’ in combating fraud. We of course would refute any suggestion that we do not, nor wish to, abide by these standards.”

It added: “We recognise a small number of our customers have had experiences with Revolut which have fallen short of our expectations. We do not recognise this as the experience held by the vast majority of customers who continue to enjoy Revolut’s products and services.

“Nevertheless, there will always be more to do to tackle this multi-industry issue and we will continue to work towards reducing fraud rates further.”
