title: I'm 66 and on the state pension - should I delay taking my tax-free lump sum?
body:
There have been several rumours about the future of tax-free lump sums prior to this month's Budget

In our weekly series, readers can email in with any question about retirement and pension saving to be answered by our expert, Tom Selby, director of public policy at investment platform AJ Bell. There is nothing he doesn’t know about pensions. If you have a question for him, email us at money@inews.co.uk.

Question: I’m 66 and have just started receiveing my state pension. I also have a private pension to take and am in two minds what to do with it. Should I start taking it now, or should I delay and let it grow? I think I can afford to do so as I’m mortgage free. Will the lump sum I’m allowed to take grow if I wait?

Answer: There are lots of benefits to using a pension to save for retirement, one of which is the ability to take up to a quarter of your pot completely tax-free from age 55. For most people, the maximum tax-free cash they can take is capped at £268,275 over the course of their lifetimes.

However, just because you can do something doesn’t mean you necessarily should – and there are plenty of good reasons to hold off on taking your pensions tax-free cash if you can afford to.

This is particularly important right now, with the near-constant rumour and speculation about what tax nightmares Chancellor Rachel Reeves could have in store in her Budget, scheduled to take place the day before Halloween. While these stories can be destabilising, it’s usually better to focus on your long-term retirement strategy rather than reacting to rumours.

How does it work?

Pension rules allow you to access up to a quarter of your “defined contribution” (DC) pension completely tax-free from age 55. This “normal minimum pension age” is set to rise to 57 in 2028. To access your tax-free cash, you need to choose a retirement income route for the rest of your fund. For most people, this will either be entering drawdown (where you keep your fund invested and take a steady income) or buying an annuity (an insurance product which pays you an agreed level of income for the rest of your life).

Taking your tax-free cash isn’t a decision that should be taken lightly, however. You will be removing the cash from an environment where it can grow tax-free, so if you do choose to access it, at the very least make sure you have a plan for it. If you just take the money out of your pension and put it in a bank account earning little to no interest, its value will likely quickly be eaten away by inflation.

If left in your pension, you tax-free cash entitlement could have the opportunity to grow tax-free too. The impact of this could be substantial. Take, for example, someone with a £200,000 pension who decides to take their maximum 25 per cent tax-free cash of £50,000 at age 55 and puts it into a current account paying 0 per cent interest. If they make no further pension contributions, they will receive no further tax-free cash entitlement – even if their remaining £150,000 fund is left untouched and benefits from investment growth.

If we assume that remaining fund grows by 4 per cent per year after charges, by age 65 it could be worth around £222,000, alongside the £50,000 tax-free cash they withdrew at age 55 (i.e. £272,000 in total).

If, however, they had left their entire £200,000 fund untouched and enjoyed the same 4 per cent investment growth post-charges, by age 65 they could have a total fund worth around £296,000, with £74,000 available tax-free. That is almost 50 per cent more tax-free cash than if they had accessed their pot at age 55.

If you have specific things you need to spend money on and your retirement pot is your only option, just accessing your tax-free cash – or a portion of your tax-free cash – can be a sensible option.

Where you also flexibly access taxable income from your pension pot, the ‘money purchase annual allowance’ (MPAA) will be triggered, reducing your annual allowance for making new contributions from £60,000 to £10,000. You will also lose the ability to carry forward up to three years of unused annual allowances from the three previous tax years. If, however, you just withdraw tax-free cash from your pension, you will not trigger the MPAA and so can retain the full £60,000 annual allowance.

If you do need to take tax-free cash from your pension, you could consider partially “crystallising” some of your pot in drawdown. Crystallising in this context just means choosing a retirement income route. This could allow you to generate the tax-free cash you need, while leaving the ‘uncrystallised’ part of your pension – including the attached tax-free cash entitlement – untouched and with the ability to continue growing.

It is also worth remembering that by withdrawing money out of your pension, you are moving it from an environment where it will usually be free from inheritance tax (IHT) – and could be passed onto your beneficiaries completely tax-free – to one where it will form part of your estate for IHT purposes.

That is not to say, of course, that people should not access their tax-free cash, but simply to emphasise the importance of considering what you plan to do with the money when you access it. And whatever you do, do not let it fall victim to the ravages of inflation.
topics: Pensions, Retirement, Subscribers

title: Average two and five-year mortgage rates rise for the first time in three months
body:
Experts say those nearing the end of their mortgage term should consider locking in a new deal

Average mortgage rates for the two most popular lengths of home loan have both risen for the first time in three months.

The average two-year deal has moved from 5.36 to 5.37 per cent since last Friday, while average five-year deal rates went from 5.05 to 5.06 per cent, according to figures from analytics firm Moneyfacts.

Although the increases are small, the change bucks the trend of rates falling for the past few months.

The last time average rates on both types of deal rose was between 9 and 10 July, when they went from 5.92 to 5.93 per cent and 5.5 to 5.51 per cent, respectively.

Some major lenders – including Barclays and Santander – have pulled their cheapest mortgages in the past week after swap rates, which influence the prices lenders can offer, rose.

Rachel Springall of Moneyfacts told i: “Last month falling swap rates encouraged lenders to cut rates, but a combination of the looming Budget, concerns over inflation and other global influences can result in market pricing uncertainty. However, there are still expectations for the Bank of England base rate to drop further before the year is over.

“All eyes will be on the pending Budget and the next base rate decision day for borrowers, but in the meantime, it would be wise for them to seek independent advice to explore the latest options. Lenders will no doubt be watching the markets closely, so they may react to changes suddenly. As a result, as we have seen in the past, some deals could be pulled as lenders try to assess their current margins.”

Lewis Shaw, owner and mortgage broker at Shaw Financial Services, added: “Multiple lenders’ increasing rates last week will have spooked buyers after months of a gradual thawing of the mortgage and property market.

“The gentle downward slope that had been mortgage rates may have come to a bump in the road, as illustrated by average two and five-year fixed rates rising for the first time since July.”

He also urged those coming to the end of their terms to seek out a new rate now.

“It’s anyone’s guess where it goes from here with so much uncertainty around the autumn Budget, the US election and global conflicts all colliding at once. One thing is for sure: don’t count your chickens. Given the febrile nature of the current market, inaction could well be painful,” he said.

David Hollingworth, of L&C Mortgages, said: “Swaps look to have eased back a little this morning although still sitting higher than they were. However, TSB has announced some rates are rising from this week so it certainly feels like there’s more evidence of increasing rates feeding through.

“It’s important not to pin too much on one day’s data but there has certainly been evidence of lenders slowing the pace of rate cuts and in a growing number of instances beginning to increase rates.

“That can in some cases be provoked by a need to calm volume, usually when a lender is at the very top of the tables but the increase in market rates will have pushed up the cost for lenders slightly and that looks to now be feeding through into some rates.

“This isn’t likely to signal a radical hike in rates but could at least put a pause on the rate cutting cycle of recent months. The base rate is still expected to fall but we will have to see how market expectation of how quickly develops, as that will have a bearing on fixed rate mortgages.”

Swap rates, and therefore mortgage rates, have fallen in recent months on expectations that the Bank of England is likely to cut interest rates further – from its current level of 5 per cent – later this year and in 2025.

But in the past week, expectations of two cuts to interest rates this year – at both the remaining meetings of the Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) – have reduced.

Part of the reason for this has been the messaging from senior staff at the Bank of England.

The Bank’s chief economist, Huw Pill, said earlier in October that interest rates should not be cut “too far or too fast”. This caused confusion among some investors as it contrasted with recent comments by the Bank’s Governor Andrew Bailey, who said “more aggressive” reductions could be on the way.

Some mortgage lenders will allow you to lock in a new rate up to six months before your current deal ends, though though some offer a smaller window of time.

If you lock in a rate, it is guaranteed even if rates go up later, but if they end up going down before your deal ends, you can transfer on to the new price.

The Bank of England cut interest rates from 5.25 per cent in August, with its next meeting coming in November.

This will be after Rachel Reeves delivers her Budget, which is expected to contain multiple tax-raising measures. She has been warned that more borrowing to fund spending commitments puts interest rates at risk of staying higher for longer.
topics: Bank Of England, Banks, Interest Rates, Mortgages, Property

title: The era of buy-to-let is over. Why young people don't want to be landlords
body:
There have been several changes in recent years that have made the sector not as attractive to younger landlords

Amateur landlords may be a dying breed as fewer younger people are able – or willing – to buy investment properties.

The average age of a landlord was last reported to be 58 in 2021, according to Government figures, which means it could well be higher now.

While landlords aren’t selling up in huge numbers, fewer people are buying new investment properties, resulting in a lack of young blood entering the market. We look at what this all means.

Why are landlords getting older?

“The growth of the private rented sector was kickstarted by the launch of the buy-to-let mortgage in 1996,” says Aneisha Beveridge, research director at the estate agency group Hamptons.

“Since then, the size of the sector has more than doubled. However, most of that growth came pre-2010, which is why the majority of landlords tend to be a little older.”

According to the 2021 English Landlord Survey, which is the most recent robust data, the average age of a landlord was 58. Around two-thirds of landlords at the time were over the age of 55, and just 2.4 per cent were under 34.

“Many of the older generations saw buy-to-let as a way to spread their risk and supplement their pension”, adds Ms Beveridge. “Over recent years, however, we haven’t seen younger generations pick up the baton.

“Not only have affordability pressures made it difficult for younger generations to purchase their first home, let alone a buy-to-let, but running portfolios requires more knowledge of the rules and regulations than ever before.”

Meanwhile, given high property prices, the barriers to entry have become trickier for any age. Hamptons has calculated that a new investor would need a minimum £50,000 deposit to purchase a typical £200,000 buy-to-let home today.

“Instead, younger generations are leaning towards more digital-based forms of investments like stocks, shares and cryptocurrency, where entry costs are minimal,” she adds.

What regulation changes have there been in recent years?

The financial uncertainty of Brexit, inflation, higher interest rates, tax changes and lower house price growth are all reasons why some will have been put off becoming landlords.

Regulation has also become tighter. There have been a few changes over the years around energy requirements, fire safety and even what fees can be charged to tenants. There are also licensing requirements in some areas.

Currently, you must have a valid energy performance certificate (EPC) when letting a property. Since 2018, that property must have a minimum E-rating. The Government is looking to extend these plans to essentially ban letting a home with less than a C-rating.

There is likely to be around a £10,000 cost cap imposed for properties that struggle to reach that rating, according to Ms Beveridge.

How is the landlord environment changing?

There has been speculation that landlords are selling off their portfolios, but the evidence for this has been based on surveys of landlord intentions.

Analysis from Hamptons suggests that this sell-off has not happened, but that, since 2016, fewer people have bought than have sold.

And those who have sold appear to be amateur landlords, who are struggling making less money, and who are finding the increased regulations too much of a hassle.

Professional landlords have become a bigger proportion of the market. They are the people who are doing this as a business and whose property company pays tax via a limited company.

Hamptons data shows that, despite a sharp fall in the number of homes bought by landlords in 2023, the number of limited companies set up to hold buy-to-let properties continued to rise.

Last year, a record 50,004 limited buy-to-let companies were set up across the UK, surpassing 2022’s previous record (48,540) by 3 per cent. Overall, there has been an 82 per cent increase in landlords who are renting through their company since the end of 2016.

This was when tax changes were announced, making limited companies a more profitable way to hold buy-to-let properties, assuming a person had enough properties to make the increased accountancy fees worthwhile.

The reason why holding property in a company is more tax efficient is that when the property is sold, instead of paying capital gains tax, the seller pays corporation tax. The rate of corporation tax is 25 per cent, a rate the Chancellor has indicated will not change at the Budget later this month. However capital gains tax (CGT) is expected to go up, possibly by a lot.

For property, the CGT rate is currently 18 per cent for basic rate taxpayers and 24 per cent for higher rate earners.

The Guardian has suggested the Treasury is considering hiking it up to 39 per cent for higher rate taxpayers, which would mean a near doubling in the amount of tax landlords paid when they sold.

Not only is it tax efficient to sell one’s home as a company but one will pay less tax on income too. Landlords paying themselves via a limited company may take most of their income out in dividends.

In this case, they will be subject to dividend tax (8.75 per cent for basic rate taxpayers, 33.75 per cent for higher rate and 39.35 per cent for additional) . This is also lower than the income tax they might have paid for income tax as an individual (20 per cent, 40 per cent and 45 per cent).

What used to be the appeal of being a landlord?

It used to be that being a landlord was a no-brainer in terms of making money. Rapid house price growth generated large returns while rent increases closely-mirrored earnings, meaning a hedge against inflation. Then there was capital growth at the end.

This, plus easy credit in the form of buy-to-let mortgages meant that between 2000 and 2017, the share of all UK residential mortgages ballooned from 1.7 per cent to 17.4 per cent, according to a recent report compiled by the Joseph Rowntree Foundation.

Now, landlords are looking at lower house price growth, higher interest rates and tighter regulation – and these are only some reasons as to why it is no longer so appealing to amateurs.

How many landlords are there?

Since 2010 the market started slowing down – and, since 2016, when the UK voted for Brexit, and the economic upheaval that came with that, followed by a war in Ukraine and double-digit inflation – the number of landlords has flatlined.

Figures from Zoopla, the property portal, show that from 2000 to 2016 the number of landlords doubled, to 5.5 million. Since then, the number of landlords has remained largely static.
topics: Buy-to-let, Landlord, Mortgage, Property, Subscribers

title: How I Manage My Money: Firm owner on £4k a month who wants a £500k pension pot
body:
Katie Guild thinks maternity pay should be much higher and runs a business to help people secure parental leave

In our How I Manage My Money series we aim to find out how people in the UK are spending, saving and investing money to meet their costs and achieve their goals.

This week we speak to Katie Guild, 32, who lives in London with her partner, Martin, 35, and their two-year-old son, Charlie. Katie, who runs Nugget Savings, thinks statutory maternity pay should be increased. Katie, who told i she’s very motivated by money, had to neglect her pension for a few years, but wants to build a £500,000 retirement pot.

My monthly income: I pay myself anything from £2,000 to £4,000 per month from my business, which I co-own, Nugget Savings, but this is variable. I have about £500 a month coming in from freelance work. We also receive £102.40 a month for child benefit. My husband has income coming in from his job in the emergency services.

My monthly outgoings: We split our outgoings equally, so I pay 50 per cent. My share is as follows – Mortgage, £500; childcare, £300; groceries, £200, council tax, £76.50; gas and electric, £46.92; water, £20; car insurance, £55; mobile, £47.09; home insurance, £10; service charge, £69.28; subscriptions, including Amazon, Disney and Hayu, £18.97; money into private pension, £100; eating out, £120; Joe Wicks App, £14.99.

Growing up, my family was well off. My dad was an investment banker and my brother and I went to private schools in north London. We had lovely family holidays and shopped at nice supermarkets. We didn’t have to worry about money.

In my early twenties I worked in tech sales, but had an urge to set up my own business. I quit my job and launched a business selling nightwear. It was much harder than I thought it would be and money was a constant worry. It was eventually successful, but the pressure of buying stock and selling it, saving enough for VAT, paying workers fairly, keeping up with consumer demand and the pandemic, was tough. Retail is very hard work and fashion retail is even harder. I’m not sure I would do it again!

I only started paying myself from the nightwear business after several years, and even then it’d be about £2,000 to £2,500 a month. I supplemented my income by being a nanny, before becoming a part-time postal worker in and around Barnet, north London. I loved the flexibility of being a postie and did lots of overtime.

It was brilliant exercise and good for your brain when you’re trying to work through a problem like having 1,000 Christmas pyjamas stuck in customs.

I was pregnant in 2021 and, financially, it was very stressful. I was lucky enough to get maternity pay from Royal Mail and continued to work on my nightwear business throughout. I didn’t qualify for Royal Mail’s enhanced maternity pay policy. I was also naive about the stress involved when it came to running a business with a newborn.

I hired temporary help and a new advertising agency to see me through and thought I had enough elements of the business automated to enable me to work very little and get passive income. However, the post-pandemic e-commerce slump came and I had to fire the advertising team and bring it back in-house.

I had no childcare for the first year and was constantly stressed about money. I got delayed postpartum depression when my baby was 18 months.

I now run Nugget Savings with the co-founder. It’s a community aimed at helping parents have a financially secure parental leave. My income from the business is anything from £2,000 to £4,000 a month, but this varies.

I think parental pay and leave isn’t working properly for several reasons. There is a lack of education about the financial realities of having a baby, a lack of transparency from employers with their parental leave policies and a lack of financial planning.

Employer parental pay and leave policies need to be more transparent and easily accessible on all job specifications and in all employee handbooks.

I’d like to see statutory maternity pay increased up to the level of the national minimum wage. This seems like an absolute no-brainer. I’m doubtful this will happen, but we can hope and we will make noise about it until it changes.

I opened a self-invested personal pension (SIPP) with Aviva in September 2024. I hope to double my pension contribution every year for the next five years. I’ve got around £10,000 in my old Royal Mail pension.

All the savings I had previously helped us buy our home in London, which we purchased in July 2022 for £390,000. I also have £1,700 in credit card debt, which I want to get paid off before I start focusing on saving again.

I’m much more invested in the idea of saving for later life than I used to be. I feel like a bit of a wally for sticking my head in the sand for so long, but I’m really motivated to turn it around and sort my pension out and open a stocks and shares ISA. I’ve always had it in my head that I’d sell a business and that would sort me out for retirement. This might still happen, but there’s no harm in having a backup plan.

I want to have at least £500,000 in my pension by the time I retire. From old work pensions, I’m projected to scrape £100,000 at present, so I’ve got a lot of work to do. I’ve got to try and compete with my partner’s Civil Service pension. I don’t think I’d be able to live solely off the state pension.

I’m very motivated by money. I’d love to give my children the financial security I had growing up. I have only truly understood the gift that was after feeling so financially insecure for the past seven years. Money stress is all encompassing. The anxiety I have felt has been truly horrible. But I love our work and our mission so much that I’m quite happy earning what we are now so long as we’re having an impact. Ideally, though, I’d love £200,000 a year.

In time, we’d like to have another baby and I’d like to be financially stable for that, particularly as it’d probably require us moving house. Other than that, I’d love to succeed in my commitment to boost my pension and get funding for Nugget Savings – so far we’ve been entirely bootstrapped.

Want to take part in How I Manage My Money? Email money@inews.co.uk

title: Over 1m people missing out on £3bn of 'unfulfilled' benefits - how you can claim
body:
Many already claiming benefits could be entitled to more help than they think, the the DWP has found

More than one million people across the country are missing out on £3bn of benefits they are entitled to.

New data from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has identified a group of claimants who already receive benefit, but whose need has grown since they first claimed, and who have not yet received the extra help theya are able to claim for.

The DWP describes the problem as “unfulfilled” benefits, and estimates that the total amount people may be missing out on is about £3.1bn in 2023/24.

This figure has increased by 34.7 per cent in a year – up from £2.3bn – according to former pensions minister Sir Steve Webb.

Previously, the DWP has published separate figures on the number of people claiming each benefit and how much they receive; plus the number of people who do not claim anything but who would be entitled to benefit – and how much these people missing out on.

Now, the DWP has begun to report separately on those whose circumstances have changed, leaving them facing the “unfulfilled” benefits problem.

Sir Steve said: “There is understandable focus on people who miss out completely on benefits to which they are entitled. But this new report shines a helpful light on another reason why people may be missing out on billions of pounds in benefits.

“These are cases where people’s circumstances have changed since they first claimed the benefit and would now be entitled to extra help but have not updated the DWP.”

title: I walked Japan's ancient pilgrimage and went home feeling uplifted
body:
The Kumano Kodo is one of the world’s greatest pilgrimages, winding through forests to tranquil shrines

“Your luck is on its way, but not in a rush,” reads my fortune as I gently unfurl it from a tiny, red plastic cat. It’s the fifth maneki-neko (“beckoning cat”) I’ve bought since I arrived in Japan’s Wakayama prefecture, south of Osaka in the Kansai Region.

A common Japanese figurine sold everywhere from temples to service stations, a maneki-neko is believed to bring good luck to its owner. Unfortunately for me, each glimpse into my future has been ambiguous to say the least.. My love fortune reads: “Nothing is nearby, do not be depressed.”

I show the underwhelming prophecy to our guide, Hatsumi, and look up at 133 metres of water thundering into a stream below. We are standing at the foot of Nachi, Japan’s tallest single-drop waterfall, which I’m told symbolises the divine power of nature.

It is at the edge of the Kumano Kodo network of pilgrimage trails. “Whatever you need luck for, you must think about it on the walk,” Hatsumi responds with a smile.

Along with Spain’s legendary Camino de Santiago, the Kumano Kodo is one of only two pilgrimage routes with Unesco World Heritage status.

Winding through the mountains of the Kii Peninsula, it has been walked by everyone from emperors to farmers on their quest for peace for more than 1,000 years.

The pilgrimage evolved from nature worship. Devotees of Shinbutsu-shugo (the syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism) believed deities lived among the evergreen trees which it winds between.

The route was also developed as a way for people to access three shrines: Hongu Taisha, Hayatama Taisha and Nachi Taisha, collectively known as Kumano Sanzan. Now, they attract visitors from all over the world.

At the Kumano Nachi Taisha shrine, standing tall in orange and white, I watch as worshippers approach the main hall and wash their hands and mouths at the purification fountain. They bow twice to show respect and clap twice to attract the attention of the deities. After clapping, they make their prayer or wish in silence, before bowing once more.

The rules seem complicated, and I’m worried about messing up but after gentle encouragement, I make my wish. We had started our 10km stretch of the trail by walking through Hosshinmon-oji, the Gate of Awakening and Enlightenment.

This centuries-old, carved wooden gate marks the entrance to the path, which is lined with towering trees and moss-covered stones. “It’s magical, isn’t it?” Hatsumi asked me.

“Some people don’t know what they’re feeling but they know they’re feeling something.” Hatsumi was first taken on the Komodo trail 20 years ago and said she immediately felt revitalised. Each time she visits, she says her peace is reaffirmed.

She was right, of course, because it is magical. As we made our way along the trail, we found ourselves enveloped in forests of maple, cypress and cedar. The paths, hugging plunging ravines, are latticed with roots, so you have to watch your step.

I paused occasionally to look out at pale-pink cherry blossoms across the valley, or to take pictures of wild azalea, juniper and camellia, checking their proper names with a plant app.. Mostly, we were encouraged to walk in silence with our thoughts.

We stopped to visit Oji shrines, poem stones and small Jizo statues that line the path, the latter of which is heralded for watching over children and travellers like me. In autumn and winter, local people dress the Jizo with red bibs and hats. Looking for them feels like searching for fairies in a garden.

We also met Akira Nakagishi, an 81-year-old walker and official trail guide from Tanabe City, who chats to foreign tourists walking the Kumano Kodo so he can improve his English. “The people I meet here are so co-operative and generous that I become very emotional,” he told me, before asking if I minded featuring on his Instagram page.

That evening, we dined at Caravanserai, a stunning French-Japanese restaurant in a renovated 50-year-old ume plum warehouse in Kamihaya, and spent the night at Akizuno Garten in Kamiakizu, a few kilometres from Tanabe City.

The former primary school is now a farmer’s restaurant, workshop and fruit picking experience, as well as accommodation. Wakayama brought many more unexpected delights. Cycling around Sandanbeki, on the prefecture’s coastline, there were breathtaking views of the Pacific Ocean.

Watching soy sauce being made at Yuasa Shoyu offered a fascinating glimpse into the meticulous fermentation process.And bathing naked in onsen, a Japanese hot spring bath that is geothermally heated by volcanic activity underground, felt both freeing and calming.

But I enjoyed it all the more having visited Koyasan, a small, secluded temple town on the wooded Mount Koya.

Founded in 816CE by an influential monk known as Kobo Daishi, Koyasan is among Japan’s most important religious centres. The birthplace of esoteric Shingon Buddhism, it was home to thousands of forest-clad temples at its peak from the 17th to the 19th century. Today, 117 remain, many of which now accommodate paying guests.

One of these temple shukubos (guesthouses) is Daienin lodge. When I arrived after dark, a grey, ethereal mist hung over the shrines and trees.

In my room, I found a futon bed and a pot of steaming tea. The floors were lined with tatami mats, made of compressed rice straw and sea grass, and a note had been left on a low side table reading: “The morning ceremony, ‘otuome’, is an opportunity to pray for peace in the world and happiness for everyone. We hope it will contribute to your good health and happiness.”

The morning prayer was a serene experience, even for a non-Japanese speaker like me. I woke early to be at the prayer room for 6am and was delighted to discover its warm air filled with the subtle scent of incense.

Monks, dressed in traditional robes, led a solemn, rhythmic and reverberating chant. After a while, I decided to close my eyes, focusing on the soothing sound of their voices and the gentle clinking of ritual implements. I and felt tingles from head to toe.

Later, we walked under umbrellas to Okunoin, a cemetery in Koyasan of more than 200,000 tombstones, the largest cemetery in Japan. Many belong to notable historical figures, including samurai and feudal lords. I walked in silence, with only occasional whispers and the gentle sound of footsteps on stone paths floating through the trees.

As we approached the mausoleum of Kobo Daishi, the founder of Shingon Buddhism, guide Nobu stopped to explain its significance. It’s believed that Kobo Daishi did not die, but instead rests in his tomb in eternal meditation, awaiting the arrival of Miroku (Maitreya), the Buddha of the Future.

It was hard not to be moved by the stream of pilgrims and visitors leaving offerings and prayers for a man who Nobu described as “the father of Japanese culture.” The devotion was palpable as the Toro-do, or Lantern Hall, near Kobo Daishi’s mausoleum, was illuminated by thousands of lanterns, some of which have been burning for centuries.

At the airport on my way back home, I realised I still had my fortune in the pocket of my shorts. “Your luck is on its way, but not in a rush.” This time, it didn’t feel underwhelming. It felt like a lesson from Wakayama to slow down, take a breath and enjoy the journey.

title: I used 90s tech for a week - and rediscovered books
body:
I was born in 2002 and have never known life without smartphones - could switching to a CD player, live TV and a film camera help me unwind?

I used to find it annoying that the size of my iPhone meant it was getting too big for my jeans pocket. But the retro personal CD player I’m currently wrestling with really is a problem. There’s no way this thing is fitting in any pocket – and the wire to my headphones is so short, it wouldn’t reach me anyway.

I’ve tried planting the thing into my jumper hood, but to no avail – the neckline nearly suffocated me, and the wire dragged my head back. I’ve resorted to carrying it. How on earth did 90s kids survive?

I’m attempting to imitate my weekly park walk with my iPhone and Airpods, but with 90s tech. If I have any chance of blaring lyrics in my ears, it’s with this retro CD player and its accompanying wired headphones.

Although I’m lucky to get a glimpse of Madonna’s voice over any car going past. As well as bluetooth technology, noise cancellation, it seems, was also revolutionary.

I’m a Noughties baby, born in 2002, and the oldest piece of technology I remember owning is a pink Nokia flip phone – the one that required a good four presses for the letter ‘S’ and a further three for the letter ‘C’ – and a red MP3 player, aged six.

By the time I was 14 I was skilled in simultaneously watching a YouTube video on my iPad, taking selfies on Snapchat, and having Netflix on as background noise. That was a standard morning, afternoon and evening but sometimes, if I really wanted to test myself, I’d do some homework on my laptop too.

Yet when I’d ask my parents and grandparents about their childhoods, I’d sometimes get a pang of jealousy about the fun they seemed to have before social media. Research from Bumble for Friends shows that 66 per cent of Gen Z-ers report meeting their friends online and according to Save the Children only one in four children play out regularly on the street compared with almost three quarters of their grandparents’ generation, who did so a few times a week.

Knocking on a friend’s door to see if they’re free to play knock and bolt rather than poring over a shared Google Calendar to fit in a quick matcha coffee date sounded much more amusing.

And what about using physical make-up testers on the high street instead of an AI-powered app to swipe through lipstick colours? This week, I decided, I would get as close to that analogue life as possible, to see what I could learn.

I’ve done digital detoxes before so I knew what to expect when it came to only using my normal phone for work: a twinge of Fomo mixed with relief and serenity. It’s like being sucked back into the real world after being transported.

But this wasn’t a normal tech ban. I was switching my phone camera for an old-fashioned instant film camera, Spotify for a Discman, and iMessages for phone calls and written letters. The Netflix subscription was out, and freeview television was in (thank God I have a TV licence).

I haven’t touched a CD since putting Olly Murs’ 2011 album into my mum’s car as she drove me to school so getting hold of one was the first hurdle. My boyfriend’s mum lent me some discs to keep me going for the week, but with only two options and without the skip ahead 10 seconds button, I was bored in the first hour. Luckily the CD wasn’t scratched, like my childhood ones were, but not having different artists at my fingertips was a struggle.

Switching on the telly in the evening, the first thing to note was that EastEnders has changed. The last episode I watched was in 2017 when Ronnie and Roxy Mitchell died; now, I barely knew the characters. That was my BBC 7.30pm slot ruined on night one. It felt like starting a Netflix limited series on episode four, and left me scrolling through the TV guide like a lost puppy. Have I Got News For You?, Channel 4 News, Coronation Street. Nothing was riveting. Without thousands of possible things to stream, pause, and then turn off if I was again, bored, and at a loss. I gave up and read a Harlan Coben book.

Before the week, I’d warned friends that if I didn’t reply to them, I was in fact alive, just banishing them for seven days. Still, I presumed my best friend might need some updates on my life, so I took to pen and paper to let her know. Granted, she’ll probably receive the letter after I have my trusty iPhone back anyway, but it passed some time, and was better than looking through awful TV options.

For someone who writes for a living, and talks to their best friend everyday, it felt incredibly difficult to tell her normal things in handwritten form. Perhaps because this missive feels more concrete.

There’s no backspace; when it’s written down, it’s in ink, it’s permanent. I’m also a triple texter – a short-but-multiple texter if you will. Instead of explaining everything in one paragraph, I do it in four separately-sent sentences that causes unnecessary buzzing of the correspondent’s phone. Now I was face to face with that annoying habit. I wasn’t paying for four tracked letters.

I tried a phone call instead. The only people I usually call are my dad, because if I text him I only receive a thumbs-up in reply, and my nan, who can’t work out how to text. When my best friend answered the phone the first thing she said was “what’s wrong?”.

We’d usually only do this under extreme circumstances – like the time I crashed my car. When I replied it was for a catch-up she laughed. “Just voice note me, I’ll listen to it later,” she said.

We managed a 10-minute conversation before she went to the gym, with the promise that we’d meet up for a coffee in two days’ time. I reiterated that I wouldn’t be checking my texts, so she couldn’t cancel.

By day three, all my time was taken up with books. I hadn’t enjoyed the CD player, TV was boring, and I was unable to communicate effectively through a pen, so it seemed the next best option.

It was a revelation. I used to be a big reader – and used to win the school competition every year for most books read. I’d definitely not enjoyed a good book for a few months, and even when I did I’d get distracted by my phone, or leave it a few days between chapters when life got busy. Coming back to it uninterrupted felt divine. I finished all 352 pages of Daisy Buchanan’s Pity Party in one sitting.

Day three is the coffee date that I’m hoping my friend turns up to. When I’m sitting in the café we agreed five minutes early, I start thinking that I’ve probably chosen my most unreliable friend for this.

Without TikTok to scroll through while I wait for her I’m recalling all the times she’s been late – most of them – or rearranged. The clock on the wall feels like it’s mocking me as I sit staring into space. I should have brought a book.

When she arrives, 15 minutes after our agreed time, I’m relieved. I watch her using Apple Pay to get an iced coffee (something I’ve missed) and she sits down to show me an Instagram post.

I realise how many of my interactions rely on modern technology. I’m obviously not a rarity as most people in the café are on their phones but it makes me upset that so many of my in-person conversations rely on the Internet. I wonder how many of the memories I could have made just by being in the moment have been tainted by my need to share them online.

There were other things I learnt. Going to sleep without scrolling through my phone beforehand had a positive impact on the quality of my snoozing – but my favourite part of being smartphone-free was waking up and getting on with my day without my habitual 20 minutes checking my screen.

My generation is obsessed with wellness and finding ways to relax and unwind. We’re all searching for the answers on our phones, but it turns out we just need to put them down.

But far and away the best piece of 90s tech, which I came to realise on day four, was the Instax Mini 10, an instant film camera first released in 1998. I admit, I wasn’t sure as I put in the first set of 10 films.

Not only was the camera difficult to work out how to use, it was bulky. As it was almost 30 years old, I was expecting a black-and-white blur that might somewhat resemble me to come out of the obscenely large piece of tech.

So it was a pleasant surprise to love what I received: multiple memories packaged up in three-by-two inch squares, with picture quality that almost seemed edgy and purposeful.

Only having one take to capture a moment was refreshing – nothing had to be perfect, I didn’t need to retake it because a hair was out of place, I didn’t need to find a filter or try and hide my skin. They were raw images. And they’re already framed in my flat.

What did I learn from my week in the 90s? Well, I’m sad I didn’t get to experience the 1996 Tamagotchi as a young girl, or the first portable DVD player in 1998, or play on the Sega Dreamcast. I didn’t miss social media as much as I thought; by day three, I didn’t even think about it, and I enjoyed focusing only on the day ahead, rather than other people’s breakfasts.

But I also live in an era where friends who live in different countries are contactable – and I did miss texting friends. At times, I was also restless with boredom. Yes, the online world can be toxic, but it’s also entertaining. Although granted, I’d probably have more hobbies if Netflix wasn’t around.

Am I still jealous of my parents and grandparents? A bit. But it’s my sister who’s really got me green-eyed with envy. Born in 1998, she got to experience both worlds – no retro Discman-in-the-Noughties required.
topics: Features, Generation Z, Technology

title: 'When I told my kids I wanted to die, I realised I had to stop drinking'
body:
Men have always drunk more than women, but now a new generation of stressed and burned-out mid-lifers are changing the face of alcohol abuse. Isabelle Aron speaks to them

Jamie Klingler had her last ever alcoholic drink on 14 April, 2020 at the age of 42. Throughout her adult life, her drinking had got progressively worse. Having a career in the media and hospitality, her work often involved drinking. “It was normalised through work and then I became an extremist. I never wanted the party to end,” says Klingler, now 46. “I was drinking a lot. I would drink two bottles of wine a day as standard. I didn’t drink a lot of spirits, but I competitively drank white wine. I was drinking until I passed out every day.”

In the pandemic, Klingler’s drinking stepped up a gear. “Things spiralled. I was buying five-litre boxes of rosé – because with the box, you don’t see how much you’re drinking, so you’re removing some of the shame,” she says.

Her rock-bottom moment came when she developed shingles and worried she had a rare strain of Covid and was going to die. “I was catastrophising and thinking I was going to die in a shitty apartment, drunk and with my elderly dog – and that would be my whole legacy.”

While Klingler had realised she had a problem about eight or nine years before giving up, and many loved ones had tried to speak to her, this was the moment that finally changed things.

“I thought: I’m either going to come out of the pandemic more depressed, more addicted and more broke. Or I’m going to use it as an opportunity.” After that last drink in April 2020, Klingler says “everything changed”, and she has been sober ever since.

Klingler was not alone in having increased her alcohol consumption during the pandemic. According to Alcohol Change UK, one in five adults in the UK were drinking more in lockdown, which is the equivalent to 8.6 million people.

But now, with the pandemic behind us, we’re starting to see a different trend: complications from alcohol use – including alcohol-related liver disease and other health problems – are rising among women aged 40 to 64 as a result of increased drinking during that time.

Yes, men generally still drink more than women – according to 2022 stats from the Health Survey for England, 55 per cent of men drank at least once a week compared to 42 per cent of women – but women are binge-drinking more. A 2023 report by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development found that British women were the biggest female binge-drinkers in the world, in a survey that looked at 33 countries.

UK research has found that the age bracket where women are most likely to exceed the recommended drinking limits are between the ages of 45 and 64.

As a result, there is an increasing disconnect between what we might think of as a problem drinker, and who actually falls into that category.

“We do that othering – we think of a problem as at the extreme end, and think of someone not like us. We might think of street drinkers, someone older, or someone who’s homeless. We tell ourselves: I’ve got a house, a job, a family – I can’t have a problem with alcohol,” says Richard Piper, chief executive of Alcohol Change UK.

Anna Donaghey, is a former alcohol addict, and now an alcohol mindset coach and host of The Big Drink Re-think podcast. In her work as a coach, she often sees women in their thirties and forties.

“I work with many women of this age. Some are clearly emotionally dependent and addicted,” she explains. “But a great number fall into the category of ‘grey area drinkers’, where drinking has yet to become so debilitating that they have experienced rock-bottom, but neither are they okay. Their drinking is creeping up and beginning to take its toll on their mental and physical wellbeing, their professional life, their relationships with others and themselves.”

There are particular issues that impact this demographic when it comes to drinking, too. While Klingler’s story highlights the way that professional workplaces can normalise excessive drinking – especially for Gen-X women who entered booze-dominated workplaces before the Noughties – but there is also the additional factor of parenthood, which Donaghey says is a big contributor.

She says that one of the big issues is becoming a mother and managing the stress that comes with that (all mothers will be familiar with the “gin o’clock” or “mum juice” content on social media that presents alcohol as a necessary tonic for the stresses of parenting) as well as grieving for your old life and resentment towards your partner if you feel they aren’t making the same sacrifices. Then, there’s balancing motherhood with your career.

Piper agrees. “There’s a definite uplift in this age of drinkers that’s linked to parenting. It becomes quite habitual. Combining parenting and work can be particularly stressful. It means we’re more susceptible to that message of: ‘Relax, have a drink’.” He adds that drinks companies are specifically targeting women, with the pink-ification of packaging, aspirational advertising techniques and using algorithms to reach women in a specific age bracket.

Elizabeth Walker, 47, says having children and being a single mum made her drinking worse. “I was doing it on my own, and drinking was my treat. I felt like parenting was such hard work – that was my only way of relaxing,” says Walker. “It’s that ‘mummy wine culture’ – at the end of the day, the mum sits down with a glass of wine, puts her feet up and goes ‘ahhh’.

“You see it on TV and I’d seen it in everybody around me. I thought that’s what you did. But it made looking after my children even worse. I never felt 100 per cent and had this feeling of letting them down. It escalated and made the whole cycle of parenting even more stressful.”

Walker started drinking as a teenager, and found it helped her feel more confident – something that continued throughout her life. Matters came to a head in 2022 when she was 44.

“I wasn’t being the mother I wanted to be. My rock-bottom moment was hearing my kids bicker in the car. I turned around and said: ‘I can’t do this anymore. If this is what my life is going to be, I want to be dead.’ Their faces just fell,” explains Walker.

She says she also fantasised about running off to Morocco and leaving her kids with her mother. “That was my moment where I thought: ‘This needs to change’ and I decided to go to rehab.”

Other issues impacting this demographic can include divorce and bereavement and “being the sandwich generation – helping children navigate the teenage years, whilst caring for parents”, says Donaghey. “Towards the upper end of this age group, it could also be that women are “anticipating a time when their children leave home – and worrying about their purpose”, she says.

After giving up alcohol, Klingler realised she had never dealt with the grief of losing her mother, who died two years before she got sober and had been worried about her daughter’s drinking. “It’s astonishing how much time it filled. If I wasn’t drinking, I was having a bad sleep or hungover. I was never out of the fog, which meant I never dealt with my pain,” she says.

Despite the increasing numbers of women in this position the stigma remains – Walker says that her decision to go to rehab wasn’t easy for that reason. “I was absolutely terrified. I was scared that I was too broken. I also worried about the stigma and what other people would think,” says Walker.

“But it was one of the best experiences of my life. There was a sense of relief that maybe it was over.” She also found solace in speaking to others and knowing that it wasn’t just her. “Suddenly, I wasn’t this broken, horrendous, bad individual. I was human.”

Stigma around drinking is something that worries Natasha*, 34, who is currently trying to stay sober, having struggled with alcohol issues since she was 18. She stopped going to pubs about five years ago as she would get “black-out drunk every night and arrive home a day later with no memory of where she’d been”.

For her, alcohol offers a level of connection and a sense of belonging, but it has had an adverse effect on her life. “It’s impacted everything – relationships, work, finances and everything in between. I’ve had half-hearted attempts at quitting over the years but I’ve always relapsed. At the moment I believe I’m so close to being long-term sober. I realise it’s now or never,” she says.

“Alcohol addiction is hugely taboo. Recovery rates would drastically improve if there was less shame, which can only happen if there’s open conversations about addiction.”

Interestingly, Piper at Alcohol Change UK says that a large proportion of the people using the tools on their website to help with drinking issues are women. “We’ve seen a lot of women realise how good it is to drink less or not at all, particularly in that thirties and forties age group. More than twice as many women use our programmes as men. Lots of women are waking up to the fact that they’ve been mis-sold alcohol as a harmless, positive, liberating thing. But actually, there’s not a liberation there, there is a dependency.”

Piper says that while we often think of alcohol issues as binary – either you have a problem or you don’t – there’s a spectrum of harm, and that something at the lower end is still harmful. “If you’re reading your kid a bedtime story, but you’re thinking about a glass of wine, you’re not present. That might not feel like a drinking problem as we have conventionally thought of it, but it absolutely is,” says Piper.

Other examples might be waking up feeling sluggish, being unproductive at work or experiencing anxiety and stress as a result of alcohol consumption.

When it comes to getting help, Donaghey says the first step is to understand that it is not your fault. “Alcohol is addictive to all humans. Alcohol is the villain in the piece, not you. You’re doing the best you can, with the tools available to you – but you need better tools.”

She says there isn’t just one pathway for recovery, either. “There are so many options these days, from traditional routes like AA, through to online programmes and coaches. Help comes in many shapes and forms. There’s also a thriving and inspiring world of ‘quit lit’ and podcasts that provide free tools and tactics for anyone questioning their relationship with alcohol. Research your options and find something, or someone, that speaks to you.”
topics: Alcohol, Features, Non-alcoholic

title: Britain set for 22°C temperatures this week - but don't expect an Indian summer
body:
The mercury is set to rise 10°C in some areas

Parts of Britain could see temperatures soar to 22°C this week as chilly conditions from the weekend give way to milder weather.

However, forecasters have ruled out an Indian summer.

The mercury is set to rise 10°C compared to this weekend in some areas as a brief spell of warmer weather is forecast for midweek.

The Met Office said East Anglia and the Home Counties could experience temperatures of up to 22°C on Wednesday.

But Met Office meteorologist Tom Morgan said the country would not be seeing an Indian summer this week, with warmer weather set to be accompanied by showers, which will persist into the weekend as temperatures return closer to the seasonal average.

While not a formal meteorological term, the expression “Indian summer” refers to spells of “summer-like weather” during the autumn, also known as “autumnal warmth”.

It is defined as “a warm, calm spell of weather occurring in autumn, especially in October and November.”

He said: “Temperatures are going to rise gradually, peaking probably on Wednesday in eastern areas, and we might well see in some spots 20°C, and 22°C is not out of the question, probably in eastern England – so East Anglia down towards the South East.

“But it will be much milder compared to now for everyone.

“It’s possible we could exceed 20°C in London, but the peak temperatures might well be up towards the Home Counties and up to Cambridgeshire.

“There’s going to be a stark contrast in temperatures between today and Wednesday.

“Some places will be 10°C warmer because today is a very chilly day for early October, so the main theme for this week is that it’s turning much milder for all.”

He added: “It’s not going to be an Indian summer – an Indian summer is a period of fine, settled weather with widely high temperatures after a period of frosts.

“We have had some frost but it’s only going to be a day or two that we see these high temperatures.”

On Monday morning, conditions differed considerably between the north and the south. In the south, it was damp with rain clearing east, and very mild on the south coast, while in many northern areas it was cold and crisp with some frost and sunshine.

Tonight is expected to be mostly dry with some clear spells, especially in the north, where a patchy frost is likely. Areas of low cloud are forecast further south and west, giving patchy drizzle. It will be mild under the cloud, the Met Office said.

Tuesday is set to be mainly dry but fairly cloudy, with northern Scotland expected to see the best of the sunshine. Patchy drizzle is forecast under areas of thicker cloud and there will be some heavier rain in the west and southwest.

In the West and Wales, it could become quite wet by midweek.
topics: UK Weather, Weather Forecasts

title: Putin and perfume that could have killed thousands: Five Novichok inquiry findings
body:
Dawn Sturgess died in Salisbury after being exposed to the nerve agent that had poisoned former spy Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia months earlier

An innocent British woman may have been “caught in the crossfire” of an international assassination attempt, a public inquiry into the Salisbury poisonings has heard.

Dawn Sturgess was fatally poisoned in Amesbury, Wiltshire by the Russian nerve agent Novichok which had been hidden inside a designer perfume bottle.

Her death, in July 2018, followed the attempted murder of former spy Sergei Skripal, his daughter Yulia and police officer Nick Bailey, who were poisoned in nearby Salisbury in March of the same year.

Ms Sturgess, a 44-year-old mother of three, died after administering the chemical weapon to her skin from the discarded perfume bottle.

The inquiry into her death, which started at the Guildhall in Salisbury on Monday, was told that there was “enough poison to kill thousands of people” inside the bottle.

Counsel for the Government told the inquiry it believes Ms Sturgess was the “innocent and unintended victim of a cruel, deliberate and reckless attack on Sergei Skripal”.

Here are five key details from the first day of the inquiry.

Dawn Sturgess died after she applied poison to her own skin believing it was perfume, after she was gifted a bottle unwittingly by her boyfriend Charlie Rowley.

Mr Rowley also fell ill after being inadvertently poisoned as he affixed the applicator to the perfume bottle before giving it to Ms Sturgess. He was admitted to hospital but recovered, although he suffers from long term health problems including issues with his vision and memory, the inquiry heard.

While Ms Sturgess was the only fatality, concerns about the wider risk to the public have been raised, especially given the significant quantity of the nerve agent in the bottle and its presence in a public place.

The perfume bottle contained “enough poison to kill thousands of people“, the inquiry was told.

Andrew O’Connor KC, counsel to the inquiry, said: “A particularly shocking feature of Dawn’s death is that she unwittingly applied the poison to her own skin.

“She was entirely unaware of the mortal danger she faced, because the highly toxic liquid had been concealed – carefully and deliberately concealed – inside a perfume bottle.

“Moreover, the evidence will suggest that this bottle – which we shall hear contained enough poison to kill thousands of people – must earlier have been left somewhere in public place creating the obvious risk that someone would find it and take it home.

“You may conclude, sir, that those who discarded the bottle in this way acted with a grotesque disregard for human life.”

Sergei and Yulia Skripal will not give live evidence to the inquiry, due to concerns for their safety, but statements from the pair will be considered.

In one statement from Mr Skripal shown to the inquiry on Monday, he alleged that Vladimir Putin was responsible for the poisonings.

“It’s my private opinion,” a police interview transcript showed that Skripal said.

The UK Government believes the attack was undertaken by agents of the Russian state, specifically by members of the Russian intelligence unit the GRU.

It is also the Government’s view that the operation was authorised by Putin.

In a witness statement provided to the inquiry, Jonathan Allen, a senior FCDO official, said it is the Government’s view that Mr Putin “authorised the operation”.

Mr Straw added: “He should look Dawn’s family in the eyes and answer the evidence against him.”

The family of Ms Sturgess also believe Mr Putin was behind the poisoning and have requested for him to be invited to give evidence.

Mr Skripal was formerly a high-ranking military intelligence officer at the GRU and was “an important asset, with high-level knowledge and intelligence” before he came to the UK, making him a “clear and obvious target of an attack from Mr Putin and his henchmen”, Mr Mansfield KC said.

Russia has denied any involvement in the poisonings and referred to the inquiry as a “circus”.

Ms Sturgess’s family have accepted that her poisoning was unsurvivable and that differences in the emergency response would not have saved her life, their lawyer Michael Mansfield KC told the inquiry.

However, among the key questions Ms Sturgess’s family seek answers to is why her treatment differed to others poisoned by Novichok. They also want to identify any deficiencies in her care.

The three individuals poisoned in March 2018, as well as Ms Sturgess’s partner Mr Rowley survived.

Apparently acting on evidence from police, doctors initially theorised Ms Sturgess’s symptoms were caused by a drug overdose, the inquiry heard.

Her family would like to know whether this theory was dismissed early enough and if lessons learned from the Skripals’ poisoning were acted on in regards to her treatment.

Wiltshire Police has apologised to the Sturgess family for wrongly identifying her condition as an overdose on the basis she was a “well known drug addict”, the inquiry was told.

Michael Mansfield KC, counsel on behalf of the family of Ms Sturgess and Mr Rowley, told the inquiry the information was false and “there was no intelligence that Dawn was a drug user”.

Earlier the inquiry was told Ms Sturgess had suffered with long-term alcohol dependence but was “settled and happy” in the months leading up to her death.

Mr Skripal was born in Russia and served as a paratrooper, and later as a member of the GRU – Russian Military Intelligence – the inquiry heard.

He was convicted of espionage charges in Russia in 2004 after he was alleged to have spied for the UK, Mr O’Connor KC said.

He was sentenced to 13 years in prison but in 2010 was given a presidential pardon and brought to Britain on a prisoner exchange, he added.

He had lived in Salisbury since 2010.

The poisoning of Sergei Skripal was “no bolt from the blue” and the threat that he could be attacked by the Russian state on UK soil was “real, substantial and foreseeable”, Mr Mansfield KC said.

“Why did the UK authorities fail to identify the risk [Mr Skripal] faced? How was it that no protection was put in place?

“These are central questions that are pressing and reveal a shocking indifference to public safety which we’ve tried to emphasise over and above the safety of Dawn herself,” he added.

The inquiry was shown CCTV evidence of the day that Sergei and Yulia Skripal were poisoned, Sunday 4 March, 2018. It shows them park their car in Salisbury, go to a pub, and then leave.

Pictures capture them walking back through the town, and then sitting on the bench where they were later found by passersby.

An ambulance was called when the public realised they were in distress, Mr O’Connor said.
topics: Novichok, Russia, Salisbury, Salisbury Poisonings, Spying, Vladimir Putin, Wiltshire

title: The GP crisis on Britain's new-build estates
body:
The number of patients per GP has risen by over a third in some areas as residents move into new homes without supporting infrastructure

New-build homes are being built without promised GP surgeries, putting pressure on local healthcare services that could worsen under Labour’s plans to ramp up housebuilding, doctors and councils have warned.

The number of patients per GP has increased by more than a third in some parts of England since 2017, as residents move into new developments built without supporting infrastructure.

Despite pleas from residents, funding for healthcare services from developers is not being spent, according to data shared exclusively with i.

At least 17 councils had more than £1m in unused healthcare funds secured via the planning system in 2023, data obtained via Freedom of Information requests shows.

Keir Starmer pledged that no new homes would be built without the infrastructure to match them – but councils told i they already have higher housebuilding targets to meet, even though changes to the planning system to match this have not yet been made.

The Government has pledged to build 1.5 million new homes within five years. It rejected claims that this ambitious target risks exacerbating the country’s GP crisis, arguing it has been clear with developers that new homes must be built alongside infrastructure – including surgeries.

South Tyneside in Tyne and Wear has had the biggest jump in patients per GP since 2017, from 1,642 to 2,408 – a 47 per cent surge, according to i analysis of NHS and House of Commons Library data.

Some 1,850 homes have been built there during the same period, official data show.

Residents recently blocked controversial plans for 1,200 homes on green belt land south of Fellgate in Tyne and Wear but told i they were worried about more housebuilding to come under Labour.

Stoke-on-Trent in Staffordshire had a 35 per cent rise in the number of patients per fully qualified GP, while Greater Preston in Lancashire had a rise of 34 per cent.

In Stoke-on-Trent, 3,060 new homes were built since 2017, while in Preston the figure was 5,250.

Portsmouth and Leicester have had some of the biggest increases in patients per GP since 2017 and now have the largest number at 3,040 and 2,919 respectively.

Professor Kamila Hawthorne, chair of the Royal College of GPs, raised concerns that the need for more GPs was not being considered carefully enough by the new Government in its housebuilding plans.

“As communities expand, it is essential that local services expand as well, and that includes increasing the size and numbers of GP practices,” she said.

“It’s vital that any new development is built in line with sufficient primary care infrastructure planning, so that patients can receive their care locally.

“It is therefore worrying that the Government’s planned changes to regulations specifically encourage planners to think about hospitals but not primary care or general practice.”

Dr David Wrigley, deputy chair of the British Medical Association’s GP committee in England, said developers have obligations to fund infrastructure and make money available to expand health services but “we know that this does not always translate into new capacity – whether that’s a new GP practice or extending an existing one”.

He said: “We know from our members that GPs often struggle to tap into these funding pots.

“There are various potential reasons for this, whether that’s developers not providing the funding in the first place, or integrated care boards (ICBs) and councils not engaging properly to ensure local needs are met.

“It’s also a problem that a one-off capital investment only goes so far – without considering the ongoing costs of running a practice, at both ICB and practice level.

“Separately, even if a developer funds an entirely new practice building, GPs are needed to take on a partnership, with all of the responsibility and financial liability that this entails, and more GPs and other staff need to be attracted to the area and recruited.”

He said issues with recruitment can be more common in rural areas of those with higher levels of deprivation, which makes existing health inequalities worse.

Helen Morgan, the Liberal Democrats’ health spokesperson, said frontline health services “are failing because of years of Conservative neglect” and called for 8,000 new GPs.

She said: “As we build the homes we desperately need we must ensure that people can see their GP. We want community-led development with the infrastructure to back it up at the heart of it.”

Megan Hinch, policy and practice officer at the Chartered Institute of Housing, said achieving Labour’s housing targets will “need some investment alongside the infrastructure reforms being put out”.

Richard Wright, planning spokesperson for the District Councils’ Network, said developers sometimes promise a GP surgery when they apply for planning permission but fail to deliver it once the homes are actually built.

As part of the planning process councils negotiate with developers to get contributions towards infrastructure and affordable housing.

There are formulas to help determine these contributions, and developers typically expect a profit margin of 20 per cent to proceed with a project, according to the Home Builders Federation.

Mr Wright, who is also the Conservative leader of North Kesteven District Council, said developers often renegotiate this after getting planning permission, saying their infrastructure or affordable housing commitments are no longer “financially viable” – meaning they cannot afford it because their costs were higher than expected.

One of the reasons costs go up for developers is that the land they intend to use for the project shoots up in value once planning permission is granted, meaning they have to pay landowners more.

Mr Wright urged the Government to change this so the increase in land value is shared with local authorities.

“The landowner walks away with the entire profit, whilst everybody else is scrambling around for health provision and such forth,” he said.

The previous Conservative government enhanced the powers of councils to use Compulsory Purchase Orders (CPOs) to buy land without the owner’s consent. Councils can ask the Housing Secretary to approve a payment that does not factor in planning permission-related increases, but Labour has pledged to further reform these powers to make them easier for councils to use.

However, Mr Wright said this is unlikely to be a practical solution for councils.

“That has to be the last resort because you haven’t been able to negotiate it,” he said. “You’ve got all your costs – your legal costs, you’re going to be in an argument and there’s going to be, obviously, bad blood between you and the owner.

“If that’s not a big developer, if that’s more of a local landowner then you could be creating issues in your community as well when you need them on side for whatever it is you’re planning to build.”

In other cases, he said it is the NHS that does not want a new GP surgery, which means it does not appear in the plans for new developments at all.

Mr Wright said the NHS typically requests funding from developers in proportion to the number of new homes built, but “that doesn’t mean that GP services are actually delivered in the new communities”.

“In this part of Lincolnshire – they call it the hub-and-spoke model – they’re trying to set up multi-purpose centres that provide services,” he said. “But of course, that doesn’t put GPs right into the centre of the new communities. So that’s often the cause of the lack of GPs.

“People forget as well that GPs are private practices – they’re a business. Unfortunately, we often get residents saying, ‘Well, if you build a surgery, you’ll get GPs.’ Unfortunately, it’s not Field of Dreams. It’s not, ‘If we build it, they will come.’ It’s got to be a viable business for them. The GP surgery has really declined in the community as a business model for both GPs and for the NHS.”

He said these bigger multi-purpose centres can often mean residents having to travel further to see a GP, even if the public transport services do not exist to help them get there without a car.

Mr Wright raised concerns that communities could be left with even more new homes without accompanying infrastructure under Labour’s plans to scale up housebuilding, saying: “It’s a developer’s dream.”

Councils have already been given higher housing targets to meet but changes to the planning system are still being consulted on.

Mr Wright said it is best to build new homes where infrastructure already exists and can be improved rather than creating it from scratch, but said: “At the moment, you’re seeing developers that would rather go into a more rural area, where they’ve got the handles on the land, and build 200 to 400 new houses that don’t attract the huge infrastructure bill that it should.

“They walk away with almost a tokenistic contribution to the infrastructure, walk away with the profit on the homes, and we’ve now extended the size of a village beyond the size it can cope, infrastructure-wise.”

In the new town of Wixams, south of Bedford, about 3,000 homes have been built since 2007 but the planned GP surgery is still missing. Another 1,500 homes are in the pipeline.

More than half of 10,000 residents are forced to make a 14-mile round trip to GPs in Ampthill, according to councillors.

For those who do not drive, it is even harder to get to a GP because public transport links are not available.

Health services for the area are overseen by the NHS Bedfordshire, Luton and Milton Keynes ICB, which now has one of the highest patient-to-GP ratios in England.

Saqhib Ali, 54, moved into his new build home in Wixams in 2011 and said residents are struggling to get GP appointments at surgeries in other areas.

He’s been told that a man died of cancer in the town after being unable to access a GP, who may have been able to detect it early.

Another woman said she travelled seven hours on public transport to see a GP eight miles away because it is difficult to reach a surgery without a car.

Mr Ali, an accountant and entrepreneur who travels to Bedford to see a GP, told i: “It’s shocking. We’re now about 3,000 homes, so if you do the math of 3,000 homes with an average price of £400,000, you can work out how much has been spent in this community, but basic facilities like a health centre have not been considered. We have a vet but we don’t have a GP.”

Graeme Coombes, a Conservative councillor at Bedford Borough Council who represents Wixams, told i: “The houses were built and all the infrastructure has been delayed, not materialised or been scaled back. If you look at the original copy of the Wixams masterplan, it’s completely different to what you’ve got now.”

Blake Stephenson, Conservative MP for Mid Bedfordshire, said the NHS ICB has been “slow” to deliver the surgery. Two councils put in £19m of their own budgets to help pay for GPs, and developers have paid more than £5m.

He told i a lot of infrastructure “needs to come before, or at least alongside housing”, adding: “There’s a big job for the Government to do to make sure Wixams doesn’t happen elsewhere.”

A spokesperson for the ICB said “£4.2m capital funding is required to deliver a surgery in the town, but funding on this scale is currently not available” to it.

They said: “We are working with local partners to identify solutions and the local authority has secured some Section 106 funding in principle for extensions to the Wixams developments; however, this is not expected to become available for several years and is dependent on the pace of housebuilding.”

Steve Turner, executive director at the Home Builders Federation, said local authorities already have millions of pounds from developers for healthcare services that they are not using.

He acknowledged there are circumstances where commitments to deliver infrastructure are not fulfilled by developers, but said “in a lot of cases” they do make contributions that then sit in bank accounts.

He told i: “That’s a frustration for us because we pay this as part of the development costs. You want that to be then spent to benefit both existing residents in that area and the new residents on the development.

“If the local authorities have sat on it for years, clearly it’s not doing what it was intended and the system’s not working in that regard.”

At least 17 local authorities in England had more than £1m in unspent healthcare contributions last year, according to data from the Home Builders Federation shared with i.

Greenwich Council in London had the biggest amount, at £4.4m, followed by Rushcliffe Council in Nottinghamshire (£2.9m) and Lewisham Council, also in southeast London (£2.1m), the data obtained under freedom of information laws shows.

South-east London is among the top 20 areas with the biggest rise in patients per GP since 2017, and is in the top 20 areas with the worst ratio currently.

Seven London councils were in the top 20 for having the most unspent healthcare funds from developers, including Islington, Kensington and Chelsea, and Lambeth.

Kensington and Chelsea’s health services are covered by the North West London ICB, which has had a 33 per cent rise in patients per GP since 2017. It is eighth among areas with the worst patient-to-GP ratio.

Some 171 councils in England and Wales – about half – who responded to the requests for information said they held a total £46m in unspent funds for healthcare services.

Councils holding on to these large sums said it was up to the NHS to decide when to use them.

When new developments were proposed in Silver End and Cressing, which is run by Braintree District Council, the NHS told developers it needed money to improve the local GP surgery.

James Abbott, a Green Party councillor who represents the area, said there are now more than 1,000 new homes that have been built over the next year – but the money has just been “accumulating for years” instead of being used.

The council had £1.76m in unspent healthcare contributions from developers last year – the fifth-largest sum among 177 local authorities who responded to the Home Builders Federation’s freedom of information requests.

“We’re caught in this limbo, as is well known locally, and we raise this on a regular basis at every meeting where we get an opportunity,” he told i. “All of these developments are just housing estates. None of them include a school or a preschool or a GP surgery or a shop or a community hall, and that’s the failure of the planning system.”

He said: “Most, if not all of the GPs are locums. There’s been complaints about how you get hold of appointments.”

Mr Abbott said the council, which owns the GP surgery building, has been told the NHS needs to authorise the expansion of the practice.

He said councillors are “very frustrated”, adding: “The community don’t feel they’re getting the services upgrade they should get with all this new housing. The councillors don’t feel they have any ability to move it forward. The people who should be making the decisions just sit on the money for years.”

He said the council’s housing targets have shot up since Labour came to power.

“What this Government – amazingly, for a Labour government – seems to be doing is putting even more power in the hands of these big-volume developers who are already the ones who are building the estates without the services,” he said. “It could get worse before it gets better.”

A spokesperson for NHS Mid and South Essex ICB said: “We are working closely with the local authority to support access to healthcare services for existing and new residents.”

A Government spokesperson said: “We don’t recognise these claims, we have been clear we expect new homes to come with infrastructure, including GP surgeries. Under our plans developers will also be expected to contribute more to help build these vital services alongside housing.

“More widely, we have already begun hiring an extra 1,000 GPs into the NHS and put an extra £311m funding into GP practices.”
